findings.description: The admin/root pattern `/\b(?:admin|root)\b\s*[:=]\s*["']([^"']+)["']/gi` only validates the captured value with isPlausibleCredentialValue, which rejects values with spaces or values in a small denylist of single words ("admin", "true", etc.) — but a descriptive label like "Administrator" or "FullAccess" has no space and isn't in the denylist, so it passes as a "plausible credential" even though it's a role display name, not a secret. Verified directly: matching `{ admin: "Administrator", root: "FullAccess" }` against the pattern and isPlausibleCredentialValue produces two hits, both `plausible: true`. Trigger: A JS object literal defining role display labels for an admin dashboard / RBAC UI, e.g. `const ROLE_LABELS = { admin: "Administrator", root: "FullAccess", editor: "Editor" };` — an extremely common pattern in CMS/SaaS admin panels, self-hosted dashboards, and forum software that show human-readable role names.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same 'sibling-key chain suggests a denylist/label-map, not a real credential' heuristic already used in vibe-code.ts's vibe-placeholder-auth (chainCount >= 3 comparisons nearby suppresses the finding): count nearby `\w+\s*[:=]\s*["'][^"']+["']` occurrences within ~150 chars of the match and skip the finding when 3+ sibling key:value pairs are present in the same object literal, since a real hardcoded admin/root credential does not typically appear as one of several role-label entries.

findings.title: sql-injection-patterns: sql-injection-patterns (critical severity) fires on a static SQL string literal inside a script tag, with no concatenation/user-input requirement
findings.description: The check only requires the SQL-shaped regex to match somewhere inside `<script>...</script>` (and not inside `<code>/<pre>`); it never checks whether the query is built via concatenation with a variable — unlike the more precise code-sqli-raw-query-string and code-sqli-template-literal-query checks a few hundred lines later in this same file, which correctly require `+`/`${}` interpolation with req/request/params/query/body. A single hardcoded SQL string constant used as sample/demo text inside an inline script satisfies this check. Verified: `<script>const sample = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = 1"; ...</script>` matches the pattern and is correctly identified as being inside a `<script>` context (not inside `<code>/<pre>`), so it fires. Trigger: A client-side SQL playground, query-builder tool, or interactive SQL tutorial page (e.g. an in-browser SQL learning tool, or an admin dashboard's "saved query" preview feature) that stores a sample query string like `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = 1"` as a JS string constant for display purposes.
findings.recommendation: Require the same concatenation/interpolation signal the sibling code-sqli-* checks already use: after a match, verify the matched text is immediately preceded/followed by `+` or `${` and a request-derived identifier (req/request/params/query/body), or at minimum verify the matched SQL text is NOT fully enclosed in a single string literal (i.e. skip when the match is bounded by the same quote character on both sides with no `+`/`${}` inside it).

findings.title: cache-control-public-sensitive: Any POST-method form (not just password/sensitive forms) triggers a HIGH-severity finding
findings.description: The check fires whenever Cache-Control includes 'public' AND the body has EITHER a password input OR any <form method=post ...> at all (`if (!hasForm && !hasPasswd) return null;`). hasForm matches any POST form regardless of what it does, so a completely public, non-sensitive page (contact form, newsletter signup, comment form, search-by-POST) served with a normal CDN cache policy gets flagged at HIGH severity as if it were leaking authenticated content. Trigger: A SaaS marketing homepage (not under /login,/signin,/signup,/register) with `<form method="post" action="/newsletter-signup"><input name="email"></form>`, served with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` by its CDN -- a completely standard, correct caching setup for a static marketing page.
findings.recommendation: Drop the generic hasForm branch; only fire when hasPasswd is true, or narrow hasForm to forms that also contain a sensitive input (password, or name/id matching /card|ssn|cvv|account.?number/i). i.e. change `if (!hasForm && !hasPasswd) return null;` to require an actual sensitive field, not just any POST form.

findings.title: stripe-key-exposed: Stripe publishable key (pk_live_/pk_test_) reported as a 'high' severity secret leak
findings.description: The detector has two branches: an sk_ (secret key) match and a pk_ (publishable key) match. Both return a non-null string, so both are reported as a finding under the same checks-data entry, which is fixed at severity 'high' with CWE-798/'Live Stripe keys can process real payments' framing. Stripe's own integration docs require pk_live_/pk_test_ to be embedded directly in client-side HTML/JS (Stripe.js, Checkout, Elements) -- this is the intended, documented, unavoidable pattern for every Stripe integration, not a leak. The detector's own codeExamples/fixSteps text even says 'pk_live_* (publishable keys) are intentionally public and safe in browsers,' directly contradicting the severity the same check assigns when a pk_ key is the only thing found. Trigger: Any site using Stripe Checkout/Elements, e.g. a page containing `<script>Stripe('pk_live_51H8x...').elements()</script>` (the standard, required Stripe.js initialization snippet) -- this alone fires 'Stripe Key Exposed' at severity high.
findings.recommendation: Return null for the pk_ branch (publishable keys are public by design, same treatment already given to Google Analytics tracking IDs and reCAPTCHA site keys elsewhere in this codebase), or split it into a separate low/info-severity check id (mirroring how twilio-credentials-exposed was already given its own 'low' severity entry with explanatory language for the non-secret Account SID case) so a bare publishable-key match never shares the sk_ branch's high-severity, CWE-798 finding.

findings.title: sql-error-exposure: PostgreSQL pattern lacks the 'ERROR:' colon requirement its sibling check was fixed to require
findings.description: The pattern `/PostgreSQL.*ERROR/i` matches any single line containing the word 'PostgreSQL' followed anywhere later by the word 'error' (case-insensitive, unbounded `.*`). The near-identical detector `sql-error-in-page` in content.ts was already hardened for exactly this false-positive class with an inline comment: 'Require "ERROR:" colon to match actual PG error format, not descriptive text like "PostgreSQL errors"' -- but that fix was never applied to this file's separate, independently-registered 'sql-error-exposure' check (category information-disclosure, severity high), which still uses the old unbounded pattern. Trigger: Any developer blog, changelog, or README rendered as HTML containing a sentence like 'We migrated our backend from MySQL to PostgreSQL. Error handling for failed queries is now centralized in a single wrapper.' -- 'PostgreSQL' and 'error' appear on the same line with no actual database error present, firing a 'high' severity 'SQL error message in response' finding.
findings.recommendation: Change the pattern to `/PostgreSQL.*?ERROR:/i` (require the literal colon after ERROR, matching real Postgres error-message format), identical to the fix already applied to `sql-error-in-page` in content.ts.

findings.title: api-key-hardcoded-in-js: No placeholder/known-test-key denylist -- flags Stripe's own publicly documented example secret key
findings.description: Lines 196-211: unlike the credit-card-pattern check (fixed earlier this session with a KNOWN_TEST_CARD_NUMBERS denylist) and hardcoded-credentials/insecure-auth (fixed with CREDENTIAL_VALUE_PLACEHOLDERS), this check has no placeholder/known-test-value guard at all. Stripe's own official API documentation uses the example secret test key `sk_test_4eC39HqLyjWDarjtT1zdp7dc` throughout its docs (confirmed via web search: this exact string appears across docs.stripe.com samples and is reproduced verbatim in thousands of third-party tutorials, gists, and Stripe CLI examples -- e.g. github.com/stripe/stripe-cli issue #1553 literally pastes it). The second regex pattern `/(?:openai|anthropic|stripe|sendgrid|twilio)\s*(?:api.?key|secret)\s*[:=]\s*["'](?!pk_)[A-Za-z0-9\-_]{20,}["']/i` matches this key whenever it's assigned to a camelCase identifier like `stripeApiKey`/`stripeSecretKey`/`stripeSecret` (a very common naming convention in beginner Stripe-integration tutorials and CodePen/demo pages that -- as bad practice -- put the test secret key in client JS): the value `sk_test_4eC39HqLyjWDarjtT1zdp7dc` is 32 chars of `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, doesn't start with `pk_`, and satisfies every condition, so it's flagged as 'treat as compromised' when it's actually Stripe's own inert, publicly-known example key. Trigger: const stripeApiKey = "sk_test_4eC39HqLyjWDarjtT1zdp7dc"; // copied verbatim from Stripe's own docs example
findings.recommendation: Add a placeholder/known-test-key guard mirroring the KNOWN_TEST_CARD_NUMBERS precedent already established in secrets-extended.ts: capture the matched value in both regexes, then skip if it equals a small KNOWN_TEST_API_KEYS denylist (at minimum Stripe's `sk_test_4eC39HqLyjWDarjtT1zdp7dc`), and/or skip values that are a repeated character run or match /^(?:x+|0+|test|example|sample|dummy|placeholder|your[_-]?api[_-]?key)/i, matching the isPlausibleCredentialValue() pattern already used in code.ts.

findings.title: webhook-ssrf-request-input-no-validation: Regex conflates server-side req/body/params/query objects with identically-named client-side variables, flagging ordinary browser OAuth/redirect JS as server-side SSRF
findings.description: The detector's assignRe pattern `(?:webhook|callback)[a-zA-Z_]*\s*[:=]\s*(?:await\s+)?(?:req(?:uest)?|body|params|query)\??\.[\w'"[\].]{1,80}` treats a bare identifier named `body`, `params`, or `query` as proof of an Express/Koa/Fastify request object, but those exact names are extremely common in *client-side* browser JavaScript that has nothing to do with server-side SSRF: `const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)` (a standard way to read OAuth/SSO callback/redirect params on a landing page) or React Router's `useParams()` hook both produce a local variable literally named `params`/`query`. Any page whose readable (non-minified) inline `<script>` does something like `const callbackUrl = params.get('callback_url'); fetch(callbackUrl)` -- a completely normal client-side OAuth callback/redirect handler -- matches this pattern and produces no nearby validation keyword to suppress it, so it fires the medium-severity 'Webhook URL From Request Passed to Outbound Call Unvalidated' (SSRF) finding on code that runs in the visitor's own browser, not on the server, and therefore cannot be SSRF at all. Trigger: Any server-rendered page (WordPress/Shopify/small business sites frequently ship unminified inline JS) containing: `<script>const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search); const callbackUrl = params.get("callback_url"); fetch(callbackUrl).then(r => r.json());</script>` -- verified against the actual regex in this file: it matches `callbackUrl = params.get`, finds `fetch(` within the 500-char lookahead, and finds none of the exclusion keywords (private/internal/loopback/etc.) nearby, so it fires.
findings.recommendation: Require the request-object source to be `req.` or `request.` immediately followed by `.body`/`.params`/`.query` rather than accepting those three names bare. Change the alternation from `(?:req(?:uest)?|body|params|query)\??\.` to `(?:req(?:uest)?)\??\.(?:body|params|query)\??\.` so the regex only matches the canonical Express/Koa/Fastify shape (`req.body.X`, `request.query.X`) shown in this very check's own 'Bad' code example, and no longer matches bare `body.X`/`params.X`/`query.X` that are equally common as client-side `URLSearchParams`/`useParams()` variable names.

findings.title: open-redirect-location-confirmed: Fires 'confirmed open redirect' on legitimate link-safety rewriting services (e.g. Microsoft Defender Safe Links) whose entire purpose is redirecting to an external host after a security check
findings.description: `REDIRECT_PARAM_NAMES` includes `url`, and the check fires whenever a query param with that exact name holds an absolute external URL and the response's Location header sends the browser to that same external host, treated as 'confirmed, not a static text guess.' Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links -- extremely common in corporate email -- rewrites every link to `https://<region>.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=<percent-encoded target>&data=...` and, when visited, legitimately issues a 302 to that exact `url=` value after a reputation check. Since `safelinks.protection.outlook.com` and the target domain are unrelated organizations, `extractRootDomain` won't suppress it, so scanning any Safe-Links-wrapped URL produces a high-severity 'Confirmed Open Redirect via Location Header' finding against a security vendor's own protective redirector, not against a vulnerability in the scanned application. Trigger: Scanning `https://nam02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.example.com%2Fpage&data=...` -- verified end to end against this file's actual logic: `reqUrl.hostname` (safelinks.protection.outlook.com) differs from `locUrl.hostname` (www.example.com), the `url` param name is in `REDIRECT_PARAM_NAMES`, its decoded value is an absolute external URL, and it matches the Location header's host exactly, so the check returns a confirmed-finding string.
findings.recommendation: Add a short skip-list of known link-safety/URL-rewriting vendor hostnames (e.g. `/\.safelinks\.protection\.outlook\.com$/i`, `/^urldefense\.proofpoint\.com$/i`, `/\.secure-web\.cisco\.com$/i`, `/\.clicktime\.symantec\.com$/i`, `/\.linkprotect\.cudasvc\.com$/i`, `/\.mimecastprotect\.com$/i`) and return null immediately when `reqUrl.hostname` matches one of them, before doing the param/Location comparison. Apply the same skip-list check to the sibling `open-redirect-meta-refresh-confirmed` detector, which shares the identical `REDIRECT_PARAM_NAMES`-based matching and the same exposure.

findings.title: RATE_LIMITS split-brain lets 11 routes bypass admin-configured rate limits
findings.description: Two exports named RATE_LIMITS exist: lib/config/constants.ts (static shipped defaults, no resolver awareness) and lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit.ts (resolver-aware, tags each entry with a 'limit' name so checkRateLimit() looks up the live admin override). checkRateLimit() only queries the DB-backed override when config.limit is truthy, so any route importing RATE_LIMITS from constants.ts instead of rate-limit.ts silently always enforces the hardcoded default, ignoring whatever the admin panel says. Confirmed live in app/api/v3/scan/verify/route.ts and 10 other routes: account/delete, admin (adminReauth), ai/chat, auth/2fa/backup-codes, auth/2fa/disable, auth/2fa/email-setup, auth/2fa/setup, history/[id]/summary, scan/verify-batch, teams/members. rate-limit.ts even has an explicit doc comment warning against the constants.ts version.
findings.recommendation: Repoint all 11 imports to @/lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit; rename the constants.ts export (e.g. RATE_LIMIT_DEFAULTS) so the name collision can't recur.

findings.title: Boot-time schema catch-up in instrumentation.ts is the only thing that closes the migration-01 gap for an existing prod DB, and one failed statement silently aborts everything after it
findings.description: instrumentation.ts's entire ~1700-line schema-creation/seed/cleanup-scheduling/sequence-repair sequence is wrapped in exactly one outer try/catch that only console.error's on failure and never calls process.exit -- the app continues booting and serving production traffic regardless. Most v3-era CREATE TABLE/ALTER TABLE calls are bare awaits with no individual try/catch, unlike the FK self-heal blocks and a handful of blocks that ARE wrapped in .catch(). Since this boot sequence is the ONLY mechanism that actually creates the tables/columns missing from the versioned migration, a single unexpected failure partway through it silently abandons every later table, every later column, badge seeding, periodic cleanup scheduling, and the sequence-repair safety net, with no forced restart and no alert beyond one buried log line.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each independent v3-era schema block in its own try/catch, matching the pattern already used for the FK self-heal blocks; consider having the top-level catch call process.exit(1) instead of only logging, so a broken schema never silently serves production traffic.

findings.title: Regression-alert diff only compares finding IDs, never severity, so a same-URL finding that escalates to critical/high is silently treated as already-known and never emailed
findings.description: checkForNewCriticalOrHighFindings diffs the current scan against the prior scan of the same URL purely by Vulnerability.id via diffFindingsByKey. id = <checkId>--<fnvHash32(url)> has no severity component. Several checks compute severity dynamically per run, e.g. page-cookie-missing-secure: severity is high if a session-like cookie lacks Secure, medium otherwise. If a site adds a session cookie without Secure on a later scan (severity medium to high), the finding id is byte-identical to the prior scan's, so the diff buckets it as unchanged/outstanding rather than added, and hasNewCriticalOrHigh stays false -- the alert email never fires even though a genuinely new high-severity issue just appeared. 100% reproducible, no attacker required, defeats the feature's stated purpose.
findings.recommendation: Track previous findings as an id-to-severity map, not just a Set of ids, and add an escalated bucket: same id present in both scans but previous severity was not critical/high and current severity is -- include these in newFindings/hasNewCriticalOrHigh alongside genuinely added findings.

findings.title: content.json metadata copy-paste drift: 4 checks show completely wrong title/description/evidence
findings.description: form-action-tel-scheme, sourcemap-reference, discord-webhook-exposed, and exposed-session-id in content.json each had title/description/evidence/riskImpact/fixSteps text belonging to a DIFFERENT check (e.g. form-action-tel-scheme's JSON said 'Forms Submitting to External Domains' while its detector actually checks for tel: scheme form actions; sourcemap-reference's JSON was entirely about cookie max-age; discord-webhook-exposed's JSON was entirely about WordPress admin paths; exposed-session-id's JSON was about missing cookie flags while the detector actually checks for a session ID in the URL). Real scan findings showed users a title/description unrelated to the actual evidence.
findings.recommendation: Rewrote all 4 JSON entries' title/description/evidence/riskImpact/explanation/fixSteps/codeExamples to match what their detector functions actually check; corrected severities (tel-scheme medium->low, discord-webhook low->medium) and the 'type' field (sourcemap-reference/exposed-session-id combined|header-value -> body-pattern, fixing an inflated engine-confidence score for a body-regex check).

findings.title: service-worker-scope always fires at high severity on ordinary PWA service worker registration
findings.description: The detector regex captured only the URL string argument of navigator.serviceWorker.register(...), never the options object, so it could never see an explicit scope option -- meaning the 'broad scope' condition was true for virtually every register() call including ones that DO narrow scope. Combined with a JSON title/description claiming 'Registered Over Insecure HTTP' (unrelated to what the code checks) at severity high, this fired at high severity on the single most common, expected PWA pattern (navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')) -- the same class of bug as the Walmart incident (standard pattern flagged as if dangerous).
findings.recommendation: Fixed the regex to capture the full register(...) call so a real scope option is actually visible; corrected the JSON title/description/evidence to describe broad-scope detection instead of HTTP insecurity; downgraded severity high -> low since broad scope is the expected default for most PWAs, not itself exploitable.

findings.title: hardcoded-secrets check flat-critical across ~30 secret patterns, double-counts Google keys
findings.description: Walmart scan: Google API keys matched by generic hardcoded-secrets (severity critical) pushed the whole scan to unsafe/10, despite two dedicated checks (google-api-key-exposed, secret-google-maps-api-key) already correctly rating the same evidence as medium. Client-exposed-by-design keys (Google/Firebase) should not carry the same severity as server-only secrets (AWS/Stripe/DB URIs).
findings.recommendation: Split hardcoded-secrets into 4 severity-tiered check ids (hardcoded-secrets critical / hardcoded-secrets-high-risk high / hardcoded-secrets-client-exposed medium / hardcoded-secrets-low-risk low) in lib/scanner/checks/code.ts + checks-data/code.json. Removed the Google API Key (AIzaSy*) pattern entirely -- google-api-key-exposed (content.json) and secret-google-maps-api-key/secret-firebase-api-key-public (secrets-extended.json) already cover that evidence at medium/low. Also fixed safety-rating.ts's dead 'Hardcoded API Keys' exploitablePatterns entry (never matched any real title) so the new tiers classify as exploitable-at-their-own-severity instead of falling into 'hardening' or being dropped -- merged with scanner-02's independent fix for the same dead pattern (broader regex, kept as-is). Shipped by agent a9eefbf8ba0b78d5c.

findings.title: Danger score / safety rating ignore AI verification verdicts entirely
findings.description: getSafetyRating/getDangerScore in lib/scanner/safety-rating.ts weight every finding by severity+title pattern only; a finding the AI already flagged possible_fp counts at full weight, defeating the verification pipeline. Confirmed on Walmart scan: several cookie findings marked possible_fp (detector cited a cookie not present in the live probe) still counted at full weight toward the unsafe/10 verdict.
findings.recommendation: Extend Finding interface with aiVerdict/aiConfidence, weight accordingly. In progress (agent adf62015a31287147).

findings.title: Cookie 'third-party' checks conflate having a Domain= attribute with being cross-site
findings.description: cookie-no-samesite-third-party, cookie-third-party-no-samesite-none-secure, and cookie-partitioned-missing all treated any cookie carrying an explicit Domain= attribute as a 'third-party'/'cross-site' cookie. An explicit Domain attribute is the standard, completely ordinary way to share a session cookie across subdomains for first-party SSO (Domain=example.com set by www.example.com so api.example.com can read it) at any company with multiple subdomains -- it cannot be determined to be cross-site from a single response at all. cookie-third-party-no-samesite-none-secure (high severity) consequently fired on ordinary Domain-scoped cookies using SameSite=Lax/Strict -- a secure, correct configuration -- and told developers to add SameSite=None instead, which is worse remediation advice, not better (it would widen CSRF exposure). cookie-no-samesite-third-party was additionally a strict-subset duplicate of cookie-third-party-no-samesite-none-secure's firing condition.
findings.recommendation: Disabled all three detectors (return null with an explanatory comment). The precise, correct version of this check already exists and doesn't depend on guessing 'third-party' from Domain=: set-cookie-samesite-none-no-secure fires only when SameSite=None is already explicitly declared but Secure is missing.

findings.title: content-disposition-inline's isBinary regex matched images/audio/video, firing 'force a download' advice on essentially every image on every site
findings.description: The 'no Content-Disposition header on binary response' branch used an isBinary regex that, in addition to genuinely downloadable types (PDF, ZIP, DOC, octet-stream, executables), also matched image/*, audio/*, and video/*. Images and video are *supposed* to render inline via /
findings.recommendation: Narrowed the isBinary check used for the 'missing header' branch to only genuinely downloadable document/archive/executable MIME types, matching what the JSON description already promised.

findings.title: x-xss-protection-block reported a finding for the correct, recommended configuration
findings.description: A second branch returned a non-null evidence string -- creating an actual finding entry -- whenever an HTML page correctly omitted the deprecated X-XSS-Protection header, with evidence text that literally read '...that's correct (deprecated); ensure CSP is the actual defense.' Omitting a deprecated, no-longer-supported header is the current best practice recommended by MDN/OWASP, not something to flag. Because this fired on every single HTML page of every site that does the right thing, it was likely one of the single largest volume contributors to inflated finding counts of any check reviewed in this sweep.
findings.recommendation: Removed the branch entirely; the detector now only fires on the genuinely bad state (X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block explicitly set), matching what the JSON title/description already described.

findings.title: secrets-extended.ts's ~51 per-provider secret-* detectors had zero placeholder filtering
findings.description: Unlike the main hardcoded-secrets detector (which filters matched values against example/your_/xxxx/0000/placeholder/test_/dummy/localhost), none of the per-provider secret-* detectors (secret-stripe-webhook-endpoint, secret-google-maps-api-key, secret-aws-secret-key, etc.) called stripExampleContent or filtered matched values at all. A .env.example served raw, or a README documenting a fake-but-correctly-shaped credential (STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_YOUR_KEY_HERE, AIzaSyXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX), would satisfy a provider's format regex and get reported as a confirmed secret, several at critical severity.
findings.recommendation: Added maskPlaceholderSecrets() (mirrors hardcoded-secrets' existing exclusion terms) plus stripExampleContent, applied via an export-time wrapper (same pattern as vibe-code.ts's stripDocBlocks wrapper) so every detector receives body with placeholder-marked tokens and doc/example HTML regions already neutralized before its format regex runs. Also fixed secret-auth0-client-secret, which fired on the bare phrase auth0_client_secret with no captured value at all, to require an assignment+value shape.

findings.title: secrets-extended.json's per-provider checks all typed 'header', overstating confidence to 93% for pure body regex
findings.description: All 51 entries in secrets-extended.json declared type 'header' even though every one of their detectors (confirmed by reading the full .ts file) only examines the response body, never headers. Per registry.ts's confidenceForType, 'header' maps to 93% confidence (near-certain) while the correct 'body-pattern' type maps to 70% -- the same mislabeling class already fixed once for a single content.json check (AUDIT-008 content-07) but present here across an entire file.
findings.recommendation: Bulk-corrected type: 'header' -> 'body-pattern' for all 51 entries in secrets-extended.json.

findings.title: ssl.ts's mixed-protocol-content had no HTTPS gate, fired 'HTTPS page loading HTTP resources' on plain HTTP pages
findings.description: detectMixedContent() matched src/href/action="http://..." anywhere in the body with no check that the scanned page itself was HTTPS. Mixed content is only a meaningful concept on an HTTPS page loading HTTP subresources -- an http:// page referencing other http:// URLs (including ordinary same-origin links) is completely normal. This fired on virtually every plain-HTTP page scanned, misreporting them as HTTPS pages with mixed content. The newer PageCheck-architecture equivalents (page-mixed-content-active/passive in page-checks/mixed-content.ts) already correctly gate on ctx.isHttps -- this older detector was the one left behind.
findings.recommendation: Added an explicit url.startsWith('https://') gate before the mixed-content regex runs.

findings.title: vibe-code category self-triggers on any page documenting its own example patterns, including this product's own /docs pages
findings.description: None of vibe-code.ts's 31 detectors scoped their regex search to actual <script> content -- they scan the full page body/text. Every detector's 'bad' example (eval(), SQL string concatenation, hardcoded password comparisons, JWT none-alg, etc.) is exactly the kind of snippet a tutorial, security blog, or API-documentation page renders as literal text inside <pre>/<code> blocks for teaching purposes. This product's own /docs/api page renders every check's codeExamples field (including the 'Bad (AI-generated)' samples) as literal HTML text, so scanning VulnRadar's own docs would self-trigger a large fraction of this entire category -- the same 'no context requirement, matches on huge blocks of unrelated/informational text' failure mode called out for this audit, just self-inflicted.
findings.recommendation: Added a new stripDocBlocks() helper (lib/scanner/_helpers.ts) that removes <code>/<pre>/<kbd>/<samp> regions but NOT <script> tags (several detectors need real script content), and wrapped every vibe-code detector to run against the stripped body.

findings.title: TOTP code replay not prevented — no totp_last_counter column
findings.description: 2FA verify accepts any valid TOTP code within its 30-second window with no replay check. The same OTP can be submitted multiple times to authenticate repeatedly. Prevention requires storing the last accepted counter value and rejecting codes at or below it.
findings.recommendation: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN totp_last_counter BIGINT; after accepting a code, UPDATE users SET totp_last_counter = <counter> WHERE id = $1; reject if counter <= totp_last_counter.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): DB migration v3.1.0 + TOTP replay + share-token hash lookup
findings.fixSummary: Migration 3.0.0-to-3.1.0.mjs adds users.totp_last_counter BIGINT. After verifyTOTP() succeeds, verify/route.ts locks the user row, compares the current 30-second step counter against totp_last_counter, rejects if used, and advances it atomically.

findings.title: GitHub Actions use mutable major version tags — supply chain risk (carry-over from AUDIT-002#ci-01)
findings.description: All GitHub Actions (actions/checkout, actions/setup-node, docker/setup-buildx-action, etc.) are pinned to floating @vN tags. A compromised upstream repository can silently replace the action code on the next CI run without any change to the workflow file.
findings.recommendation: Pin each action to a commit SHA: uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v7. Use a tool like pin-github-action or dependabot to keep SHAs current.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): BrowserBase IDOR fix, env schema, GH Actions SHA pinning
findings.fixSummary: All 11 action references across 6 workflow files pinned to commit SHAs with the mutable tag retained as a comment. SHAs fetched from GitHub API as of 2026-07-02.

findings.title: SQL INTERVAL injection via template literal in history retention query
findings.description: history/route.ts line 96 interpolated retentionDays directly: INTERVAL '${retentionDays} days'. A user whose plan lookup returned a crafted string could inject arbitrary SQL into the interval expression.
findings.recommendation: Changed to parameterized form: ($2 * INTERVAL '1 day') with Math.floor(retentionDays) as the $2 parameter.

findings.title: Share token IDOR — any team member can manage other members share tokens
findings.description: POST and DELETE /api/v3/history/[id]/share checked only that the requester and scan owner share a team (COUNT(*) > 0) with no role filter. A viewer-role team member could create or revoke share tokens on any other team member's scans.
findings.recommendation: Changed team membership query to require tm1.role IN ('owner', 'admin'). Returns 404 (not 403) to avoid leaking membership.

findings.title: Bulk scan rate limit applied once per request, not per URL
findings.description: checkApiKeyRateLimit was called once before the URL loop, consuming a single rate limit slot for up to 100 URLs. An attacker could exhaust 100x the intended scan budget per API-key slot. Additionally a second checkRateLimit call at the end of the function consumed another slot.
findings.recommendation: Moved checkApiKeyRateLimit inside the URL loop with early-exit on limit exceeded, filling remaining results with error objects. Removed the redundant end-of-function checkRateLimit call.

findings.title: Redirect-based SSRF in async scanner checks via redirect:follow
findings.description: lib/scanner/async-checks.ts FETCH_OPTS had redirect:'follow'. robots.txt and security.txt checks follow 302/301 to any destination including http://169.254.169.254/, http://10.x.x.x/, etc. A target server returning a redirect to a cloud metadata endpoint would cause the scanner to exfiltrate internal data.
findings.recommendation: Changed to redirect:'error'. fetch() throws on any redirect; the surrounding try/catch suppresses the error cleanly.

findings.title: Profile email change does not reset email_verified_at
findings.description: PATCH /api/v3/auth/update changes the email in place but leaves email_verified_at pointing at the OLD verification. The new email is implicitly trusted without proof of control.
findings.recommendation: Set email_verified_at = NULL on email change; require the user to verify the new email before they can log in.

findings.title: GH Actions pinned to mutable major tags, not SHA digests
findings.description: All actions/checkout, setup-node, setup-buildx-action, etc. use floating @vN tags. A compromised upstream republish swaps action code on the next CI run.
findings.recommendation: Replace each tag with commit SHA + comments block containing the resolved version, e.g. uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v7.0.0

findings.title: startCheckoutSession accepted userId from client (IDOR)
findings.description: The userId parameter was stamped into Stripe metadata, letting any logged-in user upgrade a victim's plan by paying.
findings.recommendation: Dropped the parameter. userId is now derived server-side from getSession().

findings.title: TOTP seed stored plaintext at rest
findings.description: users.totp_secret held the base32 TOTP seed unencrypted. DB read = full 2FA bypass.
findings.recommendation: Route through encryptApiKey/decryptApiKey (AES-256-GCM). Added idempotent backfill on startup.

findings.title: No Origin/Referer check on mutating API routes
findings.description: Cross-site POST could ride the session cookie and change the victim's email.
findings.recommendation: Middleware enforces Origin match + Sec-Fetch-Site in same-origin/same-site on every mutating /api/v3/ request. Webhooks and Discord callback are explicitly exempt (signed-payload trust boundary).

findings.title: DISABLE_CSP=1 was shipped in production env
findings.description: Operator-set env var stripped every security header (CSP, COOP, CORP, XFO, Permissions-Policy, HSTS) silently.
findings.recommendation: env validator refuses DISABLE_CSP=1 when NODE_ENV=production. Removed from .env.local.

findings.title: Docker base + compose tag both mutable
findings.description: node:22-alpine and ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar:latest are moving targets; a compromised registry push immediately ships to every self-hoster.
findings.recommendation: Pinned to node:22.11.0-alpine (self-hosters can replace with @sha256:<digest>). Compose uses :3.0.0. Added tini for PID 1 signal forwarding + HEALTHCHECK.

findings.title: API-key daily cap race: concurrent requests bypass the limit
findings.description: checkRateLimit + recordUsage were two separate statements. N concurrent requests at used=limit-1 all passed, all inserted.
findings.recommendation: Single transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on api_keys.id; recordUsage() is now a no-op kept only for back-compat.

findings.title: Discord OAuth tokens stored plaintext at rest
findings.description: discord_connections.access_token and refresh_token were plaintext. DB read = Discord account takeover via refresh token.
findings.recommendation: Encrypt via encryptApiKey; added getDiscordTokens() helper that decrypts inline; backfill migration on startup.

findings.title: Password change did not invalidate other sessions
findings.description: A stolen session cookie remained valid for the full 7-day TTL even after the legitimate user rotated their password.
findings.recommendation: Mirror reset-password: deleteAllSessions + createSession(current).

findings.title: The destructive Button renders white on hsl(0 91% 71%) at 2.75:1 in the default dark theme, so every delete and cancel confirmation is below AA
findings.description: components/ui/button.tsx:14-15 defines `destructive: "bg-destructive text-destructive-foreground"`. app/globals.css:238-239 sets the dark theme's `--destructive: 0 91% 71%` with `--destructive-foreground: 0 0% 100%`; computed contrast is 2.75:1. The light theme (:192-193, `0 84% 60%` with white) computes to 3.78:1. AA needs 4.5:1 for the button's text (h-10 text-sm, not large text) and 3:1 even as a UI component, so the dark value fails both. Dark is the default theme (app/layout.tsx:151 hardcodes className="dark", ThemeProvider defaultTheme="dark"). The same pair backs `--success: 142 70% 45%` with `--success-foreground: 0 0% 100%` (globals.css:261-262) at 2.32:1 dark and 3.35:1 light. Only `--warning` gets this right, pairing hsl(38 92% 50%) with a near-black foreground at 8.39:1 (:218-219), and the light --primary-foreground was already fixed the same way with the comment at globals.css:179-184 explaining exactly this reasoning.
findings.impact: The destructive variant is what confirms account deletion, scan deletion, team removal and subscription cancellation. Its label is the least readable text in the product for a low-vision user, on the one control where misreading it is most costly.
findings.recommendation: In app/globals.css set `--destructive-foreground` to a near-black in both blocks the way --warning-foreground already is (`0 0% 9%` gives ~8:1 on both destructive fills), or darken `--destructive` itself to about `0 72% 42%` and keep white. Apply the same treatment to --success/--success-foreground at :216-217 and :261-262.

findings.title: The AI chat textarea, the support-ticket reply box and four other user-facing inputs have only a placeholder, no accessible name
findings.description: A scan of all 144 Input/Textarea/input/textarea/select elements in app/, components/ and lib/ found these with no id + htmlFor pair, no aria-label and no wrapping <label>: components/ai-chat/chat-widget.tsx:1541 (the AI assistant's message box, mounted on every page via ChatWidget in app/layout.tsx:190); components/contact/support-tickets.tsx:609 (the reply box on a support ticket, available on every tier); components/history/history-notes.tsx:82 (scan notes); components/teams/team-detail-header.tsx:79 (rename a team); app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:406 (request-body textarea, the sibling of AUDIT-011#docs-07's :514 which cited only the param inputs); components/admin/features/support-inbox.tsx:344 (staff reply). Each has a `placeholder` only, and a placeholder is not an accessible name: it is not exposed as the field's name by the accname algorithm when it is the sole source in several screen-reader/browser pairings, and it disappears the moment the user types. This is the same defect AUDIT-011#docs-07 filed against the playground, present on the general product surface rather than in docs. app/legal/accessibility/page.tsx:88-91 publishes "Form Labels: All form inputs have associated labels for clarity."
findings.impact: A screen-reader user who tabs into the AI support widget hears "edit, blank" with no indication of what the field is for, and the same on a support-ticket reply. Voice-control users cannot say "click <field name>" because there is no name to speak. The published claim is false on the product's own support channel.
findings.recommendation: Add `aria-label` where a visible label would crowd the layout (chat-widget.tsx:1541 `aria-label="Message ${BOT_NAME}"`, support-tickets.tsx:609 and support-inbox.tsx:344 `aria-label="Reply"`, team-detail-header.tsx:79 `aria-label="Team name"`), and give history-notes.tsx:82 a real `useId()`-backed `<label htmlFor>` since it already has a visible "Notes" heading to reuse.

findings.title: The AI chat has no live region, so streamed assistant replies are never announced, and its slash-command autocomplete carries no combobox ARIA
findings.description: components/ai-chat/chat-widget.tsx contains exactly one ARIA announcement hook in 1600+ lines: `role="alert"` at :444. The message list at :1417-1419 is a plain scrolling `<div ref={scrollRef} className="h-full overflow-y-auto ...">` with no `aria-live`, no `role="log"` and no `aria-busy`, and assistant text is streamed into it token by token. The slash-command autocomplete at :1496-1528 renders a bare `<div>` of `<button>`s: the textarea has no `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` or `aria-activedescendant`, the list has no `role="listbox"`, and the items have no `role="option"` or `aria-selected`. Arrow-key movement itself is implemented (handleKeyDown at :1071-1091 handles ArrowDown/ArrowUp/Enter/Tab/Escape and tracks cmdHighlight), so the widget is operable by keyboard, it just publishes none of that state. The rest of the product does use live regions correctly, which makes this an outlier: 45 `aria-live` and 63 `role="status"` occurrences elsewhere, including components/scanner/scanning-indicator.tsx:281 and :293-297 for scan progress.
findings.impact: A screen-reader user asks the AI assistant a question and hears nothing at all: the reply streams into a silent container, so they must manually hunt back through the transcript to discover an answer arrived. Typing "/" pops a suggestion list that is never announced, and moving through it with arrows changes a highlight the user is never told about, so a blind user can select a slash command only by luck.
findings.recommendation: Add `role="log" aria-live="polite" aria-relevant="additions text"` to the scroll container at chat-widget.tsx:1419 (polite, so a stream does not interrupt continuously), and set `aria-busy={isStreaming}` on it. On the textarea at :1541 add `role="combobox" aria-expanded={cmdSuggestions.length > 0} aria-controls="chat-cmd-list" aria-activedescendant={...}`; give the list at :1497 `id="chat-cmd-list" role="listbox"` and each button `role="option" aria-selected={i === cmdHighlight}` plus a stable id.

findings.title: The post-scan AI choice modal declares aria-modal but never moves focus into itself, traps nothing, and ignores Escape
findings.description: components/scanner/ai-choice-modal.tsx:34-44 renders a fixed full-screen overlay whose panel carries `role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby={titleId}` and nothing else: no ref, no tabIndex, no focus move on mount, no Tab containment, and no Escape handler. It is rendered from app/dashboard/page.tsx:980 at the end of every scan that produced findings, and it is the gate between the scan finishing and the user seeing results (the only ways past it are the "Verify with AI" and "Skip, show the raw findings" buttons). The codebase already has the fix: lib/hooks/use-modal-a11y.ts provides role/aria-modal/aria-labelledby plus Escape, a Tab focus trap and focus save-and-restore, and eleven other hand-rolled modals use it (components/modals/tos-modal.tsx:164, components/shared/notification-center.tsx:106, components/scanner/crawl-url-selector.tsx:92, components/shared/onboarding-tour.tsx:113, components/profile/tabs/profile-billing-tab.tsx:67, components/admin/users/gift-subscription-modal.tsx:57 and five more). components/docs/docs-mobile-nav.tsx:52-61 solves the same problem inline. ai-choice-modal.tsx is the one that got neither.
findings.impact: On the main scan flow, a keyboard user's focus stays on whatever triggered the scan while a dialog that claims aria-modal="true" covers the page; they must Tab blindly forward, past the still-focusable page underneath, to find the two buttons. Escape does not dismiss it. Announcing aria-modal while leaving focus outside the dialog is worse than not declaring it, because assistive tech constrains the user to a subtree their focus is not in.
findings.recommendation: In components/scanner/ai-choice-modal.tsx, call `useModalA11y({ open: true, onClose: onViewNow })` inside Shell and spread `dialogProps` onto the panel div at :36 and `titleProps` onto each `<h2 id={titleId}>`. That is a five-line change and reuses the hook the other eleven modals already share.

findings.title: The admin panel repeats the unlabeled-input pattern from AUDIT-011#docs-07 twenty times, including a bare select
findings.description: Extends AUDIT-011#docs-07, which filed the same defect only against app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx. The identical shape (a `<label>` with no `htmlFor` sitting above an `<Input>`/`<Textarea>`/`<select>` with no `id`) recurs across the admin surface: components/admin/features/mass-email-manager.tsx:291/295, :303/307, :316/320 (a `<select>` for the recipient segment), :332/337; components/admin/features/ip-rules-manager.tsx:558/563, :602, :618; components/admin/features/engine-feedback-manager.tsx:864, :875, :903; components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:952, :991, :1413, :1428, :1490, :1724, :1780, :2187, :2196; components/admin/users/gift-subscription-modal.tsx:144 (a `datetime-local` field). Verified as genuinely unlabeled rather than implicitly wrapped: the checkboxes at engine-feedback-manager.tsx:346, :530, :915 and the cancel radios at profile-billing-tab.tsx:1572, :1603 ARE inside a `<label>` element and are fine, so the pattern was checked both ways.
findings.impact: A staff member using a screen reader hears a run of unnamed edit fields on the mass-email composer, the IP block-rule form and the user detail panel. Mass-email in particular has four unnamed controls in a row, one of which chooses who receives the blast, so an unnamed select decides whether an email goes to one person or every registered user. Admin is lower traffic than the scan flow, hence medium and not high.
findings.recommendation: Thread `useId()` through each block: `const id = useId()` then `<label htmlFor={id}>` / `id={id}` on the control. The user-facing forms already do this correctly (components/auth/login-form.tsx:121-123, components/teams/team-invite-form.tsx:88-90, components/contact/contact-form.tsx:201-208), so copy that shape.

findings.title: text-muted-foreground drops to 3.93:1 on bg-muted in light mode and 4.25:1 in dark, and the /40 through /70 opacity variants reach 1.67:1
findings.description: app/globals.css:189 sets light `--muted-foreground: 220 10% 42%` and :235 sets dark `220 8% 55%`. Computed ratios: light on --background 4.44:1 (just under the 4.5:1 AA floor), on --muted 3.93:1, on --secondary 4.13:1, on --accent 3.54:1; dark on --muted 4.25:1, on --accent 3.43:1, on --surface-3 4.32:1. `bg-muted` and `text-muted-foreground` appear together on the same element 119 times across app/ + components/. The same token is the placeholder colour for every field (components/ui/input.tsx:11 and components/ui/textarea.tsx:12 both set `placeholder:text-muted-foreground`), so light-mode placeholder text sits at 4.44:1 against the field's bg-background. Opacity variants make it far worse where they are used as real text: muted-foreground/70 computes to 2.63:1 on the light background and 3.26:1 on the dark one, /60 to 2.24:1 and 2.70:1, /50 to 1.93:1 and 2.23:1, /40 to 1.67:1 and 1.84:1 (components/ai-chat/chat-widget.tsx:1521 renders slash-command descriptions at text-muted-foreground/70, and the widget's own placeholder at /40).
findings.impact: Secondary text is the bulk of the copy in this UI: table meta, timestamps, hint lines under fields, empty-state prose, placeholder text. All of it sits at or under the AA floor on the muted and accent surfaces in both themes, and the opacity variants used for hints and descriptions are unreadable for low-vision users at under 2:1.
findings.recommendation: Darken light `--muted-foreground` to about `220 12% 35%` (≈6.3:1 on --background, ≈5.6:1 on --muted) and lighten dark to about `220 8% 65%` (≈6.4:1 on --muted) in app/globals.css:189 and :235. Then replace the /40, /50, /60 and /70 variants used for real text with the solid token; keep the opacity variants only for decorative glyphs that already carry an aria-hidden.

findings.title: Every API-key response example in the docs uses field names and a status the routes do not return (`prefix` vs `key_prefix`, a top-level `id`/`name` that does not exist, 200 vs 201)
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:727-735 documents POST /keys as returning `{ id, name, key: { raw_key, prefix, daily_limit } }`. app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:120 returns `ApiResponse.success({ key }, 201)`, and lib/api/api-utils.ts:15 emits the payload verbatim, so the real body is `{ "key": { id, key_prefix, name, daily_limit, created_at, scopes, raw_key } }` with status 201: there is no top-level `id` or `name`, and the field is `key_prefix` (lib/api/api-keys.ts:92/107), not `prefix`. GET /keys (app/docs/api/page.tsx:702-714) has the same problem: lib/api/api-keys.ts:617 selects `ak.key_prefix`, and also returns `scopes` and `usage_today`, neither of which the example shows. POST /keys/{id}/rotate (:763-767) documents `{ id, name, key: { raw_key, prefix, daily_limit } }`; app/api/v3/keys/[id]/rotate/route.ts:62-72 returns `{ success: true, key: { id, key_prefix, name, daily_limit, created_at, raw_key, scopes } }`. The docs also omit the 403 "API keys are disabled on this deployment" (app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:38) and the 400 "Invalid key ID" on rotate/revoke.
findings.impact: A client written against the documented shape reads `response.id` and `response.key.prefix` and gets undefined for both, and a client that asserts on HTTP 200 rejects the successful 201 from key creation. This is the first call any integration makes.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the three response examples in app/docs/api/page.tsx:702-795 from the actual RETURNING clauses in lib/api/api-keys.ts:92 and :617, mark POST /keys as 201, add `scopes` and `usage_today` to the GET example, and add the missing 400/403 rows to each error list.

findings.title: Key rotation is documented as a hard-delete-and-recreate in three places; the route updates the same row in place and keeps the id
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:754 describes POST /keys/{id}/rotate as "Hard-delete the key and create a new one with the same name" and its example (:763-767) shows a new id (2) replacing id 1; :1146-1147 repeats "rotate with POST /api/v3/keys/[id]/rotate, which deletes the old key in the same call"; lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:438-439 says "Delete the key and issue a replacement". lib/api/api-keys.ts:637-700 does the opposite and says so explicitly: "Rotate an API key - swaps the secret in place, same row, same id", with the comment at :664-671 explaining that the old delete-then-insert wiped api_usage rows via ON DELETE CASCADE and was deliberately replaced by `UPDATE api_keys SET key_hash = ..., key_prefix = ... WHERE id = $7 AND user_id = $8`.
findings.impact: An operator who stores key ids (audit records, per-key dashboards, allow-lists) is told rotation invalidates the id and rebuilds their mapping after every rotation, which it does not. The reverse is also missed: because the id and its usage history survive, today's consumed quota carries over to the rotated key, which the docs never mention.
findings.recommendation: Change app/docs/api/page.tsx:754 and :1146-1147 and lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:438-439 to "replaces the key's secret in place; the id, name, scopes and today's usage count are preserved", and update the response example at :763-767 to keep the original id.

findings.title: New API keys are documented as getting a daily limit of 50 from CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT; the route always passes the plan's apiRequestsPerDay instead
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:738 states "Default daily_limit comes from CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT (50)" and its example (:733) shows `"daily_limit": 50`; app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:172-174 repeats "New API keys default to CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT = 50". app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:88-97 resolves `dailyLimit = planLimits ? planLimits.apiRequestsPerDay : -1` and calls `generateApiKey(userId, name, dailyLimit === -1 ? 999999 : dailyLimit, scopes)`, always supplying a concrete value, so lib/api/api-keys.ts:70's `dailyLimit ?? getSetting("DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT")` fallback is never reached from this route. lib/billing/catalog.ts gives apiRequestsPerDay 25 (free, :118), 100 (core, :150), 5000 (pro, :182) and -1 (elite, :213, stored as 999999). app/api/v3/keys/[id]/rotate/route.ts:41-42 does the same.
findings.impact: A free-tier user is told their new key allows 50 requests/day and is cut off at 25; a Pro user is told 50 and actually has 5,000. Both numbers on the two doc pages are wrong for every plan, and the named constant is dead on this path.
findings.recommendation: Replace app/docs/api/page.tsx:738 and app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:172-174 with "a new key's daily_limit is your plan's apiRequestsPerDay (lib/billing/catalog.ts): 25 / 100 / 5,000 / effectively unlimited", and either delete CONFIG_DEFAULT_API_KEY_DAILY_LIMIT or document that it applies only to keys created outside this route.

findings.title: DELETE /history documents a `{ success: true, deleted: 47 }` response that the route never returns, and claims it deletes every scan when it excludes GitHub repo scans
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:461-468 describes DELETE /history as "Permanently delete every scan and tag for the authenticated user" with the response `{ "success": true, "deleted": 47 }`. app/api/v3/history/route.ts:226 returns `ApiResponse.success({ message: SUCCESS_MESSAGES.DELETED })`, and lib/api/api-utils.ts:15 passes the object through unchanged, so the real body is `{ "message": "..." }` with no `success` key and no count. The DELETE statements at :215-224 are scoped with `AND (scan_type IS NULL OR scan_type != 'github')`, so GitHub repo scans survive. The error list (:468) shows only 401; the route also returns 403 for an unaccepted ToS (:169) and for a key missing scan:delete (:176-180), and 429 for the key's daily limit (:186-191).
findings.impact: A client that branches on `response.success` treats every successful wipe as a failure, and one that reports "deleted N scans" prints undefined. An integrator with repo scans is told they were deleted when they were not. The scan:delete scope requirement is invisible here even though it is deliberately excluded from a new key's default scopes (lib/config/client-constants.ts:335-338), so this call 403s for most keys with no documented reason.
findings.recommendation: Correct the response example in app/docs/api/page.tsx:464-467 to the real `{ message }` body (or make the route return `{ success: true, deleted: n }` from a RETURNING count), state that GitHub repo scans are excluded, and add the 403 (scan:delete missing) and 429 rows to the error list.

findings.title: GET /history is documented as showing teammates' scans; the query is scoped to the caller's own user_id with no team clause
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:424 notes "Team members can see scans from other team members in the same team" on the GET /history card. app/api/v3/history/route.ts:117-138 issues `SELECT ... FROM scan_history sh WHERE sh.user_id = $1 AND (sh.scan_type IS NULL OR sh.scan_type != 'github') ORDER BY sh.scanned_at DESC LIMIT ...` in both retention branches: there is no team_id join and no union with team_members. Team visibility exists only on GET /history/{id} (app/api/v3/history/[id]/route.ts:15-18, getTeamResourceAccess) and on the separate GET /api/v3/teams/member-scans route, which app/docs/teams/page.tsx:409 documents correctly.
findings.impact: A team lead is told the list endpoint aggregates the team and sees only their own scans, with no error to explain the gap, and never finds /teams/member-scans, which the API reference does not mention at all.
findings.recommendation: Delete the note at app/docs/api/page.tsx:424 or replace it with "this list is your own scans only; use GET /api/v3/teams/member-scans?teamId=&userId= for a teammate's scans, and GET /history/{id} for a single scan a teammate owns".

findings.title: GET /history documents its `id` field as a number; the route returns the opaque public_id string
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:409-421 shows the GET /history response with `"id": 1`, and the code samples at :946 and :981 and the Python sample at :1011 all use the numeric form `/history/123`. app/api/v3/history/route.ts:117 and :127 both select `sh.public_id AS id`, so the returned id is the opaque non-enumerable token, not the row's integer primary key. GET /history/{id} resolves either form (lib/history/resolve-scan.ts:56-67 matches public_id first and falls back to the legacy numeric id), so the samples still work, but the documented list-response type does not match what comes back.
findings.impact: A client that declares `id: number` (or does `Number(scan.id)`) against the documented shape gets NaN for every row and cannot build a detail URL. The docs also never mention that the opaque id is the canonical form and the numeric one is legacy.
findings.recommendation: Change the example at app/docs/api/page.tsx:412 to a string public id, add a note that `id` is an opaque token and that /history/{id} also accepts the legacy numeric id, and mirror the same wording on the GET /history/{id} card at :430-456.

findings.title: History retention is documented as Free 30 days / Core 90 days; every plan's shipped retention default is -1 (keep forever)
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:408 states "Retention follows the user's plan (Free: 30 days, Core: 90, Pro/Elite: forever)". app/api/v3/history/route.ts:26-32 resolves retention through the registry keys BILLING_FREE_RETENTION / BILLING_CORE_SUPPORTER_RETENTION / BILLING_PRO_SUPPORTER_RETENTION / BILLING_ELITE_SUPPORTER_RETENTION, whose shipped defaults are all -1 (lib/config/config-values.ts:1209-1212, with the comment at :1205-1208 "-1 means keep forever on every plan"). :110-114 turns any value <= 0 into the no-retention-window branch, so on a default deployment no scan is ever aged out for any plan.
findings.impact: Free and Core users are told their history is deleted after 30 or 90 days when it is kept indefinitely, which is both a factual error and, since it is a data-retention statement, one the privacy/legal pages have to agree with. A self-hoster reading it also believes a cleanup window is running that is not.
findings.recommendation: Change app/docs/api/page.tsx:408 to say retention is admin-configurable per plan and defaults to unlimited on every plan (lib/config/config-values.ts:1209-1212), and reconcile the free plan's "30-day scan history" marketing bullet in lib/billing/catalog.ts:110 with whichever value is intended.

findings.title: The documented five X-RateLimit-* headers on a successful response are not what the documented endpoints send: session-auth scans send none
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:1376-1386 shows a 200 response carrying X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining, -Used, -Policy and -Reset, and :1405-1412 states "Both emit the same X-RateLimit-* headers". app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:280-283 goes further: "Every successful scan response includes rate-limit headers." In app/api/v3/scan/route.ts the success path at :441-452 attaches only Limit, Remaining and Reset, and only on the API-key branch; the session-cookie branch returns `NextResponse.json({ scanId, status })` at :454 with no rate-limit headers at all. The five-header helper getRateLimitHeaders (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:408-423) is the only source of X-RateLimit-Used and X-RateLimit-Policy, and across all of app/api it is called on exactly four lines: scan/route.ts:214, scan/crawl/route.ts:183, scan/bulk/route.ts:575 (all 429 paths) and scan/bulk/route.ts:732 (the one success path that uses it). GET /history, GET /history/{id} and GET /scan/status/{id} send no rate-limit headers on any path.
findings.impact: The docs' own best practice, "Read X-RateLimit-Remaining, not the 429" (app/docs/api/page.tsx:1489), cannot be followed on the endpoint it is written for when the caller uses a session, and X-RateLimit-Used / -Policy never appear on a 200 outside bulk. A client that pre-emptively throttles on those headers silently never throttles.
findings.recommendation: Either call getRateLimitHeaders on the success responses of app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:441-454 (both branches) and the history reads, or scope the claim in app/docs/api/page.tsx:1376-1412 and app/docs/rate-limits/page.tsx:280-283 to "POST /scan/bulk on the session path, and Limit/Remaining/Reset only on Bearer scan creation".

findings.title: The OpenAPI spec declares Bearer API-key security on five endpoint groups that only accept a session cookie
findings.description: lib/api/openapi-spec.ts declares `security: [{ apiKey: [] }]` on /scan/remediation (:337), /scan/remediation/bulk (:369), /keys GET and POST (:392, :403), /keys/{id}/rotate (:440) and /revoke (:466), /domains (:481, :492, :522), /domains/{id}/verify (:558), /schedules (:578, :589) and /teams (:617, :628), while each description simultaneously says "Session cookie auth.". The routes confirm the session-only gate and never call validateApiKey: app/api/v3/scan/remediation/route.ts:52, app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:23/33, app/api/v3/domains/route.ts:21/55/145, app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts (GET/POST), app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:18/50. Grepping BEARER_PREFIX/validateApiKey across app/api returns exactly 16 route files, none of them these. The apiKey scheme is the document's only securityScheme (:679-686), so there is no cookie scheme to point at instead.
findings.impact: The spec is the machine-readable contract: importing it into Postman/Insomnia/Bruno configures a Bearer token for 14 of the 26 documented operations, all of which then return 401. The playground has the same problem in reverse: it gates "Send request" on an API key being pasted (app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:452) and then succeeds only because the browser happens to attach a same-origin session cookie, so the key it demanded was never used.
findings.recommendation: Add a `cookieAuth` securityScheme (`type: apiKey, in: cookie`) to lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:679-686 and set `security: [{ cookieAuth: [] }]` on the session-only operations, so a spec consumer is told the truth and the playground can label those operations "browser session required".

findings.title: The OpenAPI spec omits ten HTTP methods that exist on paths it already documents
findings.description: Mechanically diffing the 20 path items in lib/api/openapi-spec.ts:56-677 against the exported handlers in the matching route.ts files: /history documents GET but the route also exports DELETE (app/api/v3/history/route.ts:153); /history/{id} documents GET but the route also exports PATCH (:194) and DELETE (:392); /scan/remediation documents POST but the route also exports GET (:147) and DELETE (:116); /schedules documents GET+POST but the route also exports PATCH (:223) and DELETE (:322); /teams documents GET+POST but the route also exports PATCH (:129) and DELETE (:176). Ten real operations, on paths the spec already lists, are missing. app/docs/triage/page.tsx:383-394 and app/docs/teams/page.tsx:447-509 document most of them in prose, so the spec is the outlier, not the routes.
findings.impact: The playground renders only what the spec lists (app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:61-104), so a user can create a schedule or a team from it but cannot rename, pause or delete one, and cannot clear or annotate history. Anyone generating a client SDK from the spec gets a write-only API for those resources.
findings.recommendation: Add the ten missing operations to lib/api/openapi-spec.ts (delete on /history and /history/{id}, patch on /history/{id}, get+delete on /scan/remediation with its ?url= and ?findingId= query params, patch+delete on /schedules and /teams), and extend tests/lib/api/openapi-spec.test.ts with a check that every documented path's method set matches the route file's exports.

findings.title: The webhooks doc says the free plan gets 0 webhooks in four places; lib/billing/catalog.ts gives it 1
findings.description: app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx states the free-plan webhook cap as 0 four separate times: the hero stat "0-∞" (:58), the overview paragraph (:75-79), the POST /webhooks note (:181), and the Security section bullet (:422). lib/billing/catalog.ts:121 sets `webhooks: 1` for the free plan (its own feature bullet at :112 reads "1 webhook alert"), and core_supporter is also 1 (:153), pro 5 (:185), elite -1 (:216). app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:100-107 enforces exactly that value via withinPlanLimit(count, planLimits.webhooks).
findings.impact: Free users, the largest cohort, are told a feature they have is unavailable and never set up the webhook they are entitled to. The Core tier's cap is also mislabeled: 0 to 1 is presented as the paid upgrade when the real step up is 1 to 5 at Pro.
findings.recommendation: Change all four occurrences in app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx (:58, :75-79, :181, :422) to "1 on Free, 1 on Core Supporter, 5 on Pro Supporter, unlimited on Elite Supporter", and derive them from lib/billing/catalog.ts rather than hardcoding, so the next plan change cannot desync them again.

findings.title: PATCH /webhooks (test) is documented as returning your endpoint's status code, and the test delivery is sent unsigned and without the documented User-Agent
findings.description: app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx:200 describes the test endpoint as "Returns the response status from your endpoint" and :204-207 shows `{ "success": true, "status": 204 }`. app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:293-296 returns `{ success: true, message: "Test webhook sent successfully" }`: there is no `status` field on any path. Separately, :277-281 sends the test payload with only `{ "Content-Type": "application/json" }`, while a real delivery (lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:74-78) adds `User-Agent: VulnRadar-Webhook/1.0` and `X-VulnRadar-Signature: sha256=<hmac>`. The docs state the opposite at :369 ("Delivered with ... User-Agent: VulnRadar-Webhook/1.0") and :397-405 ("Every delivery includes X-VulnRadar-Signature").
findings.impact: A consumer that follows the Security section and rejects unsigned payloads fails the Test button, which is the documented way to confirm the webhook works (:449-453), and gets a non-2xx back that the app reports as a broken webhook. Any client reading `status` off the test response gets undefined.
findings.recommendation: Fix the example at app/docs/webhooks/page.tsx:204-207 to `{ success: true, message: "..." }` and the description at :200, and make app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:277-281 build its headers through the same helper lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:74-78 uses so a test is signed exactly like a real delivery.

findings.title: The compiled AI knowledge truncates 20 of 52 docs callouts mid-sentence at 300 characters and leaks 64 raw JSX `{" "}` tokens and 19 undecoded HTML entities
findings.description: scripts/compile-docs-knowledge.mjs:274 and :284 both apply `stripJsx(...).slice(0, 300)` to every DocsCallout body. Measured across app/docs/*/page.tsx, 52 callouts are extracted and 20 exceed 300 stripped characters, so they land in lib/ai/docs-knowledge.md cut mid-word: for example the API page's Scopes callout ends at "returns 403 naming" (docs-knowledge.md:997) and the CI/CD callout ends at "before ch" (:1009). The offending pages are app/docs/api (2), config (2), github (2), rate-limits (2), scheduled-scans (2), self-hosting (4), sharing (2), account-security, developers, teams and triage. stripJsx (:82-110) also never strips the JSX whitespace literal `{" "}` (64 occurrences survive into the output) and never decodes `'`, `{` or `}` (19 occurrences), so those consume part of the same 300-char budget.
findings.impact: lib/ai/docs-knowledge.md is what the in-product AI assistant answers from. Twenty of the most important "be careful about this" notes reach it as unfinished sentences, so the assistant either invents the missing half or drops the caveat. The Scopes callout in particular loses the sentence that tells the user a 403 names the missing scope.
findings.recommendation: Raise the cap in scripts/compile-docs-knowledge.mjs:274/284 to at least 1200 characters (the longest real callout is 522), or truncate on a sentence boundary; and add `.replace(/\{\s*"\s*"\s*\}/g, " ")` plus `'`/`&#\d+;` decoding to stripJsx before the existing entity replacements.

findings.title: The API error-code table documents 422 for SSRF and private-IP rejections that actually return 400, and omits 402, 409, 413, 502 and 503
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:1458-1463 defines 422 as "The target is unreachable, blocks the request, resolves to a private IP, or fails the SSRF check", and the best-practice at :1494-1496 tells the reader a client-side check "turns a 422 round trip into a local error". app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:276-282 returns 400 for a failed validateScanTarget, :265-273 returns 400 for an invalid URL, and :285-296 returns 403 for a blocked target: POST /scan never returns 422. Grepping every route.ts for `status: 422` finds four files only: scan/authenticated (login failure, :344/:347), demo-scan (:175), and history/[id]/ports (:96). The table also omits five codes the documented surface really returns: 402 (Browserbase minute quota, app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:92), 409 (already-terminal scan cancel, app/api/v3/scan/status/[id]/route.ts, and documented on that endpoint card at :127 but absent from the table), 413 (app/api/v3/scan/github/route.ts:143), 502 (app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:392) and 503 (11 route files).
findings.impact: A generic error handler written from this table treats an SSRF rejection as a retryable 422 and never handles the 400 it actually gets, and has no branch for the 402/409/413/502/503 responses the API really produces.
findings.recommendation: Correct the 422 row in app/docs/api/page.tsx:1458-1463 to "login could not be confirmed on POST /scan/authenticated, or a target that could not be reached on the demo and port endpoints", move SSRF and private-IP rejection to the 400 row, fix the best-practice sentence at :1494-1496, and add rows for 402, 409, 413, 502 and 503.

findings.title: Half of .github/labeler.yml uses an invented schema the labeler action silently ignores, so the step named "Apply size label" has never applied a size label
findings.description: actions/labeler takes the label name as the top-level key and accepts only `changed-files`, `base-branch`, `head-branch`, `any` and `all` as matcher keys. .github/labeler.yml gets this right for four blocks (`ci` line 24, `config` line 29, `security` line 35, `docs` line 39) and wrong for the other two. The `size` block (lines 3-16) has a top-level key `size` whose entries are `{label: "size/xs", files: [...]}`, and the `dependencies` block (lines 18-21) uses `{label: "dependencies", from-branch: [...]}`. `label`, `files` and `from-branch` are not matcher keys. I confirmed against the action's source (src/api/get-label-configs.ts): an unrecognised key is not an error, it hits `core.info(\`An unknown config option was under ${label}: ${key}\`)` and produces no matcher, so the labels `size`, `size/xs`, `size/s`, `size/m`, `size/l` and the branch-based `dependencies` rule are never applied. The step at .github/workflows/label.yml:16 is literally named "Apply size label". Separately, label.yml:7-8 declares `permissions: pull-requests: write` only; declaring any permission sets every unlisted scope to `none`, including `contents`, while the action's documented usage requires `contents: read` to read the configuration file from the repository.
findings.impact: PR triage silently does not work. Maintainers see no size labels, and the `dependencies` label the stale.yml exemption logic and the auto-merge ignore flow both reason about is never applied from the branch name (dependabot supplies it from .github/dependabot.yml:12-14 instead, which masks the breakage). Nothing in the log makes this visible except an `info`-level line nobody reads.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the `size` and `dependencies` blocks in .github/labeler.yml to the real schema: one top-level key per label (`size/xs:`, `size/s:`, ...) with `- changed-files: - any-glob-to-any-file: [...]`, and `dependencies: - head-branch: ["^dependabot/"]`. Note that labeler matches on paths, not diff size, so if a real size label is wanted use a line-count action instead. Add `contents: read` to the permissions block in .github/workflows/label.yml:7.

findings.title: Any tag matching `v*`, including a release candidate or an old-line backport, overwrites `:latest` and is published as the newest release that every self-hosted updater offers
findings.description: docker-publish.yml triggers on `push: tags: v*` (lines 5-6) and unconditionally tags and pushes `$IMAGE:latest` alongside `$IMAGE:${VERSION}` (lines 51 and 54), with no check that the tag is newer than the current `latest` and no prerelease detection. release.yml:289-292 then runs `gh release create` with no `--prerelease` flag, so the GitHub release is a normal one. app/api/version/route.ts:12 fetches VERSION_CHECK_URL, which is `/releases/latest`, and passes the tag to `compareVersions`. lib/updater/version-compare.ts:29 splits on `.` and maps `Number`, so `"3.8.0-rc.1"` becomes `[3, 8, NaN, 1]` and line 45's `latestParts[i] || 0` turns the NaN into 0, making the release compare exactly equal to 3.8.0. The repository already has tags of this shape: `v1.9.4-patch.1`, `v1.9.5-patch.1`, `v2.1.0-patch.1` are in both `git tag` and the live GHCR tag list. docker-publish.yml also declares no `concurrency`, so two tags pushed close together race on `:latest`.
findings.impact: Cutting a release candidate or a patch for an older line silently republishes it as `:latest` in GHCR and as the newest GitHub release. Every self-hosted instance's version banner then reports "behind" and the admin updater offers to apply it, so a backport of 3.6.x would be pushed to installs already running 3.7.x, and an RC would be offered to production self-hosters as a stable update. There is no way to publish a prerelease from this pipeline at all.
findings.recommendation: In docker-publish.yml, gate the `:latest` tag on the tag being a clean `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` and being the highest such tag (`git tag --sort=-v:refname | head -1`), and skip it otherwise. In release.yml:289, pass `--prerelease` when the tag contains a hyphen. Give docker-publish.yml a `concurrency: group: docker-publish` block. Fix compareVersions in lib/updater/version-compare.ts to strip and compare a prerelease suffix instead of coercing it to 0.

findings.title: The published image is amd64 only: docker-publish.yml sets up buildx and then never uses it, so ARM self-hosters cannot run VulnRadar at all
findings.description: docker-publish.yml:23 runs `docker/setup-buildx-action`, then lines 49-51 invoke plain `docker build -t ... .` with no `--platform` and no `buildx build`, and lines 53-54 push each tag separately. I fetched the manifest for v3.7.2 from ghcr.io anonymously: it comes back as `application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json`, a single-platform manifest, not an OCI image index or a Docker manifest list. So only the runner's architecture (ubuntu-latest, linux/amd64) is ever built and the buildx setup step has no effect on the build.
findings.impact: Anyone self-hosting on ARM64 (Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon, an Ampere or Graviton VPS, which is the cheap tier most hobbyist self-hosters buy) gets `no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8` from `docker compose up -d`, or falls back to qemu emulation with a several-times slowdown on a scanner whose docs promise sub-3-second scans. Nothing in the self-hosting docs states the image is amd64 only.
findings.recommendation: Replace the `docker build`/`docker push` block in docker-publish.yml:45-54 with `docker/build-push-action` using `platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, `push: true`, and `cache-from`/`cache-to: type=gha`. Keep the cosign step signing the resulting index digest. If arm64 build time is unacceptable, say so explicitly in app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx rather than leaving it undocumented.

findings.title: The weekly GHCR cleanup deletes untagged digests with no age gate, so an operator who followed the compose file's own advice to pin by digest loses the ability to pull their image
findings.description: docker-compose.yml:48-51 instructs self-hosters to pin immutably: pull the tag, read the digest with `docker images --digests`, and replace the tag with `ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar@sha256:<digest>`. .github/workflows/ghcr-cleanup.yml:39-45 runs `dataaxiom/ghcr-cleanup-action` every Monday at 06:00 UTC with `delete-untagged: true` and `delete-orphaned-images: true`, and its own header (lines 15-18) states there is deliberately no `older-than` cutoff: "a digest with no tag pointing at it is orphaned the moment it's created". The header also names the exact scenario that untags a live digest (lines 6-8): "any build a tag later moved away from, e.g. a re-run while debugging the release pipeline". Re-running docker-publish.yml for an existing tag produces a new digest (the base image `node:22.11.0-alpine` is a mutable tag and the build is not reproducible), moves `vX.Y.Z` and `latest` onto it, and leaves the previous digest untagged and therefore in scope for deletion at the next scheduled run.
findings.impact: An operator who pinned by digest exactly as the compose file told them to gets `manifest unknown` on the next `docker compose pull`, container restart, or host reboot, and cannot recover the image they were running. There is no dry-run on the scheduled path (line 45 evaluates the expression to `false` for `schedule`), no notification, and no way to restore a deleted GHCR version.
findings.recommendation: Add `older-than: 30 days` to the ghcr-cleanup.yml step so a digest an operator may have pinned in the last month is never removed, or add `keep-n-untagged` so recent orphans survive. Alternatively remove the digest-pinning advice from docker-compose.yml:48-51 and tell operators to pin by version tag only, so the guidance and the retention policy agree.

findings.title: The published scan-gate composite action is documented at the mutable `@main` ref, so every consumer's CI executes whatever is on VulnRadar's unprotected main while holding their VULNRADAR_TOKEN
