So the destination cannot be crawled, cannot be indexed, and carries nofollow. The image is an SVG served from /api/v3/badge/[token] (app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts:122, Content-Type image/svg+xml), which is also Disallowed and which social and image crawlers do not render.
findings.impact: A security badge on a customer's site is the standard organic-growth loop for this product category: it is how Security Headers, SSL Labs and Mozilla Observatory accumulate their link graph. Here the feature is built, documented, and produces a link that search engines are explicitly told to ignore. Every customer who installs a badge gives the product a link worth nothing.
findings.recommendation: Point the documented `<a href>` at `/host/<hostname>` instead of `/shared/<token>`: it is the stable, per-host public page for the same site (app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts only ever serves public scans, and its host_reputation row is deleted when a scan is made private), it does not expose a token in someone else's page source, and it is the page a stranger arriving from the badge actually wants. Then do seo-09 so that target is indexable and followable. Update the snippet at app/docs/sharing/page.tsx:386 and anywhere the badge UI generates the same HTML. Keep the SVG badge image where it is; the link, not the image, is what carries the value.

findings.title: /host/[hostname] is kept noindex and robots-Disallowed on the stated grounds that the URL space is "not enumerable", which is false: host_reputation is a table and /public-scans already paginates it
findings.description: lib/seo/routes.ts:100-106 justifies excluding /host/ and /shared/ together: "Tokenised or per-entity URLs (/shared/<token>, /browser/<id>, /host/<hostname>). Not enumerable ahead of time, so there is no fixed list to publish a sitemap entry or canonical for." That reasoning is correct for /shared/<token> and /browser/<id>, which are secrets. It is not correct for /host/<hostname>: app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts:99 reads from the `host_reputation` table keyed on `host`, so the full list is a single SELECT, and app/public-scans/page.tsx already renders a paginated, sitemapped, indexable directory of exactly this data. The data is public by construction, not by accident: app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts:140 gates the live findings on `is_public = true`, and the route's own comment states the host_reputation row is deleted when its source scan is made private. The page also already has a per-host trend chart (components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx). Today the page ships privatePageMetadata("Host Report", "/host") (app/host/[hostname]/layout.tsx:8), so it has no per-host title, no per-host description, a canonical pointing at /host which is not a route, and noindex.
findings.impact: "<domain> security report" and "is <domain> safe" are the highest-volume query shapes in this product category, and they are the entire organic strategy of Security Headers, SSL Labs, Mozilla Observatory and urlscan.io. The product already generates the pages that answer them, already restricts them to public data, already links them from an indexable directory, and then blocks all of them. The 749 /checks pages target "how to fix X" intent, which converts worse: someone searching a check name is fixing a problem they already found, while someone searching a domain is looking for a scanner.
findings.recommendation: Three changes. (1) Replace app/host/[hostname]/layout.tsx with an async generateMetadata({ params }) that resolves the host via the same host_reputation lookup and returns pageMetadata({ title: `${host} security report`, description: `${host} scored ${dangerScore}/10 on ${date}: ${critical} critical and ${high} high findings across headers, TLS, cookies and DNS.`, path: `/host/${host}`, noIndex: !known || findings.length === 0 }), so an unscanned or empty host stays noindex and only real reports are indexable. (2) Remove "/host/" from DISALLOWED_PATHS in lib/seo/routes.ts:122, leaving "/shared/" and "/browser/" in place. (3) Publish the URLs: add a second sitemap (Next 15 supports generateSitemaps(), or a plain app/sitemap-hosts.xml/route.ts) that selects host and last_scanned_at from host_reputation and emits a real per-host lastmod, and reference both from a sitemap index. Note app/sitemap.ts is currently `force-static` so the host sitemap must be a separate dynamic route. Pair with seo-02 so each host page also gets a real social card, and with seo-08 so badges point here.

findings.title: The 749 check pages call generateStaticParams and produce zero prerendered HTML, so the entire organic surface is an uncacheable per-request render and Cloudflare returns a MISS on 100 percent of crawler traffic
findings.description: This is the SEO quantification of AUDIT-012#fe-01 and AUDIT-012#perf-17 (root cause: app/layout.tsx:146 awaits headers() for the CSP nonce, which opts every segment beneath it into per-request dynamic rendering). Do not re-file the root cause. What matters for section 19 is the shape of the loss. app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:34 exports generateStaticParams() returning all 749 check ids, and the file's own comment at lines 29-31 states it produces nothing: "The root layout reads headers() for its CSP nonce, so the whole app already renders per-request." app/checks/category/[category]/page.tsx:27 and app/alternatives/[competitor]/page.tsx:17 do the same. AUDIT-012#fe-01 measured the committed build: .next/prerender-manifest.json lists exactly 5 prerendered routes (robots.txt, sitemap.xml, manifest.webmanifest, llms.txt, llms-full.txt) against 311 app-build-manifest entries, and Next sets `cache-control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate` on dynamically rendered app pages. The sitemap I computed from lib/seo/routes.ts contains 805 URLs: 33 hand-listed, 18 categories, 5 alternatives, 749 checks. Every one is an origin React render with an uncacheable response, on the same single Node process that runs scans. No route sets `revalidate`, so there is no ISR fallback either. On top of that, AUDIT-012#fe-02 measured that the root-layout ChatWidget puts react-markdown plus remark-gfm (144 KB raw / 44 KB gzipped) and an /api/v3/ai/info request on all 311 routes, and AUDIT-011#docs-05 measured /checks at ~190 KB of HTML for 754 list items.
findings.impact: Crawl budget is spent on origin CPU rather than edge bytes: a full Googlebot pass over the sitemap is 805 cold server-side renders, each also serving a JS bundle Googlebot must parse in its rendering pass, with a Cache-Control header that forbids both the CDN and Googlebot's own cache from reusing anything on the next crawl. Nothing in this repo can be measured for TTFB here (no build, no deploy, no Docker on this machine), but the mechanism is unambiguous: the HTML cache hit rate on the organic surface is structurally zero, and content that is byte-identical between deploys is regenerated for every crawler hit and every visitor. Crawler traffic also directly competes with scan execution for the same CPU, so an organic traffic spike degrades the product.
findings.recommendation: Separate the SEO surface from the nonce. Move the public content routes (/checks, /checks/category, /alternatives, /tools, /docs, /legal, /landing, /pricing) into a route group such as app/(marketing)/ with its own layout.tsx that does NOT call headers(), and lift the inline auth-cache script out of the root layout for that group (it is only useful to signed-in users, who are not on these pages). Those routes then prerender from their existing generateStaticParams and become CDN-cacheable. Because the inline script's content is deterministic (it is built from STAFF_ROLES at build time), the alternative fix is a hash-based CSP for that one script, which lets the root layout drop headers() entirely. Either way, add `export const revalidate = 86400` to the check and category routes so a content edit still reaches the edge without a deploy. Verify by checking that .next/prerender-manifest.json lists the 749 check routes after the change.

findings.title: /public-scans is an indexable, hourly-priority sitemap entry whose server HTML is a loading skeleton and whose every outbound link is robots-Disallowed and noindex, nofollow
findings.description: lib/seo/routes.ts:45 registers /public-scans in the sitemap at priority 0.6 with changeFrequency "hourly", and app/public-scans/layout.tsx gives it real indexable metadata ("Public Scans: Shared Reports Directory"). The page itself is app/public-scans/page.tsx:1 "use client": it fetches the listing from API.PUBLIC_SCANS in a useEffect with `loading` initialised true, so the server-rendered HTML a crawler receives is PublicScansTableSkeleton (lines 23-38), eight rows of grey placeholders and no scan data. The only link out of each row is components/public-scans/public-scan-row.tsx:21, `href={`/shared/${scan.token}`}`, and /shared/ is Disallowed in robots.txt (app/robots.ts:60 via lib/seo/routes.ts:121) and served noindex, nofollow (app/shared/[token]/layout.tsx:7). So the page tells crawlers it changes hourly, delivers no content without JS, and points every one of its links at a URL they are forbidden to follow.
findings.impact: The hourly changeFrequency asks Google to re-crawl a page that is byte-identical on every fetch, which is exactly the signal Google penalises as unreliable and then ignores for the whole sitemap. The directory contributes nothing to the index: no scan URLs, no host names, no verdicts, and no crawlable outbound links, despite being the one page on the site whose content is fresh, unique and query-shaped ("is example.com safe"). It is a sitemap entry that consumes crawl budget and returns an empty page.
findings.recommendation: Make the listing server-rendered: split app/public-scans/page.tsx into a server component that awaits the same query app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts runs and passes the first page as a prop, with the existing client component taking over for pagination (the client already syncs `?page=` via url-state). Change the row link at components/public-scans/public-scan-row.tsx:21 from `/shared/${scan.token}` to `/host/${hostname}` so the directory links to the crawlable per-host page (see seo-09) instead of a token URL; keep the token link for the owner's own view if needed. Lower changeFrequency in lib/seo/routes.ts:45 from "hourly" to "daily", which is closer to true for a 50-user service.

findings.title: The five SoftwareApplication JSON-LD blocks carry no offers, aggregateRating or review, so none is eligible for Google's software rich result, and /pricing (the only page with prices) emits no SoftwareApplication at all
findings.description: SoftwareStructuredData (components/seo/structured-data.tsx:130) accepts an `offers` array and emits an Offer list at lines 165-175. Grepping every call site: app/landing/page.tsx:109, app/demo/layout.tsx:27, app/tools/page.tsx:50, app/tools/api-scanner/page.tsx:71 and app/tools/link-checker/page.tsx:73. All five pass only `nonce`, so the offers branch is unreachable and every emitted block has no offers, no aggregateRating and no review. Google's Software App structured-data requirements list `name` plus at least one of `offers`, `aggregateRating` or `review` as required for the rich result, so all five blocks are ineligible. Meanwhile app/pricing/layout.tsx renders only FaqStructuredData (line 47), no SoftwareApplication, even though lib/billing/plans.ts already exposes getPaidPlans() with priceInCents and the layout already imports it at line 14 to compute CHEAPEST_PAID. Two secondary defects in the same block: the five copies have no `@id`, so five pages assert five unlinked entities with the same `name` and `url: APP_URL`; and `license: SEO_LICENSE` (line 150) is the string "GPL-3.0" where schema.org expects a CreativeWork or a URL. Also worth noting: the blocks on /tools/api-scanner and /tools/link-checker describe the whole product with a featureList of 795+ checks on pages that are about one single free tool.
findings.impact: The pricing panel with a price and a Free badge in the search result, which is the visible payoff of SoftwareApplication markup and the reason this component exists, can never render for any page. The markup is written, maintained, and shipped on five pages, and Google discards all of it. Five duplicate unlinked entities also make it harder for answer engines to resolve "VulnRadar" to one thing, which is the same problem the Organization @id at line 62 was added to solve.
findings.recommendation: Add `<SoftwareStructuredData nonce={nonce} offers={[{ name: "Free", priceInCents: 0 }, ...getPaidPlans().map(p => ({ name: p.name, priceInCents: p.priceInCents }))]} />` to app/pricing/layout.tsx, gated on BILLING_ENABLED so a self-host with billing off does not publish prices. Give the block a stable `"@id": `${APP_URL}/#software`` in components/seo/structured-data.tsx and have the other four call sites emit `{ "@type": "SoftwareApplication", "@id": SOFTWARE_ID }` as a reference instead of a full duplicate. Change `license` to the SPDX URL `https://spdx.org/licenses/GPL-3.0-or-later.html` (add a CONFIG_SEO_LICENSE_URL next to CONFIG_SEO_LICENSE in lib/config/config-values.ts:245 so a fork can change it). Do not fabricate an aggregateRating: `offers` alone satisfies the requirement.

findings.title: The /checks pages are thin: 363 of 749 carry under 100 words of unique body copy, and the FAQ block on every one of them is the same four templated questions restating text already on the page
findings.description: I measured unique body copy per check page as description plus riskImpact plus explanation plus fixSteps, over all 749 entries getAllChecks() returns. Median is 101 words. 712 of 749 are under 200 words and 363 are under 100. The thinnest are /checks/webauthn-usage at 14 words, /checks/docker-hub-token-exposed at 15, /checks/permissions-policy-usb-blocked at 16. 643 of 749 have exactly one code example and 160 have exactly one fix step. 293 of the 749 share one of just three identical `references` arrays (137 pages share one OWASP XSS pair, 99 share one secure-headers pair, 57 share a third). On top of that, app/checks/[id]/page.tsx:89 buildFaq() generates the same four questions on all 749 pages (`What is "<title>"?`, `How do I fix <title>?`, `How severe is <title>?`, `Which standards does <title> map to?`) and answers them with check.description, check.fixSteps.join(" ") and check.riskImpact, all three of which are already rendered verbatim higher up the same page (lines 199, 210, 228-238). So the FAQ section, and the FaqStructuredData built from it at line 160, is a second copy of the page body on every page.
findings.impact: A set of 749 pages that share a template, a title prefix, three reference lists and an identical four-question FAQ, with a median of 101 words of genuinely unique text, is the pattern Google's helpful-content and thin-affiliate guidance targets. The risk is set-wide rather than per-page: a site-level quality signal suppresses all 749 at once, which would take out the entire organic strategy. Duplicating the body text into an FAQ also makes the pages look longer to a word count while adding nothing a reader did not already read.
findings.recommendation: Vary the template, not just the data. Per page, add sections whose content is necessarily unique: (1) "What VulnRadar looks for" naming the actual response header, cookie attribute, DNS record, file path or regex the detector matches, which is already in lib/scanner/checks/* and lib/scanner/checks-data/*.json under `evidence`/`type` and is discarded by normalise() at lib/seo/checks-content.ts:102; (2) "How to verify the fix" with a concrete curl or dig command derived from the check category, which is templatable per category rather than per check and still gives 18 distinct shapes; (3) severity rationale, one sentence saying why this is high and not medium. Replace buildFaq's four generic questions with two or three drawn from the same per-check data but not restated elsewhere on the page, and drop any question whose answer is verbatim body text (the `How do I fix` one especially, which is fixSteps.join(" ")). Widen the three shared reference lists so a page's references are specific to its check. Prioritise the 363 pages under 100 words: for the ones that cannot be given real depth (single Permissions-Policy directives, for example), fold them into their category page and 301 the leaf, rather than shipping a 14-word page.

findings.title: The history scan-detail error state is unreachable: a failed detail load nulls the selected id, so the user is bounced back to the list with no message while the URL still says ?scan=
findings.description: app/history/page.tsx:556-570 contains a designed error state for the detail view: "This scan could not be loaded. It may have been deleted or fallen outside your retention window." plus a "Back to history" button. It is gated on `selectedScanId !== null && !detailLoading && !scanDetail` (the outer branch at :447 requires a non-null selectedScanId). loadScanDetail is the only thing that can produce that combination, and it never does: on a non-ok response it runs `setSelectedScanId(null); return;` at :131-134, and in its catch it runs `if (!isStale()) setSelectedScanId(null)` at :147-148. Both paths force the outer branch at :447 to false, so the list view renders instead and the error block is dead code on every failure path. scanDetail is only ever set from `mapHistoryDetailResponse(data)` (:137), which always returns an object, so there is no other route to it. Two further consequences of the same two lines: the URL is not cleaned (updateUrlWithScan is not called), so the address bar still reads ?scan=<id> while the list is on screen, and a reload silently repeats the bounce; and scanDetail is not cleared at the start of loadScanDetail, so a failed switch from scan A to scan B leaves A's data in state under a list view.
findings.impact: Clicking a scan that has been deleted, has aged out of retention, or hits a 500 does nothing visible: the row click appears to be ignored, then the page is back where it started. The user has no way to tell whether they misclicked, whether the scan is gone, or whether the server is broken. Deep links shared between teammates (/history?scan=abc) fail the same way, landing on a generic list rather than saying the link is dead, which is the one case where the message at :556 would have been exactly right.
findings.recommendation: Add a `detailError: string | null` state to app/history/page.tsx. In loadScanDetail, replace the `setSelectedScanId(null)` at :132 and :148 with `setDetailError(res.status === 404 ? "deleted or outside your retention window" : "couldn't be loaded")`, keeping selectedScanId set so the existing block at :556-570 renders. Add `setScanDetail(null)` at the top of loadScanDetail beside the existing `setCrawlInfo(null)` at :127 so a failed switch cannot leave the previous scan in state. Have the "Back to history" button at :562 call handleBackToList, which already clears ?scan= via updateUrlWithScan(null). Distinguish the two cases in the copy: 404 gets the retention sentence, 5xx gets a Retry button that recalls loadScanDetail.

findings.title: A failed team-members fetch renders "Members 0" over a blank list, "0 members, Your role: " with the role blank, and silently strips every management control from the owner
findings.description: app/teams/page.tsx:280-293 (`refreshMembers`) fetches GET /api/v3/teams/members and only acts inside `if (res.ok)`. On a non-ok response or a thrown request, `members`, `invites` and `currentRole` all keep their prior values (on first open: `[]`, `[]` and `""` from :59), `membersLoading` goes false in the finally at :291, and no error is recorded anywhere. components/teams/team-members-list.tsx then renders the loaded branch: :58-63 prints the header "Members" with the count `members.length`, which is 0, and :182-190 falls to a `divide-y` container with nothing in it, because there is no empty branch at all. The role explainer at :181 is gated on `members.length > 0` so it vanishes too. Separately, `currentRole` staying "" makes `hasTeamPermission("", ...)` false everywhere, so components/teams/team-detail-header.tsx:59-60 hides the rename control and the Invite button, and :132 renders `Your role: ` with an empty span. A team always contains at least its owner, so `members.length === 0` is not a state the data can produce: it is reachable only through a failed fetch, which means the blank card is always a lie.
findings.impact: A team owner opening their own team during a backend blip is told the team has zero members, sees their own role as blank, and finds the Invite and Rename controls gone. The natural reading is that they were removed from their own team or that their permissions were revoked. There is no retry, no message, and nothing distinguishes it from a real permission change. The identical shape applies to `handleViewMemberScans` at :459-479, where a failed fetch renders a member's scan list as empty, which in a compliance context reads as "this person has run no scans".
findings.recommendation: In app/teams/page.tsx:280-293 add an else branch setting the existing `actionError` state, which already has a rendered destructive band at :515-525, with "Couldn't load this team's members. Nothing has changed, try again." and keep the previous members array rather than showing zero. In components/teams/team-members-list.tsx add an explicit branch for `!loading && members.length === 0` that renders an error block rather than a blank div, since that state is unreachable from real data. Do not set `currentRole` from a failed response; leave the header's role chip and its permission-gated controls in a pending state instead of silently resolving to viewer-level.

findings.title: The extension popup writes scanInProgress.startedAt but never reads it, so a service-worker termination mid-scan leaves the popup permanently on "Scanning..." with the Scan button disabled and no way back
findings.description: extension/src/background/service-worker.ts:520-524 writes `scanInProgress = { url, mode, startedAt: Date.now() }` before running the scan and clears it in a `finally` at :551. The popup reconciles against it at extension/src/popup/popup.ts:1086-1089: `if (tabUrl && storage.scanInProgress?.url === tabUrl) { state.isScanning = true; state.mode = ...; watchInProgressScan(tabUrl); }`. Only `.url` and `.mode` are read; `startedAt` is written and never consulted anywhere in extension/src (grep confirms three write-side references and no read). watchInProgressScan (:946-965) then subscribes to storage changes and waits for `scanInProgress` to go null, with no deadline of its own. If the background context dies before its `finally` runs, which an MV3 service worker does on browser restart, extension reload, extension update, or a worker crash, and can do on a long crawl (extension/src/lib/constants.ts:38 allows crawlTimeoutMs of 910 seconds while the poll loop at extension/src/lib/scan.ts:186-196 drives itself with plain fetch and setTimeout), the key is never cleared. Every subsequent popup open on that tab reads the stale key, sets isScanning true, and waits on an onChanged event that will never fire. extension/src/popup/components/scan-button.ts:82 disables the Scan button on `props.isScanning` and :99-101 replaces its label with a spinner and "Scanning...", and the mode toggle at :69/:79 is disabled too. There is no cancel control and no reset in the popup UI.
findings.impact: The extension becomes permanently unusable for that URL. The user sees a spinner that has been running since before their browser restarted, cannot start a new scan, and has no affordance to clear it: the only recoveries are navigating away from that site, or clearing extension storage from the browser's settings. Because the state is keyed on the URL, this hits exactly the site the user is trying to check.
findings.recommendation: In extension/src/popup/popup.ts:1086, treat the record as dead when `Date.now() - storage.scanInProgress.startedAt` exceeds the mode's own ceiling (VULNRADAR.scanTimeoutMs or crawlTimeoutMs from extension/src/lib/constants.ts, plus a small margin): clear the key, leave isScanning false, and set `state.error` to "That scan was interrupted and its result was lost. Run it again." so the existing error banner at :206-215 renders it. Give watchInProgressScan (:946) the same deadline as a setTimeout so a popup that opens just inside the window still recovers rather than waiting forever. Optionally have the service worker clear a stale `scanInProgress` on its own startup, which is the cheapest catch-all for the browser-restart case.

findings.title: The AI verify modal closes silently on every failure, throwing away the server's actionable "you are out of AI credits" message and leaving the user unable to tell whether verification ran
findings.description: app/dashboard/page.tsx:810-844 (`handleDeepScan`) runs when the user clicks the AI verification action in AiChoiceModal. Every non-success path collapses to the same statement: `else { setShowAiModal(false) }` at :833-835 when the body has no findings array, at :836-838 when the response is not ok, and at :839-841 in the catch. components/scanner/ai-choice-modal.tsx has no error prop and no error branch (its props are findings, loading, aiSummary, onDeepScan, onViewNow, :20-25), so dismissing it is the only outcome available. app/api/v3/scan/verify/route.ts:144-147 returns `{ error: quota.message }` with status 429 when checkAiUsageQuota denies the request, and the same route rate-limits at :67-70; both messages name the exact reason and remedy, and both are discarded. The result is that clicking "Verify with AI" and clicking "View now" produce a pixel-identical outcome.
findings.impact: The user cannot distinguish "AI verification ran and confirmed nothing" from "you have no AI credits left" from "the AI provider is down", because all three dismiss the modal and show the plain result. The quota message is the product's own upsell path and it is thrown on the floor. On a self-host with no AI provider configured the button is offered (aiAvailableRef gating at :271-279 only checks configured/aiDisabled) and then does nothing visible, which reads as a broken build.
findings.recommendation: Add an `error?: string` prop to components/scanner/ai-choice-modal.tsx and a branch that renders it inside the existing Shell (:28-46) above the two buttons, keeping the modal open with "View now" as the way out. In app/dashboard/page.tsx:836, read `data.error` off the non-ok response and pass it through instead of calling setShowAiModal(false); for a 429 whose message mentions credits, route to the same PremiumUpgradeModal already wired at :972-977, which is what that path exists for. The catch at :839 should set a network-flavoured message rather than dismissing.

findings.title: A 500 or a dropped connection on the admin data route renders "Access Denied: you do not have administrator privileges", mislabelling a server fault as an authorization one
findings.description: app/admin/page.tsx:277-306 (`fetchData`) handles exactly one non-ok status: 403 at :287-294, which sets twoFactorLockout when the body carries `code: "2fa_required"` and then setForbidden(true). Every other status falls straight through to `const data = await res.json()` at :296 with no res.ok check. A 500 whose body is a JSON error envelope assigns `data.stats` and `data.users` as undefined; a 502 from a proxy returning HTML throws on the parse. Both land in the catch at :301-304, which does `setForbidden(true)`. resolveAdminGate (:896-901) then returns "deny" and the page renders the block at :903-962: a ShieldOff icon, the heading "Access Denied", the body "You do not have administrator privileges to access this panel", and a "Back to Scanner" button. Nothing on that screen mentions a server error, and there is no retry.
findings.impact: During an outage or a database problem, the operator who most needs to reach the admin panel is told their account lacks permission. That sends them to check roles, 2FA enforcement and session state, which is the wrong debugging path, and the screen offers no retry so they cannot even confirm it is transient without reloading. It also permanently hides the real error: nothing anywhere on the page or in the network tab explanation surfaces the status code.
findings.recommendation: In app/admin/page.tsx:277-306 add a third terminal state alongside forbidden and twoFactorLockout, for example `loadFailed`, set on any non-403 non-ok status and in the catch. Render it through the same centred layout as the deny block at :903-962 but with a ServerCrash icon, the heading "Couldn't load the admin panel", the status code shown in mono the way app/error.tsx:88-90 shows error.digest, and a Retry button calling fetchData. Reserve setForbidden strictly for a real 403. Also move the `await res.json()` at :296 behind a res.ok check with a `.catch(() => null)` so a non-JSON body does not decide the state.

findings.title: A failed notification fetch renders "All caught up! You're on top of everything", so a pending team invite that could not load reads as an empty inbox
findings.description: components/shared/notification-center.tsx:289-311 fetches /api/v3/notifications/active. Its catch at :305-308 does `console.error` only, and the finally at :308-310 sets loading false. Nothing sets an error state; there is no error state to set. The render at :483-504 is a three-way ladder: loading, then `count === 0`, then the list. A failed fetch leaves the notifications array untouched (empty on first load) and lands on the middle branch, which prints a Bell glyph, "All caught up!" and "You're on top of everything". The dropdown carries per-user actionable items, not just marketing banners: the same list renders team invites with Accept buttons at :506-540, so a failure hides an action the user needs to take behind a confident claim that there is nothing to take. The poll interval at :313-317 means it self-heals on the next tick, which bounds the exposure but does not remove it, and a persistent 500 or a revoked session keeps it wrong indefinitely.
findings.impact: A user who was invited to a team, or who has an unread staff notification, is told they have nothing waiting. Invites have expiry windows, so a missed one is a real loss rather than a cosmetic one. The copy compounds it by being maximally confident, and it is the only place in the product that uses an exclamation mark and a platitude, which is exactly the voice the project rules out.
findings.recommendation: Add an `error` state to components/shared/notification-center.tsx set in the catch at :305 and on a non-ok response, and render a fourth branch before the `count === 0` branch at :491: a muted line reading "Couldn't load notifications" with a small text button that recalls fetchNotifications. Keep the empty branch for a genuine empty response, and rewrite its copy in the house voice while you are in there: "Nothing waiting" with "Invites, scan alerts and staff notices land here." instead of "All caught up! / You're on top of everything".

findings.title: Both privacy controls in the scan actions menu fail silently: the publicly-listed toggle rolls back with no message and "Make private" leaves the label unchanged, so the user cannot tell what their scan's visibility is
findings.description: components/scanner/scan-actions-menu.tsx:309-328 (`toggleSharePubliclyListed`) is the only optimistic mutation in the codebase (`setSharePubliclyListed(next); // optimistic` at :313). Its rollback is correct in mechanics and silent in effect: `if (!res.ok) setSharePubliclyListed(previous)` at :323 and the same in the catch at :325, with nothing set anywhere that the UI could render. The switch animates on, then animates back, and that is the entire feedback. `togglePrivacy` at :330-348 is the sibling: on a non-ok response it simply does not call `onPrivacyChanged`, and its catch at :344-346 carries the comment "Silently fail, matching requestShare's existing behavior"; the menu item label at :589-596 is derived from `currentIsPublic`, so after the spinner stops it reads exactly as it did before the click. `requestShare` at :289-306 is the third: on a non-ok response the share modal simply never opens. AUDIT-011#form-01 filed the same class for five other handlers including this file's Delete action at :505, and named app/shares/page.tsx:100-121's separate copy of the publicly-listed toggle, but not these three.
findings.impact: These are visibility controls on security scan results. A user who turns off public listing, or switches a scan to private, and whose request fails, is left with no signal at all and a reasonable belief that the change took: an optimistic toggle that snaps back within a few hundred milliseconds is easy to miss entirely, and the privacy menu item gives no motion to miss. The scan stays publicly listed and reachable at /host/<hostname> and via any share link. A silently reverted privacy control is worse than one that refuses loudly, because the user stops checking.
findings.recommendation: Add a shared `actionError: string | null` to components/scanner/scan-actions-menu.tsx, set it in the non-ok and catch branches of all three handlers (:289-306, :309-328, :330-348), and render it as an inline destructive line inside the menu, matching the pattern already used for githubError at :355-360. Copy: "Couldn't change this scan's visibility. It is still public." The state of a privacy control must never be changed on screen without server confirmation or an explicit failure message; if the optimistic update at :313 is kept, pair the rollback with the message rather than letting it be the only signal.

findings.title: The extension popup has no first-run empty state and repeats the web app's "no findings equals clean" conflation with "No vulnerabilities detected."
findings.description: Two gaps in the popup's state set. First, the history sections at extension/src/popup/popup.ts:216-247 are each wrapped in `siteHistory.length > 0 ? ... : null` and `otherHistory.length > 0 ? ... : null`, so a freshly installed extension renders only the connect pill, the scan button and the footer: nothing tells the user what the panel will contain once they scan, and nothing distinguishes "you have not scanned anything" from "the history fetch failed" (extension/src/lib/scan.ts's refreshHistoryFromServer is called at :1054 and its failure just yields an empty array). Second, the result panel's zero-findings branch at :415 renders the bare string "No vulnerabilities detected.", and :381 adds a green `badge clean` chip when `r.summary.total === 0`. That is the same unqualified all-clear as the web app's, on a surface whose ScanResult also carries the `incomplete` field described in state-01, which the popup likewise never reads.
findings.impact: A first-run user sees an almost blank panel and cannot tell whether the extension is working. On the result side, an extension popup is the fastest, most casual read of a scan in the product, which makes it the place where a false all-clear is most likely to be believed and acted on. The `clean` badge is a positive assertion rendered from an absence.
findings.recommendation: Add an else branch to the history block at extension/src/popup/popup.ts:216 that renders a short prompt in the existing `.section` styling: "No scans yet. Hit Scan this page and the result lands here, with a trend arrow once you scan the same site twice." Add a distinct branch for a failed history load so it does not share that copy. Change the zero-findings copy at :415 to "No findings from the checks that ran." and gate the `clean` badge at :381 on `!r.incomplete?.length`, rendering a warn-toned chip naming the branches that did not finish when it is non-empty, which is the same fix as state-01 on the smaller surface.

findings.title: The coverage gate is dead: CI runs `npm run test` without coverage, and the only command that enforces thresholds currently exits non-zero with eight failures
findings.description: The CI test job runs `npm run test` (ci.yml:107), which is `vitest run` with no --coverage, and the comment two lines above it says so outright: 'Coverage is informational only for now; thresholds are enforced locally via npm run test:coverage'. So nothing in CI checks coverage. Meanwhile the local command that is supposed to be the gate is red. I ran `vitest run --coverage` on the current tree: all 356 files and 10,158 tests pass, but the threshold check reports eight errors and exits non-zero. lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit.ts is at 88.23% lines against a 90% threshold and 85.71% statements against 90%; lib/config/client-constants.ts is at 48.48% against 90% on both; lib/updater/copy-with-excludes.ts misses its 100% functions and statements thresholds; lib/updater/job-store.ts misses its 100% functions threshold; app/api/v3/assets/route.ts is at 68% branches against 70%. tests/README.md documents a workflow ('run npm run test:coverage, read the per-file percentage, set the threshold a few points below it') that no one can follow while the command fails for unrelated files.
findings.impact: The project has a written coverage policy, a per-file threshold map, and a documented workflow, and none of it is enforced anywhere. Coverage on a security-critical file can fall to zero between releases and nothing reports it. Worse, because the gate command is already red, a developer who runs it learns to ignore its output, so it will not catch a real regression even when someone does run it. This is also why the 0% files in cov-01, cov-02, and cov-06 could land: nothing was watching. Concretely: deleting every test for lib/updater/checksum.ts, the stated security control for the self-update flow, drops it from its declared 100 percent threshold to 0 percent and CI stays green. tests/README.md:41 tells contributors a coverage regression fails the build, which is not true of any job that actually runs, and the stale coverage/ directory (2026-08-13) means nobody sees the real number either.
findings.recommendation: Fix the eight stale thresholds in vitest.config.ts to the measured values (rate-limit.ts to 85/85, client-constants.ts to 45, copy-with-excludes.ts functions to 90, job-store.ts functions to 90, assets/route.ts branches to 65), then change ci.yml:107 to `npm run test:coverage` so the gate runs on every PR. Once green, add a modest global threshold under coverage.thresholds (lines 75, branches 65 against the measured 81.02% / 71.24%) so a new untested file drags the global number down instead of being silently exempt.

findings.title: Coverage measures only .ts, so 419 React files and 95,294 lines are invisible, and with environment:node and no jsdom the suite cannot render a component even if someone wrote a test
findings.category: whole layer outside the test harness
findings.description: coverage.include is ["lib/**/*.ts", "app/**/*.ts"] (vitest.config.ts:31). The glob `*.ts` does not match `.tsx`. The coverage run confirms it: exactly 412 files are measured, which is 250 lib/*.ts plus 162 app/*.ts, and not one .tsx. Unmeasured: 266 components/*.tsx plus 47 components/*.ts (313 files, 65,147 lines), 152 app/*.tsx (30,147 lines), and 1 lib/*.tsx. Separately, test.environment is "node" (line 23) and package.json lists no jsdom, no happy-dom, and no @testing-library/* in either dependencies or devDependencies, so no test can mount a React tree at all. The eight files under tests/components/ cover 8 of 313 component files (2.6%), and six of those eight targets are plain .ts utility modules (queue-status-utils.ts, settings-registry-utils.ts, use-unsaved-changes-warning.ts, admin/utils.ts, schedule-time-utils.ts, ai-review-gate.ts); only danger-score-trend.tsx and auth-provider.tsx are .tsx, and those tests can reach only their non-rendering exports.
findings.impact: Every form-validation rule, every conditional that hides a paid feature behind a plan check, every auth-state branch in a client component, and every result renderer is untested and unmeasured. A regression that shows a Pro-only control to a free user, or that renders a scan as clean when findings exist, reaches production with a green CI. The measurement gap makes it worse than it looks: the 81.02% headline reads as broad health while a third of the app's lines are simply not in the denominator.
findings.recommendation: Two steps, and the first is cheap. Change coverage.include to ["lib/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "app/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "components/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "middleware.ts"] so the real denominator is visible even before any test is written; expect the headline to drop, which is the accurate number. Then add jsdom plus @testing-library/react as devDependencies and an environmentMatchGlobs entry mapping tests/components/** to jsdom, and start with the highest-risk components: components/scanner/scan-form.tsx, the plan-gated controls, and the shared ScanResultDetail renderer.

findings.title: middleware.ts, the 546-line request gate for every route in the app, sits outside coverage.include so its 365-line test suite produces no measurable coverage
findings.description: middleware.ts is 546 lines and lives at the repo root, so it matches neither "lib/**/*.ts" nor "app/**/*.ts" in coverage.include (vitest.config.ts:31). It does not appear in the coverage-summary.json I generated: filtering the 412 measured files for 'middleware' returns nothing. tests/middleware.test.ts exists and is 365 lines, so the file is not untested, but there is no way to tell which of its branches the suite reaches. This matters because middleware is where the public-path allowlist and the auth redirect live, and AUDIT-012 filed three separate HIGH findings against that allowlist (authz-01, authz-02, authz-03: the public host report API, all three staff-oidc endpoints, and the public contact form all missing from PUBLIC_PATHS, each breaking the feature for logged-out visitors). lib/config/public-paths.ts reports 100% statements but only 1 statement, because it is a data table: line coverage says nothing about whether the table is correct. instrumentation.ts is excluded outright (vitest.config.ts:38) and is 3,639 lines holding 72 CREATE TABLE and 97 CREATE INDEX statements.
findings.impact: The single file that decides whether a request is authenticated, redirected, or allowed through unauthenticated has an unknown tested fraction. A branch added to it, for example a new public path or a new bypass condition, is invisible to both the coverage report and to a reviewer asking 'is this covered?'. The AUDIT-012 authz findings show the concrete cost: three features silently broken for every logged-out visitor and crawler, shipped past a green suite.
findings.recommendation: Add "middleware.ts" to coverage.include in vitest.config.ts so the file is measured, then read the resulting branch percentage and fill the gaps in tests/middleware.test.ts. Separately, add a table-driven test that walks every entry in PUBLIC_PATHS and asserts each named route file actually exists, and walks every route.ts the app serves unauthenticated and asserts it is listed, which is the drift the three AUDIT-012 authz findings all were.

findings.title: The two Stripe events that reverse money, charge.refunded and charge.dispute.created, are the only two of nine handled event types with no test
findings.description: app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts measures 68.18% statements and 58.3% branches over 264 statements. The handler switch has nine cases: checkout.session.completed (183), customer.subscription.created (296), updated (475), deleted (626), invoice.payment_succeeded (686), invoice.payment_failed (770), payment_intent.succeeded (803), charge.refunded (940), charge.dispute.created (982). Extracting the event-type string literals from tests/app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.test.ts yields eight, and the two missing are charge.refunded and charge.dispute.created. Those two branches each call reverseAiCreditPurchase, reverseGithubCreditPurchase, and reverseBrowserbaseCreditPurchase in a Promise.all (lines 958-962 and 997-1001). The reversal functions themselves are well covered (lib/billing/ai-usage.ts 98.27%, browserbase-usage.ts 100%, github-review-usage.ts 98.59%), so what is untested is the wiring: the partial-refund early-break at line 947, the payment_intent extraction that must handle both a string and an expanded object (lines 953-956 and 989-992), and the dispatch itself. lib/billing/stripe-webhook-setup.ts:29-30 does register both events with Stripe, and tests/lib/billing/stripe-webhook-setup.test.ts covers REQUIRED_EVENTS, but nothing asserts the REQUIRED_EVENTS list and the switch labels agree.
findings.impact: If either case label is renamed, or the payment_intent extraction breaks when Stripe sends an expanded object rather than a string, a refunded or charged-back customer keeps every AI token, GitHub review token, and Browserbase second they paid for. That is direct revenue loss on the exact transactions where the money has already left, and it is silent: the webhook still returns 200, the reversal functions still pass their own unit tests, and the only evidence is a console.log that never fires.
findings.recommendation: Add two describes to tests/app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.test.ts. For charge.refunded assert: refunded:false logs and reverses nothing; refunded:true with a string payment_intent calls all three reverse functions with that id; refunded:true with an expanded payment_intent object extracts .id. For charge.dispute.created assert the same extraction and the three reverse calls. Add one drift test asserting the set of `case` labels in the route equals REQUIRED_EVENTS in lib/billing/stripe-webhook-setup.ts, so registering an event without handling it (or vice versa) fails.

findings.title: The Browserbase client is at 16.87% and page-screenshot at 7.44%, leaving the session-teardown call that stops a paid third-party meter untested at all three of its call sites
findings.description: lib/browserbase/client.ts is the largest sub-50% file in the tree: 243 statements at 16.87% statements / 27.05%-adjacent branches, 662 lines, ten exports (createBrowserSession:112, getBrowserSession:165, getBrowserLiveUrls:189, endBrowserSession:213, pickLiveViewerUrl:273, isBrowserBaseConfigured:279, navigateBrowserSession:298, openCdpPageSession:416, getBrowserSessionLogs:573, parseNetworkRequests:594). tests/lib/browserbase/ contains one file, concurrency-queue.test.ts, which tests a different module. lib/browserbase/network-capture.ts is at 27.05% and lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts at 7.44% (94 statements, 21.42% functions). endBrowserSession has three call sites that must run or the session keeps billing: app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:199 (the create-failed cleanup) and :325 (explicit delete), lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts:560, and lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:267. None of those teardown paths is exercised.
findings.impact: Browserbase is a real paid third party billed by session-seconds, and the credit ledger charges the user for it. A regression where the teardown is skipped on an error path (the exact shape of the route.ts:199 cleanup) leaks a live session per failed scan. Nothing in the product notices: the scan reports a normal failure, the user is charged whatever the ledger recorded, and the overage shows up on the operator's Browserbase invoice at the end of the month. sessions/route.ts:199 already writes `.catch(() => {})`, so even a thrown teardown error is swallowed.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/browserbase/client.test.ts mocking the Browserbase HTTP boundary and assert createBrowserSession sends keepAlive:true, endBrowserSession issues the delete for the right id, and openCdpPageSession honours its timeout argument. Then add teardown assertions at the three call sites: in tests/app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.test.ts assert endBrowserSession is called when the post-create work throws, and add a page-screenshot test asserting endBrowserSession runs in the failure path as well as the success path.

findings.title: lib/api/api-keys.ts is at 48.4% and its validateApiKey tests cover IP binding, ToS gating, and scope migration but never the account-state gate, which is the exact branch AUDIT-012 found missing
findings.category: auth gate tested around its weak point
findings.description: lib/api/api-keys.ts measures 48.4% statements over 188 statements. It exports nine functions: generateApiKey (64), passesApiKeyIpBinding (213), validateApiKey (326), checkRateLimit (477), peekRateLimit (570), recordUsage (605), getUserApiKeys (615), revokeApiKey (629), rotateApiKey (639). tests/lib/api/api-keys.test.ts has four describes and seventeen tests: one for passesApiKeyIpBinding and three narrow integration slices of validateApiKey, named for IP binding, terms-of-service gating, and the scopes-column migration. generateApiKey, checkRateLimit, peekRateLimit, getUserApiKeys, and recordUsage have no direct test. This is the file AUDIT-012#auth-02 filed a HIGH against at this exact line: 'Suspending an account does not stop its API keys: validateApiKey never checks users.disabled_at'. The existing tests prove the point about where coverage is aimed: three separate describes cover peripheral conditions of the same function while the account-state condition was never asserted at all.
findings.impact: API keys are the unattended auth path, so a gate failure here is the one least likely to be noticed by a human. The concrete instance already happened: a banned user kept full API access, including scan quota consumption, until an audit found it. checkRateLimit at line 477 is the per-key daily quota, and it having no direct test means the same class of gap sits on the metering side too.
findings.recommendation: Extend tests/lib/api/api-keys.test.ts with a describe per account-state condition on validateApiKey: a key whose owning user has disabled_at set must be rejected, a key past expires_at must be rejected, a revoked key must be rejected, and a key whose user row is missing must be rejected. Add a describe for checkRateLimit asserting it increments once, blocks at the cap, and rolls over on a new day. Make the disabled_at case the first test so the regression AUDIT-012 found cannot come back.

findings.title: The browser extension is 7,048 lines across 25 TypeScript files with zero tests, no test script, and a CI job that only typechecks, formats, and builds it
findings.category: shipped product with no test suite
findings.description: extension/src/ holds 25 .ts files totalling 7,048 lines. `git ls-files 'extension/**'` matches zero files named *.test.* or *.spec.*, and extension/package.json declares no "test" script: its scripts are dev, build, build:chrome, build:firefox, icons, package, package:source, clean, typecheck, format, format:check. The CI extension job (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs npm ci, typecheck, format:check, and build for Chrome and Firefox, and nothing else. The untested surface includes the pieces that make security decisions: lib/auth.ts (74 lines, API-key handling), lib/api.ts (259 lines, the calls to the VulnRadar API), lib/storage.ts (249), lib/scan-target.ts (62), lib/url-patterns.ts (108), plus popup/popup.ts at 1,116 lines and background/service-worker.ts. lib/scanner/scan-target-classify.ts in the main app carries an explicit comment that 'the browser extension keeps its own small copy of classifyScanTarget (it's a separate build)', so there is a deliberate duplicate of classification logic on both sides with a test on neither (the app-side copy measures 37.14% statements / 16% branches).
findings.impact: The extension is a published Chrome and Firefox Web Store product with a review and rollback cycle measured in days, so a regression is far more expensive to correct than a web deploy. A typecheck-and-build gate cannot catch a wrong URL pattern that scans the wrong host, a storage change that drops a stored API key, or a classification drift where the extension and the app disagree about what a given URL is. Because the extension holds a user's API key, an api.ts regression that sends it to the wrong origin would also ship green.
findings.recommendation: Add vitest (or node:test, matching the CLI's pattern) to extension/package.json with a "test" script, and add an extension test step to the CI extension job so it gates merges the same way the app's does. Start with the pure modules where a test is cheap and the failure is expensive: url-patterns.ts, scan-target.ts, format.ts, categories.ts, plans.ts. Then add a shared fixture list of URLs asserted identically against lib/scanner/scan-target-classify.ts in the app and the extension's own copy, so the two builds cannot drift apart unnoticed.

findings.title: lib/scanner/protocol-findings.ts is at 0% while the banner parser it consumes is at 85%, so the entire ssh/smtp/imap/pop3/mongodb scan branch can report clean with no test failing
findings.description: lib/scanner/protocol-findings.ts measures 0% statements / 0% branches / 0% functions (25 statements, 265 lines) and there is no tests/lib/scanner/protocol-findings.test.ts. Its header states it holds the 'Vulnerability builders for the non-HTTP protocol scan branch in execute-scan.ts (a URL whose scheme is ssh://, smtp://, imap://, pop3://, or mongodb://)' and that 'Finding IDs are derived deterministically from a checkId prefix + URL (see generateId), so the prefixes here MUST stay stable: changing one changes the ID of an existing finding type and breaks diffing between a user's older and newer scans of the same target'. The parsing layer beneath it is covered: lib/scanner/protocols/banner.ts is at 85.52%, with dedicated suites at tests/lib/scanner/protocols/banner-analysis, banner-tls-and-capability, and mongo-probe. So the suite proves the banner is parsed correctly and proves nothing about whether a finding is produced from it. For contrast, the three other low-coverage files under lib/scanner/checks/ (email.ts 3.03%, active-probes.ts 16.66%, reputation.ts 25%) are deliberate placeholders whose detectors return null, and are correctly not a gap.
findings.impact: Two silent failures. A regression that drops a finding builder makes a protocol scan of a genuinely vulnerable host report clean, and the user has no signal that anything is wrong because the scan completes normally. A regression that changes an idPrefix silently breaks the scan-to-scan diff the file's own comment warns about, so the history view shows a resolved finding plus a new finding instead of one persistent one, in a product whose value proposition is tracking a host over time.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/scanner/protocol-findings.test.ts feeding a fixture BannerResult and MongoAuthProbeResult for each protocol and asserting: the expected finding is produced for a vulnerable banner and none for a clean one, and the finding id for a fixed (checkId, url) pair matches a hard-coded expected string. Pinning the ids in the assertion is what makes the prefix stability the header demands actually enforceable.

findings.title: No test in the repo executes real SQL: 192 of 356 test files mock the pg pool and there is no test database, so column typos, broken CTEs, missing row locks, and schema drift are all invisible
findings.description: Scope: the whole suite plus vitest.config.ts and the schema. 192 of the 356 test files contain `vi.mock("@/lib/database/db")`, and 195 reference a fake pool shape. Nothing in the repo starts a Postgres: no docker-compose service for tests, no testcontainers dependency, and the only tests that read DATABASE_URL do so to assert configuration behaviour, not to connect. Even tests/lib/database/db.test.ts, which cannot mock the module it tests, mocks one level lower at pg's Pool class with a FakePool. The result is that every SQL string in lib/ and app/ is treated as an opaque token: a mocked client returns whatever the test scripted regardless of what the query says, so a wrong column name, a dropped WHERE clause, a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` that lost its lock, or a CTE that no longer returns its RETURNING row all pass. instrumentation.ts, the canonical schema at 3,639 lines with 72 CREATE TABLE and 97 CREATE INDEX statements, is explicitly excluded from coverage (vitest.config.ts:38) and only two test files reference it at all. There is also a documented contradiction: CLAUDE.md lists 'Mocking the database in tests' under What to avoid, while tests/README.md instructs 'Mock at the network and database boundary, not below it', and the suite follows the README.
findings.impact: This is the structural reason a whole class of AUDIT-012 findings existed. Credit-ledger atomicity, the nine missing indexes in AUDIT-012#perf-15 that force full scans inside the cleanup transaction, and the function-wrapped columns in AUDIT-012#perf-16 that defeat an index are all properties of SQL text that the suite by construction cannot evaluate. The failure mode in production is a query that throws at runtime on a column that no longer exists, or an aggregate that returns silently wrong numbers, after a green CI run and a green deploy.
findings.recommendation: Do not rewrite 192 files. Add one narrow integration suite gated on an env var, tests/integration/, that spins Postgres in the CI test job as a services: container, runs instrumentation.ts to build the schema, and exercises only the queries where correctness cannot be asserted any other way: the credit ledger reversals, reserveConcurrentScanSlot, incrementDailyCountCapped, and lib/database/cleanup.ts. Then resolve the doc contradiction by amending CLAUDE.md to match what the project actually does, so the next contributor is not choosing between two rules.

findings.title: components/admin/config.ts is a graveyard of superseded copies: its tab table lists 5 of the panel's 13 tabs and its action-label map is a stale subset of one inlined in app/admin/page.tsx
findings.category: superseded dead code that still looks authoritative
findings.description: Four of the eight exports in components/admin/config.ts are dead, and each has a live replacement that was inlined into app/admin/page.tsx instead of being edited here. (1) ADMIN_TABS (declared line 7, block 6-17) declares five tabs: users, teams, notifications, admins, audit. The live tab set is built at app/admin/page.tsx:861 as ALL_ADMIN_TABS by flattening NAV_GROUPS, and it drives every render path: the nav at :1004 and :1077, the header at :1036, the role-fallback redirect at :889-892, and the per-tab render switch at :1182-1187, which alone names access-rules, blocked-data, content, security-alerts, settings and broadcast. (2) ACTION_LABELS (declared line 262, block 261-288) maps 25 admin action names to success-toast text. app/admin/page.tsx:530-561 declares a local const labels with the same 25 entries verbatim plus six more (notify_account_changes, toggle_ai_ban, verify_email, unverify_email, send_notification, send_email) and uses it at :566 via showToast(labels[action] || 'Action completed.'). The exported copy is a stale subset. (3) DEFAULT_AUDIT_PAGE_SIZE and DEFAULT_STAFF_PAGE_SIZE (lines 330-331), replaced by the inline literal in useState(10) at app/admin/page.tsx:210. DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE on line 329 is also unreferenced but shares a name with the live CONFIG_PAGINATION_DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE, so I left it out of the count. The four names occur nowhere in the repo but their own declarations; config.ts is imported four times and only for ACTION_META and PASSWORD_GATED_ACTIONS. The same pattern appears one file over: parseAdminHash and buildAdminHash at components/admin/utils.ts:234-269 parse and build '#users/user-12' hashes for a hash-routing scheme the panel abandoned; state now goes to query params through updateUrlWithUser at app/admin/page.tsx:255-274, which calls setQueryParam/setQueryParams. Neither helper has a caller anywhere, including tests, and parseAdminHash:246 hardcodes the same stale five-tab whitelist. Total: 42 lines in config.ts (6-17, 261-288, 330-331) plus 36 lines in utils.ts (234-269), 78 lines.
findings.impact: A developer adding an admin tab or a new admin action reaches for components/admin/config.ts, the file literally named 'Admin panel configuration - tabs, action metadata, filters', edits ADMIN_TABS or ACTION_LABELS, and nothing happens: the real copies are inline in app/admin/page.tsx. Adding a label to ACTION_LABELS is the likeliest version of this, because a new admin action needs one and the map here looks like the place. The result is a new action that silently falls back to the generic 'Action completed.' toast. The same trap catches anyone adding a deep link, who will find and extend parseAdminHash rather than updateUrlWithUser. This is dead code that is actively misleading, not merely unused.
findings.recommendation: Pick one direction and apply it to the whole file. Preferred: move the live copies down into components/admin/config.ts, that is, replace the local labels const at app/admin/page.tsx:530-561 with an import of ACTION_LABELS after adding its six missing entries, and move ALL_ADMIN_TABS/NAV_GROUPS out of app/admin/page.tsx:861 into ADMIN_TABS with the full 13-tab set. Otherwise delete ADMIN_TABS (6-17) with its now-unused lucide-react and AdminTab imports on lines 3-4, ACTION_LABELS (261-288), and lines 330-331. Separately delete parseAdminHash and buildAdminHash (components/admin/utils.ts:234-269) either way, since query-param routing has no use for them.

findings.title: Twenty-seven of the seventy-one runtime dependencies have zero imports anywhere in the app, dragging 78 transitive packages and 77.6 MB into the production dependency graph
findings.description: AUDIT-012#fe-13 found two of these (jspdf, jspdf-autotable). Extending that grep to all 86 declared packages, ripgrep for any quoted specifier (static import, `require(`, dynamic `import(`, type-only import) across app/, lib/, components/, tests/, scripts/, middleware.ts and every config file, with node_modules/.next/coverage/marketing/extension/cli/audits excluded, returns package.json itself as the only hit for twenty-five entries. Three groups, each with a different history. (1) Vercel AI SDK: `ai` (package.json:82), `@ai-sdk/anthropic` (:48) and `@ai-sdk/openai` (:49). `git log -S 'from "ai"' -- lib app components` returns nothing, so they were never wired in: the app talks to providers over raw fetch through lib/ai/provider.ts and hand-rolls SSE in lib/ai/anthropic.ts:212 (`createAnthropicSseTranscoder`, consumed at app/api/v3/ai/chat/route.ts:342). The 19 apparent hits for `ai` are the string literal 'ai' used as a profile tab id (app/profile/page.tsx:79) and as a `scan_tags.source` value (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:878). (2) `jsonwebtoken` (:91) and `@types/jsonwebtoken` (:122): the only mentions in source are a comment at lib/scanner/checks/code.ts:1736 and a UI label at lib/scanner/checks/page-checks/jwt.ts:140. The app's one real JWT verification, lib/auth/staff-oidc.ts:24, imports `jose`. (3) shadcn/v0 scaffold leftovers from the initial commit 26e639c5, none of which ever got a components/ui wrapper (there is no command.tsx, calendar.tsx, carousel.tsx, drawer.tsx, resizable.tsx, input-otp.tsx, sonner.tsx, form.tsx, accordion.tsx, collapsible.tsx, context-menu.tsx, hover-card.tsx, menubar.tsx, navigation-menu.tsx, radio-group.tsx, toggle.tsx or toggle-group.tsx in components/ui/): `@hookform/resolvers` (:50), `@neondatabase/serverless` (:51, named only as prose in app/docs/architecture/page.tsx), `@radix-ui/react-accordion` (:52), `-aspect-ratio` (:54), `-collapsible` (:57), `-context-menu` (:58), `-hover-card` (:61), `-menubar` (:63), `-navigation-menu` (:64), `-radio-group` (:67), `-toggle` (:76), `-toggle-group` (:77), `cmdk` (:86), `date-fns` (:87), `embla-carousel-react` (:88), `input-otp` (:89), `react-day-picker` (:101), `react-hook-form` (:103, no `useForm` or `FormProvider` anywhere), `react-resizable-panels` (:106), `sonner` (:110, the app uses components/ui/toaster.tsx over @radix-ui/react-toast) and `vaul` (:116). Separately `tslib` (:115) was added by commit b8bc8f83 'to resolve import error in react-remove-scroll'; react-remove-scroll@2.7.2 still declares `tslib: ^2.1.0` itself, so the direct entry buys nothing and only freezes the hoisted copy at an exact 2.8.1. Walking the lockfile closure, these twenty-five roots plus the two jspdf packages are the sole path to 78 packages totalling 77.6 MB installed, the largest being jspdf 28.8 MB, date-fns 10.4 MB, ai 6.4 MB, html2canvas 3.2 MB, @ai-sdk/openai 2.8 MB, @ai-sdk/anthropic 2.1 MB, dompurify 1.7 MB, pako 1.6 MB, undici 1.6 MB, canvg 1.3 MB and core-js 1.3 MB. core-js is also one of only three packages in the entire tree with `hasInstallScript: true`.
findings.impact: Every production install and every Docker image layer carries 78 packages that no line of code can reach, which is 78 more npm accounts whose compromise would land executable code in the runtime of a security product. core-js arrives with a postinstall script purely because jspdf wants canvg. Operationally the list also misleads: a reader of package.json reasonably concludes there is a PDF export path, a Vercel AI SDK integration and a Neon serverless driver, and will go looking for all three. The jsonwebtoken entry is the sharpest edge, because a contributor adding a signed token has a JWT library already installed and one grep away that is not the vetted one (`jose`) the auth layer standardised on, so the wrong library gets used with no review signal.
findings.recommendation: Delete those twenty-five entries, the two jspdf entries from AUDIT-012#fe-13 (package.json:92-93), and `@types/jsonwebtoken` (package.json:122) from `dependencies`/`devDependencies`, and drop `tslib` (:115) since react-remove-scroll pulls it transitively. Update the stale comment at tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8 that still references jspdf being in package.json. Also prune .github/dependabot.yml, whose `security` group (lines 59, 61, 64) and `scanning` group watch several of these. Regenerate package-lock.json on Linux or graft the entries by hand, per the lockfile-platform constraint this repo already documents: a Windows regeneration strips the Linux native bindings this lockfile currently has intact.

findings.title: vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 sit in dependencies, pulling 82 packages and a 20 MB rolldown native binary into the production graph, and the Dockerfile never passes --omit=dev so the devDependencies ship as well
findings.description: This extends AUDIT-012#fe-13, which named the misplacement but attributed the cost to `npm ci --omit=dev` in the Docker build. This Dockerfile does not use that flag. Two separate mechanisms compound. First, `vitest` 4.1.11 (package.json:117) and `@vitest/coverage-v8` 4.1.11 (:81) are declared under `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`. Resolving the lockfile closure of the `dependencies` list with and without those two roots, 82 packages / 42.9 MB are reachable only through them: `@rolldown/binding-win32-x64-msvc` at 20.4 MB (on a Linux runner the equivalent `@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-gnu`), `vite` 8.2.2 with its own nested `lightningcss` 1.33.0 and full 11-platform native matrix at 9.1 MB for the local binary, plus @babel/types, @babel/parser, rolldown, magic-string, magicast, istanbul-reports, chai and the rest of the runner. That second lightningcss is a straight duplicate: @tailwindcss/node 4.3.3 already brings lightningcss 1.32.0 with its own full platform matrix, so the tree carries two copies of an 11-binary native package. Second, Dockerfile:24 runs `npm ci --silent --ignore-scripts` with no `--omit=dev`, and Dockerfile:77 then does `COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/node_modules ./node_modules` into the runner stage. Measuring the lockfile's dev-flagged entries on disk gives 89 MB that is copied verbatim into the published ghcr image: typescript 23.2 MB, prettier 9.5 MB, lightningcss-win32-x64-msvc 9.1 MB, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 3.9 MB, axe-core 2.9 MB, eslint 2.8 MB, es-abstract 2.7 MB, @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin 2.0 MB and so on.
findings.impact: The published ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar image ships a full test runner, a bundler with two native binaries, a TypeScript compiler, ESLint and Prettier into the runtime a self-hoster exposes to the internet. That is roughly 130 MB of pure image weight plus a much larger attack surface than the app needs, on a container that runs as a long-lived network service. It also means the fix AUDIT-012#fe-13 recommended (move the two packages to devDependencies) would not by itself shrink the image at all, because the Docker build installs dev dependencies unconditionally.
findings.recommendation: Two changes, both one line. Move `vitest` and `@vitest/coverage-v8` from `dependencies` to `devDependencies` in package.json. Then change Dockerfile:24 to a two-stage install: keep `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the builder (the build needs typescript and the tailwind toolchain) and, in the runner stage, replace the `COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules` at Dockerfile:77 with a separate `npm ci --omit=dev --ignore-scripts` layer, or add `RUN npm prune --omit=dev` in the builder after `npm run build` and copy the pruned tree. Either removes both the 89 MB of dev tooling and the 42.9 MB vitest subtree from the shipped image.

findings.title: Node 22.11.0 and Postgres 16.4 base images are roughly a year of security releases stale, and dependabot.yml has no docker ecosystem to ever bump them
findings.category: stale base image, no update automation
findings.description: Dockerfile:11 and Dockerfile:62 both pin `node:22.11.0-alpine`. Node 22.11.0 is the release that promoted the 22 line to LTS; the 22 line is currently at 22.23.0 (the Node running in this very workspace reports v22.23.0), so the published image is twelve patch releases behind, a window that includes every Node security release cut since. docker-compose.yml:18 and docker-compose.dev.yml:22 pin `postgres:16.4-alpine`, which is roughly a year of Postgres minor releases behind on the 16 line. Both pins are deliberate and commented (Dockerfile:6-10, docker-compose.yml:13-15 both say to bump intentionally and offer digest-pinning instructions), which is the right instinct, but .github/dependabot.yml declares exactly two ecosystems: `npm` at directory `/` (line 4) and `github-actions` (line 83). There is no `docker` ecosystem entry, so nothing ever opens the bump PR the comments assume a human will remember to open. The same gap covers `gcr.io/projectsigstore/cosign:v2.4.1`, the third pinned image, at Dockerfile:60.
findings.impact: The container a self-hoster pulls from ghcr, and the one this SaaS itself deploys, runs a Node runtime and an Alpine userland with a year of published, unpatched CVEs, on a product whose whole pitch is finding unpatched software on other people's sites. The scanner's own `software-inventory` check would flag this stack on a customer's site. Because the pin is manual and unautomated, the drift only grows: it has already gone from 'pinned last release' to 'twelve patches behind' with nobody noticing.
findings.recommendation: Add a third block to .github/dependabot.yml: `- package-ecosystem: "docker"` with `directory: "/"` (which covers Dockerfile) and a second entry for the compose files, on the same weekly schedule and with the same labels as the npm block. Then take the first PR it opens to move Dockerfile:11 and :62 to the current node:22.x-alpine patch and docker-compose.yml:18 / docker-compose.dev.yml:22 to the current postgres:16.x-alpine.

findings.title: The overrides block forces ESLint 10 into three eslint-config-next plugins whose peer ranges stop at ESLint 9, and eslint.config.mjs already documents one total lint crash this caused
findings.category: peer conflict papered over by an override
findings.description: package.json:130 declares `eslint: ^10.9.0`. eslint-config-next 16.3.2 (package.json:131) declares `peerDependencies: { eslint: ">=9.0.0" }`, which ESLint 10 satisfies, but its own hard dependencies do not: the lockfile shows `node_modules/eslint-config-next/node_modules/eslint-plugin-import` 2.32.0 with `peerDependencies.eslint: "^2 || ^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7.2.0 || ^8 || ^9"`, `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` 6.10.2 with `"^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9"`, and `eslint-plugin-react` 7.37.5 with `"^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9.7"`. ESLint 10 is outside all three. The `overrides` block at package.json:146-154 forces it in anyway with three nested `{ "eslint": "$eslint" }` entries, which is what makes `npm ci` resolve instead of throwing ERESOLVE. That override is not cosmetic: eslint.config.mjs:47-55 documents the first thing it broke, in the repo's own words, 'eslint-config-next sets settings.react.version to "detect", which makes eslint-plugin-react probe the filesystem via context.getFilename(). ESLint 10 removed that legacy context method, so detection crashes the whole run', worked around by hardcoding `react: { version: "19.2.8" }` at eslint.config.mjs:55. Two more unguarded uses of removed ESLint 10 context APIs remain in the installed plugin (eslint-plugin-react/lib/rules/forward-ref-uses-ref.js:60 `context.getSourceCode()`, jsx-filename-extension.js:64 `context.getFilename()`); those two rules are off in core-web-vitals today, so they are latent rather than live. Running `npx eslint .` in the current working tree reproduces the failure class end to end: `TypeError: scopeManager.addGlobals is not a function at addDeclaredGlobals (node_modules/eslint/lib/languages/js/source-code/source-code.js:221)`, zero files linted, whole run aborted. To be precise about what that proves: this workspace's node_modules has drifted to eslint 10.8.1 while the lockfile pins 10.9.0, and CI on main is green, so this exact crash is not what CI runs. What it demonstrates is that the plugin set has no floor under it, because ESLint 10 patch releases are free to keep removing legacy APIs that three unsupported plugins still call.
findings.impact: `npm run lint` is a required, merge-blocking CI job (.github/workflows/ci.yml, the `lint` job), and it depends on three plugins that upstream does not claim to support on this ESLint major. When one of them next touches a removed API, lint does not report findings, it aborts with a TypeError and zero files checked. The failure mode is the bad one: a crash that reports no problems reads, to anyone skimming, a lot like a clean run, and the repo has already had to hand-patch one instance of it inside eslint.config.mjs.
findings.recommendation: Pick one of two. Either drop `eslint` back to `^9` in package.json:130 (which is what eslint-config-next 16.3.2's whole plugin set is tested against) and delete the three nested overrides at package.json:146-154, or keep ESLint 10 and stop depending on the unsupported plugins: replace `eslint-config-next/core-web-vitals` in eslint.config.mjs:13 with `@next/eslint-plugin-next`'s recommended rules plus `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` 7.1.1 (which is the one plugin in the set that already declares `^10.0.0` support) and configure jsx-a11y/import rules explicitly or not at all. Whichever is chosen, add a comment to the overrides block naming why it exists, since an override that silences a real peer conflict is invisible once ERESOLVE stops firing.

findings.title: Severity ordering is redeclared in nine private tables under three mutually incompatible numeric conventions, two of which share the identifier SEVERITY_RANK, and the info label already differs between the app and the ~750 public /checks pages
findings.description:
There is a canonical severity ordering: SEVERITY_PRIORITY at lib/config/constants.ts:628 (critical 5, high 4, medium 3, low 2, info 1), consumed with a `b - a` comparator by components/scanner/results-list.tsx:335, app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:236, app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:252 and app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:427. Eight further private tables encode the same idea:

Convention A, critical is 5 down to info is 1 (same as canonical): lib/scanner/dedupe.ts:18 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/reports/compliance-report.ts:37 `SEVERITY_RANK`.
Convention B, critical is 0 up to info is 4 (inverted): lib/ai/scan-summary.ts:47 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/ai/auto-tag-suggest.ts:136 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:78 `SEVERITY_ORDER`, lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 `SEVERITY_ORDER`.
Convention C, info is 0 up to critical is 4 (a third numbering): lib/scanner/software-inventory.ts:715 `SEVERITY_RANK`.

So the identifier `SEVERITY_RANK` means three different things in five files, and the comparator direction flips with it: compliance-report.ts:150 sorts `severityRank(b) - severityRank(a)` while scan-summary.ts:77 and auto-tag-suggest.ts:166 sort `severityRank(a) - severityRank(b)`, and both are correct only for their own table. Lifting either constant into a shared module, or copying a comparator between these files, silently reverses the ordering with no type error, because every table is `Record<Severity, number>`.

The name `SEVERITY_ORDER` is separately overloaded: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:12 exports it as `readonly Severity[]` (consumed by six other components: results-list.tsx:345, dashboard.tsx:428, ai-choice-modal.tsx:154, ai-verify-result-modal.tsx:60, repos/page.tsx:49 and github-scan-result-modal.tsx:59), lib/reports/markdown-report.ts:23 declares another `Severity[]`, and execute-scan.ts:78 / execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 declare it as a numeric Record.

The label layer has already drifted user-visibly. components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:71 (SEVERITY_TONE), lib/reports/markdown-report.ts:31 and lib/reports/compliance-report.ts:29 all label the lowest level "Info". lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:25 labels it "Informational", and that is the SeverityPill rendered on app/checks/[id]/page.tsx and app/tools/api-scanner/page.tsx, which is the ~750-page public SEO surface. There are also two different components exported as `SeverityPill` (components/history/severity-pill.tsx:11, which delegates to severityTone(), and lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:41, which inlines its own hsl alphas of 0.1/0.25 against SEVERITY_TONE's /15 and /40), plus four colour maps: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx SEVERITY_TONE, components/docs/docs-types.ts:75 SEVERITY_COLORS, lib/reports/pdf-report.ts:18 SEVERITY_COLORS as RGB tuples, and lib/config/client-constants.ts:304 SEVERITY_COLORS, which has zero consumers.
findings.impact: Today: the same info-severity finding reads "Info" in the product and "Informational" on the public check pages, and the same severity pill has two different tints depending on which surface renders it. Tomorrow: a developer who consolidates `SEVERITY_RANK` (a natural cleanup, since the name is already shared) or copies a working comparator between two of these files inverts a sort with no compile error, and findings list least-severe-first in a report, an AI summary, or the dedupe winner selection. lib/scanner/dedupe.ts:175 uses its rank to pick which duplicate finding survives, so an inversion there would keep the info-level copy and discard the critical one.
findings.recommendation: Put one table in lib/config/client-constants.ts next to SEVERITY_LEVELS: keep SEVERITY_PRIORITY's convention (critical highest) and export both it and the ordered array.
