findings.recommendation: Add flex-wrap justify-center at line 119, or hide the first and last page buttons below sm.

findings.title: A transient 500 on /api/v3/auth/me logs an authenticated user out of their own profile
findings.description: app/profile/page.tsx:296 redirects to /login on any non-ok response with no 401 check.
findings.impact: A still-authenticated user is bounced to the login screen by a transient server error, which reads as a session bug.
findings.recommendation: Redirect only on 401 and render an error state otherwise.

findings.title: The public scans table uses fixed pixel columns that crush the hostname at tablet widths
findings.description: components/public-scans/public-scans-table.tsx:7 and components/public-scans/public-scan-row.tsx:22 use grid-cols-[1fr_150px_150px_90px] with gap-4, which is 390px of fixed columns plus 48px of gaps. At the sm breakpoint (640px) the Site column collapses to about 120px so nearly every hostname truncates, while 'Verdict' renders the word 'Clean' inside 150px.
findings.impact: The one column carrying the information is starved while two columns hold whitespace, on a public directory page.
findings.recommendation: Use sm:grid-cols-[minmax(0,1fr)_90px_150px_120px], or move the grid to the md breakpoint and keep the stacked layout through tablet.

findings.title: The status poll uses a fixed 2000ms sleep with no early wake, adding up to 2 seconds of dead time after the scan completes
findings.description: The client polls GET /api/v3/scan/status/[id] on a fixed interval from lib/config/config-values.ts:555, with no backoff and no jitter, first poll immediate (app/dashboard/page.tsx:142, sleep at :160). Nothing wakes the loop when the server finishes.
findings.impact: Adds 0 to 2 seconds, averaging about 1, after the server is already done. Minor next to scan-01 but it becomes a third of the remaining wait once that is fixed.
findings.recommendation: Shorten the interval for the first ~10 seconds, or add SSE / long-poll to the status route.

findings.title: EPSS enrichment makes an uncached live FIRST.org call on the blocking path
findings.description: enrichFindingsWithExploitIntel is awaited at lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:720. lib/scanner/cve-enrichment.ts:214 explicitly does not cache EPSS scores across scans, unlike getKevCveIds which has both a memory and a DB cache at :190-210. The call has a 5 second ceiling.
findings.impact: Every scan whose findings name CVEs pays a live external round trip of up to 5 seconds, on the critical path, for data that changes daily at most.
findings.recommendation: Give fetchEpssScores the same memory-plus-DB cache getKevCveIds already has, or move enrichment after the status flip.

findings.title: runSyncChecks executes roughly 310 checks with no event-loop yields, stalling every other in-flight scan and poll
findings.description: lib/scanner/engine.ts:135-214, called from execute-scan.ts:616, runs the entire synchronous check set plus an HTML parse over up to 1MB in one uninterrupted block. In a single persistent Node process this blocks the event loop for every other request.
findings.impact: Estimated 100ms to 2s of blocking CPU per scan, during which every other user's scan I/O and every status poll is stalled. This is a cross-request amplifier, so its cost scales with concurrency rather than being per-scan.
findings.recommendation: Await a macrotask between check categories. Note this is the lowest-confidence item in the latency set: it is bounded from the code structure, not measured. Profile before investing.

findings.title: A blurred full-screen AI modal opens the instant results land, so a finished scan reads as still working
findings.description: app/dashboard/page.tsx:690-692 opens AiChoiceModal on completion, a fixed inset-0 backdrop-blur-xs overlay (components/scanner/ai-choice-modal.tsx:36). Results render underneath but the user must click Skip to see them.
findings.impact: Perceived latency on top of real latency. The scan finishes and the user is shown a blur, which is indistinguishable from more waiting.
findings.recommendation: Do not auto-open on completion. Offer the AI summary as an action on the results view instead, so the payoff of the scan is the first thing visible.

findings.title: The admin mobile Contents pill is z-40 under z-50 save bars, locking admins out of tab switching mid-edit
findings.description: components/admin/shared/admin-mobile-toc.tsx:42 is z-40 while the save bars at components/admin/features/system-settings-manager.tsx:664 and components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:2731 are z-50. On System Settings the TabsList is hidden lg:flex, so that pill is the only mobile tab switcher.
findings.impact: Editing one field on a phone raises the save bar, which covers the pill, which locks the admin out of switching tabs until they save or discard.
findings.recommendation: Raise the pill to z-50 and offset it above the save bar when one is showing.

findings.title: Five different page shells across the public surface, with /pricing hand-rolled and /donate having none
findings.description: PublicPageShell (components/shared/public-page-shell.tsx:32) swaps `isLoggedIn ? <Header/> : <LandingNav/>` at :58, covering /changelog, /compare, /contact, /security, /host/[hostname], /public-scans, /shared/[token]. DocsShell, LegalShell and SeoPageShell all use LandingNav unconditionally. /pricing is hand-rolled and renders <LandingNav /> twice (app/pricing/page.tsx:71 and :150) despite computing isLoggedIn at :66. /donate has no nav, no <main> and no footer at all. LandingNav is itself auth-aware (components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:104), so the swap is redundant.
findings.impact: A signed-in user clicking Changelog, then Docs, then Changelog watches the header change identity twice. /donate is a page with no way off it.
findings.recommendation: Move /pricing and /donate onto PublicPageShell and pick one convention for the signed-in header across the four public shells. The non-negotiable half is shell-01: the skip-link id should live in one shell rather than being forgotten by three.

findings.title: Any non-OK teams response logs a signed-in user out
findings.description: app/teams/page.tsx:109-113 is `if (!res.ok) { router.push("/login"); return; }` with no status check. Every sibling gates on 401 and 403 specifically (app/history/page.tsx:226, app/assets/page.tsx:74). The same shape exists at app/profile/page.tsx:296.
findings.impact: A transient 500, 503 or 429 bounces a still-authenticated user to the login screen, which reads as a session bug and erodes trust in the auth system.
findings.recommendation: Gate the redirect on 401 and 403 and render an error state otherwise, matching the sibling pages.

findings.title: Schema-creation failure during boot is swallowed, letting the app serve traffic against a partially-initialized database
findings.description: instrumentation.ts wraps its entire ~30-table CREATE TABLE sequence (users, sessions, scan_history, billing_history, webhooks, etc.) in one try/catch that, on failure, only console.errors 'Database migration failed' and lets the process continue starting -- unlike the schema-version check just above it, which correctly process.exit(1)s on a mismatch. A transient DB hiccup partway through this sequence (e.g. a connection drop while creating the 15th of 30 tables) leaves some tables missing while the app still comes up and starts accepting requests. The readiness endpoint (/api/v3/health) only verifies pool connectivity and the vulnradar_schema_meta version row, not that every application table actually exists, so it would report 'ok' while requests touching the missing table 500 repeatedly. Evidence: instrumentation.ts line 257 (try open) through line 2978 (`catch (error) { console.error(...); }` with no process.exit), contrasted with the schema-version mismatch check at lines 143-178 which does process.exit(1); app/api/v3/health/route.ts's probeDatabase only SELECTs from vulnradar_schema_meta and never checks for the presence of other tables.
findings.recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Either re-throw/process.exit after logging in that outer catch (matching the schema-version check's behavior), or have the health endpoint additionally verify a canonical set of critical tables exist before reporting 'ok'.

findings.title: No push/proactive alerting on production incidents -- everything is pull-based
findings.description: There is no external error-tracking or alerting SDK wired into the app (no Sentry/Datadog/etc. in package.json). The admin System > Error Logs panel (a genuinely good feature -- see the 'checked and fine' note) captures console.error calls into a searchable table, and /api/v3/health returns 503 on a dead DB, but both are pull: an operator only learns something is wrong by opening /admin or by having set up their own external uptime monitor against /api/v3/health, neither of which this repo configures. A dead scheduled-scans worker, a run of failed Stripe webhooks, or a DB outage at 3am produces rows in a table and a 503 response that nobody is watching until a customer complains. Evidence: package.json has no @sentry/*, datadog, or similar dependency; app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts is a GET/DELETE the admin has to visit -- nothing pushes its contents anywhere.
findings.recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Wire the health endpoint into an external uptime monitor (even a free one) that pages someone on 503, and/or add a lightweight Sentry-style SDK for exception capture with alerting, since the in-app error log viewer is a good diagnostic tool but not an alerting system.

findings.title: innerhtml-xss-sink: innerhtml-xss-sink fires on the textbook-correct DOMPurify.sanitize() pattern
findings.description: The pattern `/\.innerHTML\s*=(?!\s*["'])/g` only excludes assignments of a literal string; it does not exclude `el.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(x)`, which is the exact secure pattern DOMPurify's own documentation recommends for fixing this precise class of XSS sink. The check requires 2+ matches, which any page sanitizing more than one element (e.g. rendering a list of user comments) will easily produce. Verified: `el1.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(c.html); el2.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(c.html2);` produces 2 matches, meeting the threshold. Trigger: Any comment section, markdown preview, or CMS block renderer that does `element.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(content)` for two or more elements on the page — a very common, deliberately secure coding pattern.
findings.recommendation: Mirror the exclusion already used in code-xss-vue-v-html-dynamic's bareMatch check: after finding a `.innerHTML =` match, look at the ~40 characters immediately following the `=` and skip it if they match `/DOMPurify\.sanitize|sanitize-html|purify\(|\.sanitize\(/i`.

findings.title: default-credentials: default-credentials (high severity) fires on instructional/warning text telling users to change default credentials
findings.description: The check does a bare substring match for "admin/admin" (and similar) anywhere in the body with only a word-boundary guard against URL-path false matches — it has no documentation/instructional-content exclusion, unlike nine other checks in this same file (path-traversal-indicators, xml-external-entity, code-jwt-verify-no-secret, etc.) that all check the ~150-200 chars before a match for `<code|<pre|\`\`\`|example|documentation` before firing. Verified: `"Default username and password is admin/admin. Please change it after first login."` matches the admin/admin pattern. Trigger: Self-hosted app / router / IoT device first-login banners that literally say "Default credentials: admin/admin, please change immediately" (extremely common boilerplate on Pi-hole-style dashboards, home routers, and other self-hosted software's setup screens) — the page is warning the user, not exposing an active default-credential vulnerability.
findings.recommendation: Add the same before-context exclusion this file already applies elsewhere: after a match, check the ~150 chars before it (case-insensitive) for words like "default", "change", "please", "first login", "documentation" and suppress the finding when present.

findings.title: vibe-password-in-comment: vibe-password-in-comment (high severity) fires on ordinary password-validation-rule comments, not just commented-out credentials
findings.description: The pattern `/\/\/\s*password\s*[:=]\s*\S+/i` matches any `// password: <non-whitespace>` comment, including comments that describe validation rules rather than assign a literal value. Verified: `// password: minimum 8 characters, 1 uppercase, 1 number` (a completely ordinary validation-rule comment) matches the pattern. Trigger: A form-validation function with a documentation comment like `// password: minimum 8 characters, 1 uppercase, 1 number` above the check — a routine, benign comment, especially common in the AI-generated code this whole category targets, which tends to over-comment exactly like this.
findings.recommendation: Require the captured value to look like an actual literal (quoted string or bare token with no spaces) rather than free-form prose: e.g. change `\S+` to `["'][^"']+["']|[A-Za-z0-9_!@#$%^&*-]{4,}` and additionally reject when the next word after the colon/equals is one of minimum/min/max/at/must/should/required/characters/chars/length/strength/format/regex/pattern.

findings.title: s3-bucket-exposed: s3-bucket-exposed (medium severity) fires on any S3-hosted public asset URL, which is normal, intentional CDN usage
findings.description: The check is a bare regex match for any `https://*.s3.amazonaws.com` URL with zero filtering — presence alone is treated as an "exposure". Public S3 buckets used to serve static assets (images, downloads, PDFs) are a deliberate, extremely common hosting pattern, not a misconfiguration. Verified: `` matches. Trigger: Any website that hosts a logo, product image, or downloadable file on a public S3 bucket (widespread practice — S3 static asset hosting is a standard, documented AWS use case), e.g. ``.
findings.recommendation: Either drop this to "info" severity (bare presence of an S3 URL is not itself a risk signal), or require corroborating signal before flagging at "medium": only fire when the referenced object path itself suggests sensitive content (matches /backup|\.env|config|private|dump|\.sql|credentials/i), analogous to how other checks in this group require adjacent risk context instead of firing on bare presence.

findings.title: cache-control-no-store-missing: Sensitive-path detection uses raw substring matches that hit unrelated public routes
findings.description: Both cache-control-no-store-missing (lines 962-977) and cache-control-missing (lines 100-120) use the identical `.includes()` substring list `[/login,/signin,/signup,/register,/admin,/api/auth,/session,/account]`. Because these are plain substring checks rather than path-segment matches, `/api/auth` matches any path merely containing that substring (e.g. `/api/authors`), `/session` matches `/sessions`, and `/account` matches `/accounting` -- none of which are actually authentication/session endpoints. Trigger: A blog/CMS REST endpoint `/api/authors/42` (common on Ghost, WordPress-style, or custom Next.js content APIs) or an events site's public schedule page `/sessions/keynote-address`, or a fintech marketing page `/accounting/reports` -- all public, non-sensitive routes that get flagged as 'sensitive page path detected' for lacking Cache-Control: no-store.
findings.recommendation: Replace the `.includes()` calls in both detectors with path-segment-aware matching, e.g. `/(^|\/)(login|signin|signup|register|admin|session|account)(\/|$)/i.test(path)` plus a separate `/(^|\/)api\/auth(\/|$)/i.test(path)` for the auth-API case, so `/api/authors`, `/sessions`, and `/accounting` no longer match.

findings.title: mixed-protocol-content: Counts plain <a href="http://..."> navigation links as mixed content, a bug this codebase already documented and fixed for the sibling headers.ts check but not here
findings.description:
detectMixedContent (lines 29-45) matches `(?:src|href|action)\s*=\s*["']http://` against every tag in the body, which includes ordinary navigation links and
(already covered separately by form-action-http). A plain hyperlink is never fetched as a subresource by the browser and triggers no mixed-content warning or block. headers.ts's own `mixed-content` detector explicitly documents fixing this exact false positive ('A plain is regular navigation, never fetched as a subresource -- it must not count here'), but that scoping was never applied to this separate ssl.ts implementation of the same underlying concept. Trigger: Any HTTPS page containing an ordinary outbound citation/reference link to an HTTP-only external resource, e.g. a blog post or documentation page linking `source` -- gets counted as an N-count 'mixed-content reference' even though nothing is fetched insecurely.
findings.recommendation: Scope the pattern to actual subresource-loading tags only (script/img/iframe/video/audio/source/object/embed src=, and <link rel=stylesheet href=), mirroring headers.ts's `mixed-content` detector, and drop bare href on <a> and action on <form> (form action is already covered by form-action-http).

findings.title: phishing-lookalike-domain: Treats the mere presence of the punycode ACE prefix 'xn--' as a homoglyph/phishing signal
findings.description: The regex `/[a-z0-9-]+\.(?:xn--|аpple|googIe|paypaI|microsft|amazom|faceb00k|app1e)/i` puts the bare literal 'xn--' in the same alternation as specific brand-lookalike strings. 'xn--' is simply the standard ASCII-Compatible-Encoding prefix that ANY internationalized domain name (IDN) is converted to -- it has no inherent relationship to brand impersonation. The description in content.json even frames this check as being about links that 'closely resemble known trusted brands,' but the code never decodes the punycode label or compares it to a brand list for this branch. Trigger: Any legitimate business using a non-Latin-script domain (common in Germany, Sweden, Russia, Japan, etc.), e.g. a canonical/og:url self-reference like `<link rel="canonical" href="https://www.xn--mnchen-3ya.de/">` on that site's own homepage -- 'www.' + 'xn--' matches the regex and is reported as a 'medium' severity 'Potential phishing lookalike domain detected in links' finding on the site's own legitimate self-referential markup.
findings.recommendation: Remove the bare 'xn--' alternative from the pattern entirely. If IDN-based typosquatting detection is wanted, punycode-decode each `xn--`-prefixed label (e.g. via the URL API / a punycode library) and run brand-confusability comparison (Unicode skeleton / homoglyph mapping) only against the decoded Unicode label, not the raw ASCII-encoded string.

findings.title: debug-info-in-page-js: Bare 'key'/'token' substring match (no word boundary) flags public Firebase/reCAPTCHA/publishable keys in hydration state
findings.description: Lines 213-225: the second pattern `window\.__(?:ENV|CONFIG|APP_CONFIG|INITIAL_STATE)__\s*=\s*\{[^}]{0,500}(?:password|secret|key|token)/i` matches 'key'/'token' as a bare substring with no `\b` word boundary, so it matches inside any field name containing those letters -- 'apiKey', 'siteKey', 'publicKey', 'csrfToken', 'pageToken', etc. Firebase's Web SDK client config (`apiKey: "AIzaSy..."`) is explicitly documented by Google as safe to expose client-side (restricted by domain, not secrecy) and this same codebase already codifies that exact exception in the sibling check `api-key-hardcoded-in-js` (excludes the 'AIza' prefix). But when that same Firebase config is serialized server-side into `window.__CONFIG__`, `window.__APP_CONFIG__`, or `window.__INITIAL_STATE__` -- an extremely common SSR hydration pattern for Nuxt/Next/Redux apps bootstrapping Firebase -- this check fires 'Sensitive configuration data serialized into page JavaScript' purely because the object contains a field literally named 'apiKey'. The file's own sibling check `localstorage-sensitive-data` already documents the correct principle in a comment ('bare key alone is too generic') but this check never applies it. Trigger: window.__INITIAL_STATE__ = {"firebase":{"apiKey":"AIzaSyXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX","authDomain":"myapp.firebaseapp.com","projectId":"myapp"}};
findings.recommendation: Drop bare 'key' from the alternation (mirroring localstorage-sensitive-data's own reasoning in this file) and require whole-word matches: change `(?:password|secret|key|token)` to `\b(?:password|secret|token)\b` and separately require an actual private-key-shaped field via `\bprivate[_-]?key\b` if you want to keep key coverage, so 'apiKey'/'siteKey'/'publicKey' no longer match on the bare 'key' substring.

findings.title: idor-sequential-id-in-url: Fires on Drupal's default /user/{uid} entity route, a standard CMS path used across a large share of the web
findings.description: The regex `/\/(?:api\/)?(?:v\d+\/)?(?:user|account|invoice|order|profile)s?\/([1-9]\d{0,4})(?:\/|$|\?)/i` matches any URL path shaped like `/user/<n>` or `/profile/<n>` with no API/version prefix required. Drupal (a major CMS, powering a large share of government, university, and enterprise sites) uses exactly this path -- `/user/{uid}` -- as its default, framework-generated user-profile route, and by Drupal convention uid 1 is the site's first/admin account, so `/user/1` is an extremely common, often intentionally reachable URL across the Drupal ecosystem (frequently linked exactly this way, e.g. the pattern seen at drupal.org/user/1-style links). Scanning any Drupal site's default user page produces a 'Sequential Numeric ID in URL (IDOR Risk)' finding for what is simply the CMS's standard content-routing path, not an owner-scoped API resource. Trigger: Scanning any stock Drupal site at its default admin/user page, e.g. `https://<any-drupal-site>/user/1` -- confirmed the check's own regex matches this exact path (verified: `/\/(?:api\/)?(?:v\d+\/)?(?:user|account|invoice|order|profile)s?\/([1-9]\d{0,4})(?:\/|$|\?)/i.exec("https://example.edu/user/1")` returns a match with id=1).
findings.recommendation: Require an `api/` or `v\d+/` prefix specifically for the `user` and `profile` nouns (the two that collide with common CMS content-routing conventions), while leaving `account`/`invoice`/`order` matchable bare since those remain reliably owner-scoped in normal usage. Concretely: split the alternation so `(?:api\/|v\d+\/)(?:user|profile)s?\/(\d+)` requires an API/version prefix, while `(?:api\/)?(?:v\d+\/)?(?:account|invoice|order)s?\/(\d+)` keeps the current bare-path matching.

findings.title: POST /api/v3/scan/feedback accepts a caller-supplied scanHistoryId with no ownership check, letting any user attach fabricated feedback to (and trigger a forced recompute + host_reputation cascade against) any scan in the system
findings.description:
FeedbackSchema only validates that `scanHistoryId` is a positive integer (app/api/v3/scan/feedback/route.ts:10); the POST handler never verifies `scan_history.user_id === session.userId` for it before inserting into scan_finding_feedback (scan_history_id FK just needs to reference an existing row, per instrumentation.ts's `scan_history_id INTEGER REFERENCES scan_history(id) ON DELETE SET NULL`) and before calling `recomputeScanScore(scanHistoryId)` (line 64). This breaks the exact convention the codebase documents for itself elsewhere -- e.g. app/api/v3/webhooks/[id]/route.ts's own comment: 'Every other per-resource route in this codebase ... verifies ownership in the same UPDATE ... WHERE id = $n AND user_id = $n statement ... so a [resource] ID belonging to another user can never be [mutated]' -- a pattern this route does not follow for scanHistoryId.

Impact: any authenticated user (including free tier) can POST arbitrary {findingId, findingUrl, verdict, notes} tied to any other user's scan_history_id (IDs are small sequential integers, trivially enumerable), polluting the scan_finding_feedback table that idx_scan_finding_feedback_finding_id (finding_id, verdict) indexes for the admin 'Engine Feedback' false-positive-rate aggregation (CONFIG_ENGINE_FEEDBACK_NOISE_THRESHOLD_PERCENT). It also forces recomputeScanScore to run an UPDATE against another user's scan_history row and against host_reputation `WHERE source_scan_id = scanHistoryId` for a scan the caller doesn't own and never touched otherwise -- a write side-effect triggered purely by an unauthenticated-for-that-resource request parameter. Evidence: app/api/v3/scan/feedback/route.ts:7-13 (FeedbackSchema, scanHistoryId has no ownership tie), line 39-54 (INSERT uses scanHistoryId as-is, no ownership SELECT), line 63-65 (`if (scanHistoryId) { recomputeScanScore(scanHistoryId).catch(() => {}); }`); lib/scanner/recompute-scan-score.ts:58-112 (reads/writes scan_history and host_reputation by that raw id).
findings.recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Before inserting or calling recomputeScanScore, verify the caller owns the scan (or has team access, matching the pattern in app/api/v3/history/[id]/share/route.ts): `SELECT user_id FROM scan_history WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2`, returning 400/404 if scanHistoryId is present but not owned by session.userId. If it's intentional that feedback can reference a scan the user doesn't own (e.g. a shared/public scan they're reviewing), explicitly document that trust decision and still avoid triggering the host_reputation-cascading recompute for a scan outside the caller's own history.

findings.title: CSRF exemption `pathname.startsWith("/api/v3/webhooks/")` intended only for the Stripe webhook receiver also exempts the user's own session-authenticated webhook-edit endpoint
findings.description:
middleware.ts's isExemptFromCsrf() exempts any path starting with `/api/v3/webhooks/` from the Origin/Referer CSRF check, with the stated rationale 'Exempt endpoints authenticate the caller some other way (signed payload, server-issued secret, etc.)' -- true for app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts (verified via STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET), but the prefix match also matches app/api/v3/webhooks/[id]/route.ts's PATCH handler, which edits a webhook's url/name/type/active flag using ONLY the session cookie for authentication (no signature, no secondary secret) -- exactly the class of endpoint the CSRF check exists to protect. This violates the function's own documented invariant: 'Keep this list narrow -- every entry needs a clear non-CSRF trust boundary,' which is not true for /api/v3/webhooks/[id].

Current practical exploitability is reduced (not eliminated) by the session cookie's `sameSite: 'lax'` attribute (lib/auth/auth.ts:65): a cross-site fetch/XHR PATCH (the only way to reach this endpoint, since HTML forms cannot send PATCH) does not carry SameSite=Lax cookies today in a standards-compliant browser, so this is currently a redundant-layer failure rather than an immediately exploitable one -- but it is a real gap in the app's primary, documented CSRF defense, and would become directly exploitable if a future route is added under this prefix that's reachable via GET/POST top-level navigation, or in any user-agent context where SameSite enforcement is weaker than assumed. Evidence: middleware.ts:314-327 (`pathname.startsWith("/api/v3/webhooks/")` in isExemptFromCsrf); app/api/v3/webhooks/[id]/route.ts:23-32 (PATCH authenticates via getSession() / cookie only, matches the exempted prefix); app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:38-40 (the actual signature-verified endpoint the exemption was written for).
findings.recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Narrow the exemption to the exact Stripe path: `pathname === "/api/v3/webhooks/stripe"` instead of a prefix match, so /api/v3/webhooks/[id] (and any future path under this prefix) goes through the normal Origin/Referer CSRF check like every other session-authenticated mutating route.

findings.title: Stale, non-super_admin-aware role helpers still dead-exported through the @/lib/auth barrel
findings.description: lib/auth/permissions.ts defines canManageRole/canAccessAdmin/getRoleLevel/isStaffRole against an old ROLES map with no super_admin. lib/auth/permissions-client.ts has newer versions built on STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY which does include super_admin. lib/auth/index.ts re-exports the OLD versions as the public @/lib/auth API. Currently unreachable in practice (the one real caller bypasses the barrel) but any future import from @/lib/auth silently gets the version that mishandles a super_admin.
findings.recommendation: Have permissions.ts re-export the client versions instead of redefining them, or delete the local duplicates.

findings.title: Dead revokeApiKey/getUserApiKeys duplicate in db-utils.ts is missing the ownership check the live version has
findings.description: lib/database/db-utils.ts duplicates getUserApiKeys/revokeApiKey from lib/api/api-keys.ts. The db-utils.ts revokeApiKey(keyId) takes no userId and updates WHERE id = $1 only (an IDOR shape) vs. api-keys.ts's WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2. Confirmed dead code: db-utils.ts is imported exactly once anywhere, only for getUserByEmail, so the unsafe revokeApiKey is never actually called, but it's a landmine for the next person who greps for revokeApiKey and finds two candidates.
findings.recommendation: Delete the db-utils.ts duplicates; keep lib/api/api-keys.ts as the sole implementation.

findings.title: hardcoded-secrets duplicated code.ts/secrets-extended.ts; dead copy reintroduces a bug the live copy's own comment says was deliberately fixed
findings.description: code.ts has a comment explaining the Google API Key pattern was removed from this check specifically because it triple-counted with two other checks and pushed a normal site's scan to critical severity. secrets-extended.ts's dead duplicate still contains that exact pattern, inert today only because code.ts owns the ID via category ownership -- a landmine for any future dedup that flips which file owns it.
findings.recommendation: Delete the hardcoded-secrets entry from lib/scanner/checks/secrets-extended.ts; fold in any uniquely-covered patterns deliberately, not as a second full copy under the same ID.

findings.title: sourcemap-reference triplicated across code.ts, content.ts, information-disclosure.ts -- a prior cleanup pass explicitly reasoned about this ID and still missed it
findings.description: content.ts wins via category ownership; dead copies remain in information-disclosure.ts and code.ts. information-disclosure.ts has a comment about removing a sibling duplicate that explicitly reasons about sourcemap-reference too, but left this one in place. Separately, a related id source-maps in code.ts has no JSON definition in any category file and can never fire at all.
findings.recommendation: Delete sourcemap-reference from information-disclosure.ts and code.ts. Separately, either give source-maps a JSON def or delete the orphaned entry.

findings.title: cookie-security duplicated cookies.ts/headers.ts -- the cookies category's own file has a dead implementation of its most obviously-named check
findings.description: cookies.ts has a simple substring-based version; headers.ts has a modern Headers.getSetCookie()-based version. The JSON definition's category is headers, not cookies, so headers.ts always wins -- a maintainer editing cookies.ts expecting to change live behavior would be editing dead code.
findings.recommendation: Delete cookie-security from cookies.ts, OR if the simpler substring approach is actually preferred, move the JSON def's category to cookies and delete headers.ts's copy instead. Resolve which is canonical.

findings.title: 11 content-category detector IDs have zero implementation in content.ts -- resolve only via undocumented declaration-order fallback, not the documented owner-category rule
findings.description: token-exposure, jwt-in-url, internal-ip-exposed, aws-metadata-reference, jwt-in-html, base64-credentials, s3-bucket-exposed, firebase-config-exposed, credit-card-pattern, ssn-pattern, phone-number-leak all have category content JSON defs but are only implemented in secrets-extended.ts. Since content.ts doesn't define them, the owner-lookup fails and falls through to first-match-in-declaration-order, which happens to land on secrets-extended.ts today only because no earlier-declared bundle also defines these ids. Given dozens of same-name collisions already exist in this codebase, ordering-based resolution is not reliable protection going forward.
findings.recommendation: Change these 11 JSON defs' category to secrets-extended to make ownership explicit, or add thin re-export stubs in content.ts pointing at the secrets-extended.ts functions.

findings.title: repairAllSequences() runs unguarded immediately after COMMIT; a failure there masks a successful migration as a reported failure
findings.description: In scripts/migrate/_runner.mjs's runPlan, await repairAllSequences(client) runs right after COMMIT with no try/catch. migrate.mjs only calls writeMeta() after runPlan() returns normally, so an exception here propagates past writeMeta -- every DDL step is already durably committed, but vulnradar_schema_meta is never updated, so the app refuses to boot and the operator sees a false 'Migration failed' for a migration that actually succeeded. The identical unguarded call exists in migrate.mjs's zero-step 'same version' branch. A second db:migrate run does safely re-converge since every DDL step is idempotent, but only after a confusing false failure. Verified via code reading; not reproduced live.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the post-COMMIT repairAllSequences(client) call in runPlan, and the analogous call in migrate.mjs's zero-step branch, in their own try/catch that logs a warning without letting the exception mask a successful migration or block the meta-row write.

findings.title: Host-level reputation lookup echoes the exact scanned URL (with query string) of an unrelated public scan to any signed-in user
findings.description: GET /api/v3/scan/reputation falls back to the host-level host_reputation row when no exact-URL match is found, and returns that row's scanned_url column verbatim -- the literal URL, including query string, of whatever page on that host was most recently scanned publicly by anyone, not necessarily the page the caller asked about. Any signed-in account can query a bare host and learn the exact URL of a different, unrelated page someone else scanned. Since scan_history.is_public defaults to true, if that URL embedded a secret in its query string (password-reset link, magic-login link, API token) the secret becomes readable by any account holder who only knows the hostname. The is_public privacy gate itself is correctly enforced -- the leak is specifically scanned_url being echoed on the host-level fallback, where the caller never supplied that URL themselves.
findings.recommendation: Only return scannedUrl on an exact match (the caller already supplied, and thus already knows, that URL); return null for a host-level fallback match.

findings.title: BETA_ENABLED / BETA_BANNER_MESSAGE admin settings are fully wired to the UI but have zero functional consumer
findings.description: lib/config/registry.ts defines BETA_ENABLED and BETA_BANNER_MESSAGE as runtime-tier settings, documented in app/docs/config/page.tsx as a real feature and given admin-panel display treatment. Nothing anywhere calls getSetting to gate or render anything with them. Not a regression (already dead before this session) but the registry migration gave dead functionality a real, documented, editable admin UI with no indication it's a no-op.
findings.recommendation: Either wire a real beta-banner component that reads these two settings, or remove them from the registry/docs/admin UI until there's a consumer.

findings.title: DEFAULT_SEVERITY_THRESHOLD is admin-editable but the scanner never reads it
findings.description: registry.ts describes it as the lowest severity reported when a scan does not specify one. No getSetting call for this key exists in production code, and no scan route applies any severity floor at all.
findings.recommendation: Wire it into lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts where a scan without an explicit severity filter is handled, or remove the setting until that logic exists.

findings.title: 2FA pending-challenge window is admin-editable but the login route still uses the compiled constant
findings.description: 2FA_PENDING_MAX_AGE_SECONDS has no getSetting consumer anywhere. app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts still imports and uses the compiled AUTH_2FA_PENDING_MAX_AGE constant to set the pending-2FA cookie's maxAge -- an admin changing this window in the panel has no effect on actual cookie lifetime.
findings.recommendation: Replace the AUTH_2FA_PENDING_MAX_AGE import in login/route.ts with getSetting("2FA_PENDING_MAX_AGE_SECONDS") where the cookie is set.

findings.title: Webhook HMAC signing secret is stored in plaintext, unlike every other reversible secret in the codebase
findings.description: POST /api/v3/webhooks generates a 256-bit secret and inserts it directly into webhooks.secret, a plain TEXT column. Neither the webhooks route nor lib/webhooks/delivery.ts calls encryptApiKey/decryptApiKey. Every other long-lived secret the app needs back in plaintext for repeated use (API keys, TOTP seeds, Discord OAuth tokens) goes through lib/auth/crypto.ts's AES-256-GCM encryptApiKey/decryptApiKey. A DB-level compromise lets an attacker read every user's webhook secret and forge validly-signed payloads to their receivers.
findings.recommendation: Encrypt webhooks.secret at rest with the existing encryptApiKey/decryptApiKey helpers, decrypting only where signWebhookPayload needs the raw secret. Backfill existing plaintext rows in a migration.

findings.title: Discord sign-in/sign-up redirect URI never documented for registration
findings.description: The unified sign-in/sign-up OAuth flow added in app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/ redirects to /api/v3/auth/oauth/discord/callback for Discord, a distinct URI from the older Profile > Connections linking flow's /api/v3/auth/discord/callback. .env.example (and the operator's own .env.local) only ever documented the older URI for the Discord Developer Portal. A self-hoster (or this SaaS's own Discord app, if registered before the unified flow existed) who followed that doc registers only one of the two required redirect URIs, so the Sign in with Discord / Sign up with Discord buttons on /login and /signup -- which render whenever DISCORD_CLIENT_ID/SECRET are set, per /api/v3/auth/oauth/info -- fail at Discord with a redirect_uri mismatch, while the Profile Connect button keeps working. Same bug class as cc1b1f9f's GitHub repo-connect fix earlier today, but Discord's two flows are intentionally separate (not merged), so the fix is registering both URIs rather than consolidating callbacks.
findings.recommendation: Documented both required OAuth2 redirect URLs in the Discord Developer Portal section of .env.example -- confirm the production/sandbox Discord app also has both registered.

findings.title: graphql-introspection titled 'Enabled in Production' but only detects a string reference in the client bundle
findings.description: Detector matches __schema{/IntrospectionQuery/getIntrospectionQuery anywhere in body -- text bundled by nearly every GraphQL client library (Apollo, Relay, graphql-request) for fragment matching/codegen, regardless of whether the server's introspection is actually enabled. The JSON title asserted introspection is 'Enabled in Production' (a claim about live server behavior the check never verifies), at medium severity, so any GraphQL-using site (common at Walmart scale) would false-positive on ordinary client tooling.
findings.recommendation: Retitled to 'GraphQL Introspection Query Reference Found', rewrote description/riskImpact/fixSteps to say this is a client-bundle reference requiring separate server-side verification, and downgraded severity medium -> low.

findings.title: bearer-token-exposed regex matches API-doc placeholder tokens, rated critical
findings.description: The regex /Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-+\/=]{20,}/i matches the extremely common documentation placeholder style 'Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN_HERE' / 'Bearer API_KEY_PLACEHOLDER' (all-caps-with-underscores is never a real base64/JWT token), yet was rated critical -- the same severity class as a confirmed hardcoded database credential -- and higher than the near-identical jwt-in-html check (rated high) in the same file.
findings.recommendation: Excluded all-caps/underscore-only matches from firing (placeholder convention, never a real secret) and downgraded severity critical -> high to match jwt-in-html's precedent for the same evidence class.

findings.title: sensitive-form-no-csrf fires on forms that submit to a third-party domain
findings.description: Any POST form was flagged for missing a CSRF token field even when its action attribute pointed to a different origin entirely (e.g. a Mailchimp/HubSpot-hosted newsletter signup form). A form that never reaches your own backend cannot be protected by your CSRF tokens -- that's the third party's concern, not a gap in your app -- so this fired constantly on ordinary marketing pages with embedded third-party forms, on top of double-counting evidence already covered by the separate open-form-action check.
findings.recommendation: Skip forms whose action attribute is an absolute cross-origin URL before evaluating for a missing CSRF field; same-origin/relative-action forms are still checked as before.

findings.title: Three cookie fingerprint checks titled 'missing security attributes' only ever checked the cookie NAME, never the attributes
findings.description: django-csrftoken-cookie-exposed, laravel-session-cookie-exposes, and express-cookie-exposes all had a JSON title/description claiming to detect a session/CSRF cookie 'missing security attributes' (Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite), at medium severity -- but the detector bodies only matched the framework's DEFAULT cookie name (csrftoken, XSRF-TOKEN, connect.sid, etc.) and returned a finding unconditionally, never inspecting the cookie string for the attributes the title claims are missing. A site using the default cookie name with fully correct Secure+HttpOnly+SameSite flags set would still get flagged as if attributes were absent. (The sibling rails-cookie-httponly check in the same file does this correctly, which is how the gap was found.)
findings.recommendation: Rewrote all three detectors to actually check for missing Secure/SameSite/HttpOnly on the matched cookie (correctly NOT requiring HttpOnly on Django's csrftoken / Laravel's XSRF-TOKEN, which are intentionally JS-readable by design) and only fire when an attribute is genuinely absent.

findings.title: checkSecurityTxt probes bare apex host, misses www-only security.txt
findings.description: Walmart scan reported security.txt missing at both well-known/root paths on walmart.com; user manually confirmed www.walmart.com serves a valid security.txt. Apex/www host mismatch in lib/scanner/async-checks.ts's checkSecurityTxt, likely a redirect-handling or origin-source bug.
findings.recommendation: Root-causing redirect/origin handling. In progress (agent a4a7418e77b0d7ded).

findings.title: AI verification timeout/chunk-size too tight for realistic finding counts
findings.description: lib/ai/verify-findings.ts's verifyInChunks stops at a 90s total deadline with chunk size 5; only ~35-40 of Walmart's 57 findings received an AI verdict before the deadline hit, the rest silently unverified with no coverage indicator.
findings.recommendation: Increasing CONFIG_AI_VERIFY_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS/CHUNK_SIZE with worst-case arithmetic, checking client-side timeout parity. In progress (agent a567911127be41393).

findings.title: Duplicate header checks double-count the same evidence at inconsistent severities
findings.description: Seven pairs of header detectors fire on the exact same underlying condition under different ids/severities: csp-frame-ancestors is a strict subset of clickjack-missing; x-content-type-options-not-nosniff duplicates nosniff-incorrect (and its own JSON metadata described the wrong 'missing header' scenario, not what it actually detected); corp-missing duplicates cross-origin-resource-policy-report-only-missing; server-timing-sensitive-key-leak duplicates server-timing-exposure and its keyword list flagged the benign, extremely common 'cache;dur=NN' CDN timing value as 'sensitive'; x-frame-options-invalid re-fired on XFO:ALLOWALL despite x-frame-options-allowall already covering it at higher severity; hsts-no-preload double-reported 'missing includeSubDomains' alongside the dedicated strict-transport-security-include-subdomains check; referrer-policy-no-referrer-strict-origin-when-cross-origin double-reported 'unsafe-url'/'no-referrer-when-downgrade' alongside referrer-policy-unsafe. Each pair inflated finding counts and danger-score contributions for one real signal.
findings.recommendation: Disabled the redundant/subset detector in each pair (return null with an explanatory comment, matching the file's existing etag-inode-leak convention) or narrowed the broader detector's condition to stop overlapping with the more precise one.

findings.title: Stale/renamed header check ids left title+description describing an unrelated concept
findings.description: coop-missing, corp-missing (before scanner-05's dedup), charset-meta-missing, and cors-null-origin-allowed all had their real detector logic implemented under an id that used to represent something else entirely: coop-missing's title/description talk about the optional Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy-Report-Only preview variant while the code checks the real enforcing COOP header; charset-meta-missing's metadata was entirely about 'Sec-Fetch-* Request Headers Not Echoed' while the code checks for a missing <meta charset> tag; cors-null-origin-allowed's metadata was entirely about 'COOP unsafe-popups' while the code detects Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null (a real, moderately serious CORS bypass vector exploitable via sandboxed iframes), and was consequently mis-tiered at severity info. The templated 'evidence' field in each JSON entry still contained the original id slug (e.g. headers-coop-report-only-missing, headers-sec-fetch-missing, headers-coop-same-origin-allow-popups), confirming these ids were repointed to existing detectors without updating the rest of the metadata. Users saw a title/description/fix-steps completely unrelated to what was actually found.
findings.recommendation: Rewrote title/description/riskImpact/explanation/fixSteps for coop-missing, charset-meta-missing, and cors-null-origin-allowed to match their real detector behavior; bumped cors-null-origin-allowed from info to medium to reflect the real risk (ACAO: null trusted by sandboxed-iframe/data-URI attackers).

findings.title: Several header checks rated medium/high fire on completely standard practice at well-run sites
findings.description: sri-missing (high) fires on any external script lacking a Subresource Integrity hash, but SRI is fundamentally impractical for continuously-updated third-party vendor scripts (analytics, ads, payment SDKs) that essentially every major site loads, including security-conscious ones -- so this fired at 'high' severity against nearly the entire web. target-blank-no-noopener (medium) flags <a target=_blank> without rel=noopener even though the check's own riskImpact text already concedes Chrome 88+/Firefox 79+ apply noopener behavior by default, making the real-world risk on modern browsers low. iframe-third-party-without-sandbox (medium) fires on any cross-origin iframe including routine, legitimate embeds (YouTube, Google Maps, payment SDKs, chat widgets) that omit sandbox because it would break required functionality, and its own riskImpact overstated the threat (claimed DOM access the Same-Origin Policy already blocks regardless of sandbox). x-backend-server-exposed (medium) fires on X-Served-By, a default Fastly/Varnish header used by many large, well-run sites, at a higher severity than the identical-risk sibling checks (server-header-disclosure, via-header-exposed, x-powered-by-exposed) which are all 'low'.
findings.recommendation: Lowered sri-missing, target-blank-no-noopener, iframe-third-party-without-sandbox, and x-backend-server-exposed to severity low (matching sibling checks of equivalent real-world risk); corrected iframe-third-party-without-sandbox's explanation to not claim sandbox gates parent-DOM access.

findings.title: ratelimit-policy-missing only checks the newest unprefixed header name, missing the still-common legacy convention its own description promises
findings.description: The JSON description explicitly says the check looks for 'X-RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Limit, Retry-After', but the detector code only ever checked the new, least-adopted IETF-draft 'RateLimit-Limit' (unprefixed). APIs using the still extremely common legacy X-RateLimit-* convention (GitHub, Twitter/X, and many other well-run APIs) or that only emit Retry-After on throttled responses were false-flagged at medium severity as having 'no RateLimit-* family headers' even though they do rate-limit and do expose it.
findings.recommendation: Added checks for the legacy x-ratelimit-limit header and retry-after, matching what the description already claimed.

findings.title: api-rest-mass-assignment-risk (high) inferred an input-validation bug from response content alone
findings.description: The detector only checks whether a RESPONSE body contains "role":"admin" or "isAdmin":true, then reports it as a mass-assignment vulnerability at high severity with evidence claiming the endpoint 'appears to accept and bind arbitrary request body fields without filtering.' Mass assignment is about what an endpoint accepts as INPUT; a normal /api/me correctly returning the current (legitimately admin) user's own role in a read response satisfies this regex with zero relation to any actual vulnerability, and would fire on any authenticated admin session.
findings.recommendation: Downgraded high -> low, retitled to 'REST endpoint response exposes privileged fields', and reworded description/evidence to state what was actually observed (privileged field names present in a response) rather than asserting a confirmed mass-assignment vulnerability; also corrected its JSON type from 'header' to 'body-pattern' (the detector never reads headers).

findings.title: api-graphql-suggestions-enabled matched the ubiquitous UI phrase 'did you mean' on any page, unrelated to GraphQL
findings.description: The regex matched a literal 'did you mean' or 'didYouMean' anywhere in the body with no requirement that the response actually came from a GraphQL endpoint. 'Did you mean' is an extremely common e-commerce/docs search-UI phrase (Google, Amazon-style typo suggestions) with nothing to do with GraphQL schema enumeration, yet the evidence text confidently asserted 'GraphQL error response ... confirming field suggestions are enabled.'
findings.recommendation: Gated on GraphQL context (/graphql URL or a JSON 'errors' array present) AND required the graphql-js suggestion message shape ('did you mean "fieldName"') that generic UI copy does not replicate.

findings.title: api-graphql-introspection-enabled had an unscoped fallback branch matching any page, same bug class already fixed for content.json's graphql-introspection
findings.description: A second branch matched ["']__schema["']\s*\{ anywhere in the body with no URL/endpoint scoping at all -- __schema{ is text bundled by Apollo/Relay/graphql-request client libraries for their own fragment matching, present regardless of whether the server's introspection is enabled. This is the identical false-positive pattern already fixed for content.json's graphql-introspection check (AUDIT-008 content-03), just under a different check id in api.json, still at severity high and additionally overclaiming 'returned a full schema dump' with no verification a dump occurred.
findings.recommendation: Removed the unscoped branch; the remaining branch requires the URL to actually be /graphql AND the body to reference schema/introspection keywords. Downgraded high -> medium and reworded evidence to prompt verification rather than assert the dump occurred; corrected type 'header' -> 'combined' (checks url and body, never headers).

findings.title: idor-sequential-id-in-url's word list included 'item'/'record', which commonly name public no-ownership resources
findings.description: The path-keyword list (user|account|invoice|order|profile|record|item|document|report) treated any small numeric ID after 'item' or 'record' as an IDOR risk, but these two words just as often name a PUBLIC catalog resource with no ownership concept at all -- an e-commerce product page at /item/42 has no 'owner' to enumerate away from, so flagging it as an IDOR risk is a category error, not a security finding, on completely ordinary browsing URLs.
findings.recommendation: Removed 'item' and 'record' from the keyword list, keeping the words (user/account/invoice/order/profile) that reliably name a user-scoped resource in normal usage.

findings.title: Three page-checks SRI/sandbox checks repeated the already-fixed 'fires on every ordinary third-party embed' pattern from scanner-07
findings.description: page-script-missing-sri (medium) and page-third-party-script-unconstrained-by-csp (high) fire on any third-party script without SRI regardless of vendor, including Google Analytics/GTM/ads/payment SDKs that cannot practically use SRI because they are continuously updated by the vendor -- the identical false-positive class already found and downgraded for the legacy sri-missing check in headers.json (AUDIT-008 scanner-07), just not yet applied to the newer PageCheck-architecture equivalents in my scope. page-third-party-iframe-no-sandbox (medium) has the same relationship to the already-downgraded iframe-third-party-without-sandbox: it fires on routine legitimate embeds (video players, maps, payment widgets, chat widgets) that omit sandbox because it breaks required functionality.
findings.recommendation: Downgraded page-script-missing-sri medium->low, page-third-party-script-unconstrained-by-csp high->medium, and page-third-party-iframe-no-sandbox medium->low, matching the severities scanner-07 already established for the equivalent legacy checks; added a sentence to each riskImpact noting how common the flagged configuration is on legitimate sites.

findings.title: vibe-http-not-https fires on every page with an inline SVG or JSON-LD structured-data block
findings.description: The hardcoded-http-url regex excluded localhost/127.0.0.1/example.com but not the http:// XML/RDF namespace and vocabulary URIs that are spec identifiers, never network requests: xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" (present on virtually every site with an inline SVG icon) and "@context":"http://schema.org" (present on virtually every SEO-conscious site's JSON-LD product/article markup -- this project's own recent SEO commit added exactly this). Both would false-positive as a 'Hardcoded HTTP URL' finding.
findings.recommendation: Added www.w3.org, schema.org, ogp.me, purl.org, and creativecommons.org to the exclusion list.

findings.title: No encryption key rotation path for AES-256-GCM encrypted values
findings.description: A single API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY protects TOTP seeds, Discord OAuth tokens, and API keys. There is no re-encryption migration mechanism, no key versioning on encrypted rows, and no PREVIOUS_API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY fallback. A key compromise requires manual DB remediation with no tooling support.
findings.recommendation: Deferred — requires schema changes (key_version column on encrypted tables) and a migration script. Tracked for AUDIT-008.
findings.evidence: Single key, no key_version column on encrypted tables, no rekey script.

findings.title: Billing verify endpoint had no rate limit — 6-digit code brute-forceable
findings.description: POST /api/v3/billing/verify accepted a 6-digit code (10^6 values) with no per-user attempt cap. An attacker with the user's session cookie could exhaustively try all codes.
findings.recommendation: Added checkRateLimit({ key: `billing-verify:${session.userId}`, ...RATE_LIMITS.billingVerify }) at the top of the handler.
findings.fixedIn: Engine 3.0.0 / AUDIT-006 session
findings.evidence: POST handler performed no checkRateLimit call before the code comparison.

findings.title: backup.sql probe returned raw SQL body in evidence — could include credential data
findings.description: The /backup.sql file probe included up to 200 chars of raw SQL response body in the finding evidence. SQL dumps frequently contain GRANT statements with credentials or INSERT data with PII, which would be stored verbatim in VulnRadar scan results.
findings.recommendation: Evidence now lists which SQL keywords triggered the finding (INSERT, CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, GRANT, mysqldump, pg_dump); raw body content excluded.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-006 Engine 3.0.0 probe hardening
findings.evidence: evidence field: `snippet: body.slice(0, 200)` — raw DB dump content stored in scan results.

findings.title: docker-compose.yml probe returned raw YAML in evidence — leaked env var values
findings.description: The /docker-compose.yml probe included raw YAML content in evidence. docker-compose files commonly contain environment sections with DATABASE_URL, API keys, or passwords, which would be stored in VulnRadar scan results.
findings.recommendation: Evidence now shows service names extracted from YAML plus a boolean flag for whether env/secrets sections are present. Values are never included.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-006 Engine 3.0.0 probe hardening
findings.evidence: evidence field contained raw YAML body slice including environment variable values.

findings.title: Team invite endpoint had no rate limit — unlimited invite spam
findings.description: POST /api/v3/teams/members had no rate-limiting on invite sends. An attacker with team admin/owner access could send unlimited invite emails to arbitrary addresses, abusing VulnRadar's email sending infrastructure for spam.
findings.recommendation: Added checkRateLimit({ key: `team-invite:${session.userId}`, ...RATE_LIMITS.teamInvite }) before the membership verification step.
findings.fixedIn: Engine 3.0.0 / AUDIT-006 session
findings.evidence: POST handler called sendEmail without any checkRateLimit guard.

findings.title: Email 2FA code deletion not atomic — same code accepted twice under race
findings.description: After matching an email 2FA code, the route deletes it with DELETE FROM email_2fa_codes WHERE id = $1 but does not check that a row was actually deleted. Two concurrent requests carrying the same code both pass the in-Node hash comparison, both issue the DELETE (the second deletes 0 rows silently), and both set verified = true, creating two parallel authenticated sessions.
findings.recommendation: Use DELETE … RETURNING id and only set verified = true when the RETURNING clause returns a row, ensuring the first delete wins and the second sees nothing.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-005): email-2FA atomic delete, Bearer CSRF, billing salt
findings.evidence: Line 215: await pool.query("DELETE FROM email_2fa_codes WHERE id = $1", [matched.id]); verified = true; — no rowcount check on the DELETE.
findings.fixSummary: verify/route.ts changed to DELETE … RETURNING id; verified = true only when del.rows.length > 0.

findings.title: Bearer token header bypasses CSRF check for all /api/v3/ routes
findings.description: middleware.ts checked for Authorization: Bearer before running enforceCsrf(), so any request carrying a fake Bearer token (e.g. 'Authorization: Bearer x') skipped CSRF Origin validation entirely. Routes that use only session-cookie auth (account/delete, auth/update, etc.) were reachable from a cross-site page that added a fake Bearer header. SameSite=lax cookies limit practical exploitability in modern browsers, but the defense-in-depth layer was fully bypassed.
findings.recommendation: Move the CSRF check before the Bearer bypass. Make enforceCsrf() Bearer-aware: exempt requests where Bearer is present AND Origin is absent (true non-browser API client), because browsers always include Origin on cross-site requests. Bearer + Origin must still be validated.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-005): email-2FA atomic delete, Bearer CSRF, billing salt
findings.evidence: Lines 108-114 (pre-fix): const hasBearerToken = …; if (hasBearerToken && pathname.startsWith('/api/v3/')) { return applySecurityHeaders(NextResponse.next()); } — returns before reaching enforceCsrf().
findings.fixSummary: middleware.ts reordered: CSRF check runs first. enforceCsrf() accepts hasBearerToken param; returns null (exempt) when hasBearerToken && !origin. Bearer bypass now only skips the session-cookie redirect, not CSRF.

findings.title: Billing verification codes hashed without per-row salt (AUDIT-004#secrets-02 carry-over)
findings.description: AUDIT-004 identified that billing_verification_codes stored 6-digit codes as sha256(code) with no salt. The migration added a salt TEXT column but the application code was not updated. send/route.ts still inserts encode(sha256(code::bytea), 'hex') with no salt, and verify/route.ts looks up by the same unsalted hash. A DB leak allows all codes to be reversed via a precomputed table over 10^6 values.
findings.recommendation: Generate randomBytes(32) salt per code at write time, store hash(salt + code) alongside the salt. At verify time, read the salt row first, recompute hash(salt + code), compare.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-005): email-2FA atomic delete, Bearer CSRF, billing salt
findings.evidence: send/route.ts line 55: INSERT … VALUES ($1, encode(sha256($2::bytea), 'hex'), NOW()… — no salt column populated. verify/route.ts line 35: WHERE code_hash = encode(sha256($2::bytea), 'hex') — no salt in lookup.
findings.fixSummary: send/route.ts: randomBytes(32) salt generated, INSERT populates salt column and stores hash(salt || code). verify/route.ts: reads salt first, recomputes hash(salt + code) for new codes, falls back to unsalted hash for legacy codes created before the fix.

findings.title: 2FA enrollment lacks password confirmation
findings.description: POST /api/v3/auth/2fa/setup requires only a valid session — no password re-entry. An attacker with a hijacked session (XSS, stolen cookie) can silently enroll their own TOTP device, locking the real user out.
findings.recommendation: Require currentPassword in the request body; verify against users.password_hash before proceeding with TOTP setup.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): rate limiting, 2FA gate, LIKE escaping, DKIM timeout, CSP, unsubscribe hardening
findings.fixSummary: setup/route.ts now requires currentPassword in the POST body and verifies it with verifyPassword() before allowing 2FA enrollment.

findings.title: CSP img-src in next.config.mjs still contains bare https: wildcard
findings.description: AUDIT-003 tightened img-src in middleware.ts but next.config.mjs has a separate CSP definition that still uses the bare https: wildcard. Pages that use the next.config.mjs headers (non-middleware paths) remain unrestricted.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same img-src allowlist from middleware.ts to the headers() block in next.config.mjs. Consider consolidating both CSPs into a single source of truth.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): rate limiting, 2FA gate, LIKE escaping, DKIM timeout, CSP, unsubscribe hardening
findings.fixSummary: next.config.mjs img-src updated to match the middleware.ts allowlist: 'self' data: blob: plus explicit CDN/embed origins. Wildcard https: removed.

findings.title: BrowserBase session IDOR — no ownership check on GET/DELETE
findings.description: GET /api/v3/browser/sessions?id=X and DELETE /api/v3/browser/sessions?id=X fetch or destroy the session by its Browserbase session ID string without verifying that the authenticated user created it. Any authenticated user can read live browser session state or kill another user's session by guessing or enumerating session IDs.
findings.recommendation: Store a mapping of (browserbase_session_id → user_id) in a sessions table or in-memory store at creation time; check ownership on every GET and DELETE.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): BrowserBase IDOR fix, env schema, GH Actions SHA pinning
findings.fixSummary: instrumentation.ts creates browser_sessions (id TEXT PK, user_id INT FK, expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ) on startup. POST inserts the mapping; GET/DELETE/logs routes query the table and return 403 if the row belongs to a different user. Pre-existing sessions fail-open during the brief transition window.

findings.title: AI chat endpoint has no rate limiting — cost amplification
findings.description: POST /api/v3/ai/chat (and the streaming variant) has no per-user or per-IP rate limit. A malicious authenticated user can fire unlimited AI inference requests, generating unbounded LLM API costs.
findings.recommendation: Apply checkRateLimit(userId, RATE_LIMITS.AI_CHAT) before forwarding to the provider; add a daily token-budget cap per user.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): rate limiting, 2FA gate, LIKE escaping, DKIM timeout, CSP, unsubscribe hardening
findings.fixSummary: chat/route.ts now calls checkRateLimit with key=ai-chat:{userId}, 60 requests per hour (RATE_LIMITS.aiChat). Returns 429 if exceeded.

findings.title: Admin PATCH endpoint has no rate limit on re-auth attempts
findings.description: The password re-authentication gate added in AUDIT-003 is correct but the PATCH /api/v3/admin endpoint has no rate limit. An attacker with a compromised admin session (but not the password) can brute-force the admin password by replaying PATCH requests at unlimited speed.
findings.recommendation: Apply a strict per-admin-user rate limit (e.g. 5 failures per 15 minutes) on the PATCH endpoint before the password check.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): rate limiting, 2FA gate, LIKE escaping, DKIM timeout, CSP, unsubscribe hardening
findings.fixSummary: admin/route.ts PATCH checks checkRateLimit with key=admin-reauth:{userId}:{ip}, 10 attempts per 15 minutes (RATE_LIMITS.adminReauth). Returns 429 if exceeded.

findings.title: Share tokens stored plaintext in scan_history (ref: AUDIT-002#secrets-01)
findings.description: scan_history.share_token holds the raw 64-char hex token. A DB read yields all active share URLs. Share token hashing requires a schema change to store the hash and update the lookup query in /api/v3/shared/[token] and /api/v3/badge/[token].
findings.recommendation: ALTER TABLE scan_history ADD COLUMN share_token_hash TEXT; store sha256(token) at write time; look up by hash; backfill existing rows; then DROP COLUMN share_token.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): DB migration v3.1.0 + TOTP replay + share-token hash lookup
findings.fixSummary: Migration adds scan_history.share_token_hash as a PostgreSQL GENERATED ALWAYS AS column (encode(sha256(share_token::bytea),'hex') STORED). All existing rows are auto-backfilled. shared/[token] and badge/[token] routes now look up by sha256(token) computed in Node.js.

findings.title: billing_verification_codes missing per-row salt
findings.description: Verification codes in billing_verification_codes are hashed without a per-row salt. If the table is leaked, codes can be cracked with a rainbow table over the small (typically 6-digit numeric) code space.
findings.recommendation: ALTER TABLE billing_verification_codes ADD COLUMN salt TEXT; generate random salt per code; store hash(salt || code); verify by re-hashing with the stored salt.
findings.fixSummary: Migration 3.0.0-to-3.1.0.mjs adds billing_verification_codes.salt TEXT. Application code (billing-verify routes) must be updated to write random salts and verify via hash(salt+code). Column exists but write/verify logic is pending.

findings.title: CSP img-src bare https: wildcard permits image-based data exfiltration
findings.description: middleware.ts had img-src 'self' data: blob: https: which allows images to be loaded from any HTTPS host, enabling CSS/image-based side-channel exfiltration and widening the XSS surface.
findings.recommendation: Replaced bare https: with an explicit allowlist: https://www.browserbase.com https://static.cloudflareinsights.com https://*.tawk.to https://va.tawk.to https://cdn.discordapp.com

findings.title: Internal AI endpoint URL exposed in unauthenticated GET /api/v3/ai/info
findings.description: The GET handler in ai/info/route.ts returned url: baseUrl ?? '' in its JSON response with no authentication check. This exposes the internal provider base URL (e.g. a self-hosted Ollama or custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint) to any unauthenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: Removed the url field entirely from the response.

findings.title: Per-request DDL migration and unbounded payload in ai/conversations
findings.description: ai/conversations/route.ts called a migrate() function on every POST request that executed CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS on every invocation — a DDL lock on every chat message. The same route also stored JSONB messages with no size limit, allowing a malicious client to write arbitrarily large rows.
findings.recommendation: Removed migrate() function and all calls. Added 100KB size limit (JSON.stringify(messages).length > 100_000 → 413).

findings.title: Protocol-relative URL bypass in notification link validation
findings.description: admin/notifications/[id]/route.ts validated link fields with lower.startsWith('/') to allow relative paths. Protocol-relative URLs (//attacker.com/path) also start with '/' and pass this check, causing the browser to navigate to an attacker-controlled HTTPS URL.
findings.recommendation: Changed check to startsWith('/') && !startsWith('//').

findings.title: Self-account-delete has no password challenge or grace period
findings.description: POST /api/v3/account/delete destroys the account immediately. No password re-entry, no email confirmation, no grace period.
findings.recommendation: Require currentPassword before deletion; send confirmation email with revocation link; implement a 7-day grace period (mark disabled instead of hard-delete).

findings.title: 4 admin routes bypass logAuditAction (audit-log regression)
findings.description: After AUDIT-001 added logAuditAction with email redaction, 4 admin sites still use raw pool.query to insert audit log rows. The plain emails (team.owner_email, etc.) leak into the 365-day-retained details column.
findings.recommendation: Replace raw INSERT INTO admin_audit_log calls with logAuditAction() helper from lib/auth/authorization.ts.

findings.title: Signup rate-limited only by IP, not by email
findings.description: Per-IP signup throttling only. No per-email cap. Attacker can rotate IPs to enumerate which emails are registered (409 vs success differentiates them) and DoS by flooding signup tables.
findings.recommendation: Add per-email throttling (e.g., 5 per hour per email).

findings.title: docker-compose postgres uses mutable postgres:16-alpine tag
findings.description: Postgres image is on a moving tag, not pinned to a specific minor or digest. A poisoned upstream push silently propagates.
findings.recommendation: Pin to postgres:16.4-alpine or @sha256:<digest>.

findings.title: URL-length cap missing in bulk/crawl/discover
findings.description: AUDIT-001#scanner-02 fixed MAX_URL_LENGTH in scan/route.ts but the sibling routes (bulk, crawl, discover, crawl/discover) iterate user URLs through validateScanTarget + safeFetch + DB INSERT without the same length pre-check. A 50MB URL string is accepted.
findings.recommendation: Add if (url.length > SCANNING.MAX_URL_LENGTH) return 400 to each handler, OR extract a shared assertUrlLength helper.

findings.title: Share tokens stored plaintext in scan_history
findings.description: share_token is a 64-char hex random in plaintext. A DB read yields all share URLs, granting indefinite read access to long-lived shared scans.
findings.recommendation: Store sha256(share_token) at rest; look up by hashed value; return raw token only at creation time (already done).

findings.title: Team invite tokens stored plaintext
findings.description: team_invites.token is plaintext. No rate limit on accept-invite either.
findings.recommendation: Hash tokens at rest; add per-IP rate limit on accept-invite.

findings.title: Password reset does not clear device_trust rows
findings.description: reset-password deletes sessions but NOT device_trust. An attacker who previously compromised the device (got the device_trust cookie planted) can still bypass 2FA on subsequent logins.
findings.recommendation: Add DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1 in the same transaction as the session wipe.

findings.title: Login timing oracle leaks registered emails
findings.description: No-user path returned ~5-20ms; user-exists path ran scrypt (80-200ms). Observable delta.
findings.recommendation: No-user path runs verifyPassword against a precomputed dummy hash to equalize timing.

findings.title: account/delete blocked by FK violation on admin_audit_log
findings.description: admin_audit_log.target_user_id and access_rules.created_by had no ON DELETE clause; user self-delete returned 500.
findings.recommendation: Self-healing idempotent migration adds fk_admin_audit_target_user ON DELETE SET NULL and fk_access_rules_created_by ON DELETE SET NULL on startup.

findings.title: SMTP transport fell back to plaintext
findings.description: secure:false without requireTLS meant misconfigured relays could send password-reset + 2FA codes in cleartext.
findings.recommendation: Port 465 -> secure:true. Port 587/25 -> requireTLS:true. Min TLSv1.2.

findings.title: Audit-log IPs read leftmost X-Forwarded-For (spoofable)
findings.description: 7 routes trusted the client-supplied IP without consulting TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDR.
findings.recommendation: Replace with await getClientIp() everywhere.

findings.title: browser/sessions had no per-user cap (financial DoS)
findings.description: A compromised session could rack up real BrowserBase costs by spawning unlimited sessions.
findings.recommendation: Added RATE_LIMITS.browserSession (20/hour per user).

findings.title: window_start at ms precision created a fresh bucket per request
findings.description: ON CONFLICT(key, window_start) matched exact ms; attacker firing N requests in 1ms got N buckets at count=1.
findings.recommendation: Quantize window_start to floor(epoch_ms / window_ms) * window_ms.

findings.title: access-rules catch block failed open
findings.description: DB error in blacklist query silently allowed every scan through — turning a DB outage into a blacklist bypass.
findings.recommendation: Catch block now returns { allowed: false } — fail-closed.

findings.title: No URL length cap at scan API boundary
findings.description: CONFIG_MAX_URL_LENGTH was defined but never enforced — a 50MB URL string hit DNS resolution and DB INSERT.
findings.recommendation: Reject with 400 before any DNS / DB work when url.length > SCANNING.MAX_URL_LENGTH.

findings.title: scan_history.response_headers stored Set-Cookie values
findings.description: Scan-target session cookies persisted to DB indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: redactSensitiveResponseHeaders strips Set-Cookie / Cookie / Authorization / etc. before insert.

findings.title: Bulk scan limit hardcoded to 10 instead of MAX_URLS_IN_BULK (100)
findings.description: Self-hosters configuring MAX_URLS_IN_BULK got silent bypass.
findings.recommendation: Use SCANNING.MAX_URLS_IN_BULK.

findings.title: admin_audit_log.details stored raw user emails (365-day retention)
findings.description: Emails leaked in audit log long after the user changed or deleted their address.
findings.recommendation: Central logAuditAction helper masks any email-like substring via redactEmailsInDetails before insert.

findings.title: Two more product-surface tablists declare tab roles with no tabpanel, aria-controls or arrow-key navigation
findings.description: Extends AUDIT-011#docs-11, which covered components/docs/docs-code-tabs.tsx:30 and app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:420. The same incomplete pattern exists twice more, outside docs: components/scanner/issue-detail.tsx:896-916 renders `role="tablist" aria-label="Code examples"` with `role="tab" aria-selected` buttons over a `<CodeBlock>` at :921 that is not `role="tabpanel"` and carries no id, and no button has `aria-controls`; app/assets/page.tsx:159-183 renders the My-scans / All-public-hosts scope toggle as `role="tablist"` + `role="tab" aria-selected` where the thing it switches is the page's own list, with no tabpanel, no aria-controls and no roving tabindex. Neither has an onKeyDown for ArrowLeft/ArrowRight, so the arrow-key roving focus the tab role promises is absent in both. Of the five tablists in the repo, only app/docs/api/page.tsx:1235-1263 is complete (aria-controls="code-tabpanel" at :1246 with a matching role="tabpanel" at :1263).
findings.impact: Assistive tech announces "tab, 1 of 3" and then arrow keys do nothing, which is worse than announcing plain buttons because the user is told a navigation model that is not implemented. On issue-detail this is the fix-example switcher inside every finding, so it is on the product's main output path rather than in docs.
findings.recommendation: For app/assets/page.tsx:159, drop the tablist/tab roles entirely and use `aria-pressed` toggle buttons, which is what the control actually is (the codebase already uses that shape 27 times). For components/scanner/issue-detail.tsx:896, either do the same or complete the pattern: give CodeBlock a wrapper with `role="tabpanel" id` and `aria-labelledby`, give each button an id and `aria-controls`, and add ArrowLeft/ArrowRight roving focus.

findings.title: The signed-in app header marks the current page with colour alone, with no aria-current, while the landing nav next to it does it correctly
findings.description: components/scanner/header.tsx:153-183 is the primary navigation for every signed-in page. It computes `const active = isNavActive(href)` at :155 and expresses it only as `bg-primary/10 text-primary font-medium` at :166, with no `aria-current`. The `<nav>` at :153 also has no `aria-label`, and neither does the mobile one at :234, so a screen reader lists two or three unnamed navigation landmarks per page. Thirteen other places in the codebase do set aria-current, including the landing nav that renders in exactly the same slot for signed-out users (components/landing/landing-nav.tsx:82 and :159), the docs sidebar (components/docs/docs-sidebar.tsx:53), the legal nav (components/legal/legal-nav.tsx:43) and the pagination control (components/ui/pagination-control.tsx:171). The admin link at header.tsx:171-181 has the same gap.
findings.impact: A screen-reader user in the signed-in app is never told which nav item corresponds to the page they are on, and the visual cue that would tell a sighted user is a colour that itself fails contrast in light mode (see a11y-02: text-primary on bg-primary/10 computes to 2.08:1). WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color plus a missed 4.1.2 name-role-value.
