Also absent and load-bearing: `rate_limits` (lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit.ts:148, every rate-limited endpoint), `notification_preferences` (inserted on every signup at app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:200 and on every OAuth signup at oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:239), `processed_stripe_events` (the Stripe webhook idempotency guard at app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:168, whose own instrumentation.ts comment at :536-543 documents what happened the last time it was missing: every Stripe retry reprocessed as a new event), and the three payment idempotency ledgers ai_credit_purchases, github_credit_purchases and browserbase_credit_purchases, each of which is the sole guard against double-crediting a purchase (lib/billing/ai-usage.ts:160-172). Every one of those tables is created inside a `.catch()` that only console.errors, exactly the failure mode this list exists to catch.
findings.impact: The health endpoint is the operator's only signal that the boot-time schema sequence half-completed. Today it can report schema_ok with no missing tables while sessions, rate_limits or processed_stripe_events do not exist, which means a monitor watching /api/v3/health stays green through an outage that makes login impossible or through a state where every Stripe webhook replay re-grants a plan.
findings.recommendation: Add sessions, rate_limits, notification_preferences, processed_stripe_events, ai_credit_purchases, github_credit_purchases and browserbase_credit_purchases to REQUIRED_TABLES, plus staff_invites and admin_audit_log_archive once schema-02 is fixed. The docstring's argument against exhaustiveness (drift with instrumentation.ts) holds for a full 66-name list but not for the seven tables whose absence takes down auth, rate limiting, signup or billing idempotency.

findings.title: The five most load-bearing enum columns (users.role, users.plan, team_members.role, domains.status, gifted_subscriptions.plan) have no CHECK constraint, while a dozen cosmetic ones do
findings.description: CHECK coverage on enum-like text columns is inverted relative to importance. Constrained: admin_notifications.type/variant/audience (:969-971), access_rules.rule_type/value_type (:1007-1008), security_alerts.severity (:1097), broadcast_messages.message_type/status (:1135, :1141), broadcast_recipients.status (:1157), scan_finding_feedback.verdict (:1463), finding_remediation.status (:1506), scan_history.status (:1623), scan_tags.source (:2449), promoted_auto_tag_rules.min_severity (:2944), host_badges.scope (:3411), support_tickets.category/status (:3435-3437). Unconstrained: users.role (:292, values user/beta_tester/support/moderator/admin/super_admin plus the billing, security_analyst, content_manager and ops roles in STAFF_ROLES at lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:22), users.plan (:295), gifted_subscriptions.plan (:949), team_members.role (:898) and team_invites.role (:909), domains.status (:3178, whose 'verified' value is the gate that authorizes intrusive active probing, see lib/domains/scope.ts), scheduled_scans.frequency (:458), webhooks.type (:477), data_requests.status (:873), billing_history.status (:527), user_notifications.type (:1662), email_logs.status (:675), scan_history.source (:424) and .scan_type (:2076), users.auth_provider (:1878), .two_factor_method (:315), .subscription_status (:298) and .billing_interval (:2683). The concrete consequence is in lib/database/cleanup.ts:152-195: the per-plan scan retention runs four DELETEs whose WHERE clauses match the literals 'free' (or NULL), 'core_supporter', 'pro_supporter' and 'elite_supporter'. A users.plan value outside that set matches none of them, so those scans are retained forever with no error and no log line. lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:96 compounds it by casting an arbitrary column value straight to the enum type (`return effectivePlan as PlanType`) with no membership check, after which lib/billing/plan-limits.ts indexes PLAN_LIMIT_KEYS with it. Every current write path does validate (app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1869-1880 for update_plan, :1652-1657 for gift_subscription, and the billing routes write literals or the output of getPlanFromProductId), so this is a latent constraint gap rather than a live bug: the paths that can introduce a bad value are the SQL repair scripts, scripts/restore-db.mjs, and hand-run SQL, all of which the self-hosting docs point operators at.
findings.impact: The database does not enforce the value sets that authorization and money decisions are made from. A users.plan value outside the four known literals silently exempts that account's scan history from every retention rule in lib/database/cleanup.ts, so their data is kept forever with no error, and lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:96 hands the same unchecked string to the plan-limits resolver. A users.role value outside the known set fails closed for staff checks but is invisible in the admin panel, and a domains.status other than 'verified' or 'pending' is treated as unverified with no signal that the row is malformed. Every one of these is reachable through the documented self-hosted repair and restore scripts, which is precisely the situation a CHECK exists for.
findings.recommendation: Add CHECK constraints for the five that carry real authorization or money semantics: users.role against the union of STAFF_ROLES plus user, beta_tester and super_admin; users.plan and gifted_subscriptions.plan against the four PlanId values in lib/billing/catalog.ts:12; team_members.role and team_invites.role against the team role set; domains.status against pending/verified/reverify_failed. Use the drop-and-recreate pattern already used for scan_tags_source_check at instrumentation.ts:2469-2475 so widening one later stays possible. Separately, make lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:96 validate membership before the cast and fall back to 'free' instead of casting blind, and make the cleanup retention in lib/database/cleanup.ts cover the else case rather than silently skipping it.

findings.title: broadcast_recipients has no UNIQUE(message_id, user_id), so the mass-email send loop uses a read-then-insert guard that two concurrent sends both pass
findings.description: broadcast_recipients (instrumentation.ts:1151-1162) has a surrogate `id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` and two separate single-column indexes on message_id and user_id, and no uniqueness on the pair. The send handler and the resend handler each compensate in the application, with a comment that says so verbatim: "broadcast_recipients has no unique key, so this is an app-level guard rather than ON CONFLICT" (app/api/v3/admin/features/route.ts:555-557 and the duplicated copy at :717-719). The guard is `SELECT 1 FROM broadcast_recipients WHERE message_id = $1 AND user_id = $2 AND status = 'sent' LIMIT 1` followed, if the select returned nothing, by sendEmail and then a plain INSERT (:559-573 and :721-735). Nothing serialises the two steps, and the same recipient is only marked after the SMTP round trip completes, so the window between the SELECT and the INSERT is the full duration of one email send. Two admins hitting send and resend for the same message, or one admin double-clicking, or the resend path racing a still-running first send, both pass the SELECT for the same recipient and both send.
findings.impact: The whole verified user base can receive the same broadcast twice, from a feature whose stated design goal in that comment is that it must not. AUDIT-012#perf-07 already established that this loop iterates every verified user with no LIMIT and does one SELECT plus one INSERT plus one sequential SMTP call per recipient, so the race window per recipient is large and the number of recipients is unbounded. Duplicate mass email is the fastest way to get a sending domain reputation-flagged.
findings.recommendation: Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_broadcast_recipients_message_user ON broadcast_recipients(message_id, user_id);` in instrumentation.ts and replace both read-then-insert blocks with an insert-first claim: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (message_id, user_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING id, send the email only when a row came back, then UPDATE the status. That also satisfies AUDIT-012#perf-15's item (8), which asked for a plain composite index on the same two columns for the read side, so one unique index covers both findings.

findings.title: users.unsubscribe_token is the sole lookup key of a public unauthenticated endpoint and has neither an index nor a UNIQUE constraint
findings.description: unsubscribe_token is added at instrumentation.ts:1248-1250 as `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS unsubscribe_token UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` with no NOT NULL, no UNIQUE, and no CREATE INDEX anywhere in the file (grep for the column name in instrumentation.ts returns only that one line). It is the only credential the unsubscribe flow has: app/api/v3/account/unsubscribe/route.ts:33 runs `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE unsubscribe_token = $1` for the GET and :68 runs `SELECT id FROM users WHERE unsubscribe_token = $1` for the POST, both unauthenticated, and the token is embedded in every outbound notification email by lib/notifications/notifications.ts:98-105. Every other token column in the schema that identifies a row is declared UNIQUE (scan_history.share_token :425, team_invites.token :910, host_badges.badge_token :3362, staff_invites.token in lib/admin/staff-invites.ts:37) and most also carry an index. Collision is not realistic given the UUID default (the volatile default makes ADD COLUMN rewrite the table and evaluate gen_random_uuid per existing row, so every row gets a distinct value), but the database does not guarantee it and nothing prevents an out-of-band UPDATE or a restore from creating a duplicate, in which case `rows[0]` picks an arbitrary one of the two accounts and unsubscribes the wrong user.
findings.impact: Both unsubscribe lookups sequentially scan the entire users table on every click of an unsubscribe link in any notification email, which is the one link in the product that must work reliably for CAN-SPAM and GDPR compliance. The uniqueness the code depends on to identify an account is a convention, not a constraint, on the one column the app trusts to authenticate an unauthenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: In instrumentation.ts, next to the ALTER at :1248, add `UPDATE users SET unsubscribe_token = gen_random_uuid() WHERE unsubscribe_token IS NULL;` then `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_unsubscribe_token ON users(unsubscribe_token);`, following the same backfill-then-unique-index pattern already used for scan_history.public_id at :2609-2619. That fixes the sequential scan and the missing guarantee in one statement.

findings.title: users.updated_at is exported as the account's last-modified timestamp in both GDPR data exports while roughly two dozen UPDATE paths never bump it
findings.description: users.updated_at is `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW()` (instrumentation.ts:321) with no NOT NULL and no trigger; no table in the schema has an updated_at trigger, so the column is only correct where a hand-written `updated_at = NOW()` appears in the UPDATE. Eight sites do that (app/actions/stripe.ts:110, app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1884, lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:94, :110, :149, instrumentation.ts:2725, and the two role-change paths). About two dozen do not, including every security-relevant one: `UPDATE users SET role = $1` (app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:652, :703, :718), `UPDATE users SET disabled_at = NOW()` and the re-enable (:898, :935), the entire 2FA lifecycle (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:69, :153, :187; 2fa/disable/route.ts:57; 2fa/email-setup/route.ts:55, :122; 2fa/backup-codes/route.ts:110; 2fa/verify/route.ts:180), OAuth link and unlink (app/api/v3/account/oauth/[provider]/route.ts:143, :150; account/discord/route.ts:240), the privacy toggles (account/privacy/route.ts:45, account/share-privacy/route.ts:59, account/posture-digest/route.ts:48) and every `UPDATE users SET stripe_customer_id` (app/actions/stripe.ts:130, :401, :614, :759). The column is nonetheless surfaced to users as fact: the admin export_data handler selects it at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1275 and the self-service GDPR export selects it at app/api/v3/data-request/route.ts:129-131, in both cases as the account's last-updated timestamp.
findings.impact: A user who exercises their right of access gets an updated_at that can be months stale, having missed their own 2FA enrolment, every role change, an account suspension and un-suspension, and every OAuth connection change. For an operator debugging "when did this account change", the column is misleading rather than merely absent, which is worse.
findings.recommendation: Add one trigger function and attach it to the tables that expose updated_at, rather than auditing two dozen call sites: `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;` then a `BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW` trigger on users, notification_preferences, discord_connections, github_connections, user_ai_configs, staff_activity and support_tickets. Add it to the boot block in instrumentation.ts guarded by CREATE OR REPLACE and DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS so it stays idempotent. While there, add NOT NULL to created_at and updated_at, which the newer tables already declare (compare :640 and :678 against :320).

findings.title: users.email UNIQUE is case-sensitive, so the one-account-per-address invariant is a convention repeated across eight call sites rather than a database guarantee
findings.description: `email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL` (instrumentation.ts:284) gives a case-sensitive unique index, so 'Alice@example.com' and 'alice@example.com' are two legal rows. Every read and write currently normalizes by hand: lib/database/db-utils.ts:40 (`[email.toLowerCase().trim()]`), lib/auth/auth.ts:287 for createUser, :355 and :387 for createOAuthUser, app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:155 before both the identity lookup and the collision check at :204, app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts:61-63 before storing an invite email, and app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:129 for the per-email rate-limit key. That convention currently holds everywhere I checked, so this is a latent gap rather than a live bug, but it is enforced only by every author remembering it. app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts:202 inserts `invite.email` straight into users with no normalization of its own; it is correct today only because the admin route lowercased the value before storing the invite. Two paths look up by raw email without a visible lowercase in the same file: app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:254 (`SELECT unsubscribe_token FROM users WHERE email = $1`) and app/api/v3/admin/features/route.ts:543 (the broadcast segment filter `AND u.email = $1`).
findings.impact: If any future write path forgets the lowercase, the resulting row is invisible to getUserByEmail, so that account can never sign in with a password and a second account can be created for the same human without tripping the UNIQUE constraint. The failure is silent at write time and only surfaces later as "I can't log in" plus two accounts for one address, which is expensive to untangle once billing and scan history exist under both.
findings.recommendation: Replace the plain UNIQUE with a case-insensitive one in instrumentation.ts: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_email_lower ON users(lower(email));` (it also replaces the redundant idx_users_email from schema-05), keeping the existing constraint until the new index is verified. That makes the invariant a database guarantee, and it is also the index that would serve a lookup rewritten as `WHERE lower(email) = $1`.

findings.title: The four manifests disagree about Node: cli declares >=18 (EOL since April 2025) while root and extension declare >=22, marketing declares nothing, and CI only ever runs the CLI on Node 22
findings.description: `cli/package.json:16` declares `"node": ">=18"`, `package.json:8` declares `"node": ">=22.0.0"`, `extension/package.json:9` declares `"node": ">=22.0.0"`, and `marketing/package.json` declares no `engines` field at all. The Node 18 claim is repeated to users in three places: `cli/README.md:5` ("no dependencies (Node 18+ for global fetch)"), `cli/vulnradar.mjs:4` ("No dependencies: Node 18+ (global fetch) is all it needs"), and the docs page at `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:95` ("It needs Node 18 or newer"). Node 18 reached end of life on 2025-04-30 and receives no security updates. It is also never exercised: the only place the CLI runs in CI is `.github/workflows/ci.yml:110`, `node --test` with `working-directory: cli`, inside the `test` job whose `setup-node` step pins `node-version: "22"` (line 47). So the supported-floor claim is asserted in three user-facing places and validated in none. Node's own `--test` runner also behaved differently in 18 (experimental, narrower default file-glob) than in 22, so `node --test` with no path argument is not guaranteed to discover `cli/vulnradar.test.mjs` there.
findings.impact: A user or a CI pipeline pinned to Node 18 follows the documented floor, runs the CLI on a runtime that has had no security patches for over a year, and hits any regression alone because nothing tests that version. Meanwhile a contributor who reads the root manifest reasonably assumes Node 22 is the repo-wide floor and may use a Node 20-or-22-only API in cli/lib.mjs without any check catching it.
findings.recommendation: Raise `cli/package.json:16` to `">=20"` (the oldest Node still in maintenance) or to `">=22"` to match the other three manifests, and update the three copy sites: `cli/README.md:5`, the header comment at `cli/vulnradar.mjs:4`, and `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:95`. If Node 18 support is genuinely wanted, add a matrix entry to the CLI test step in `.github/workflows/ci.yml:110` that runs `node --test` on 18 as well. Also add `"engines": { "node": ">=22.0.0" }` to `marketing/package.json` so all four agree.

findings.title: The root is on TypeScript 6.0.3 and the extension on 5.9.3, so extension source is type-checked by 5.9 in CI while a root-level editor and root eslint analyze the same files with 6.0
findings.description: `package.json:135` pins the root to `"typescript": "6.0.3"`; `extension/package.json:36` declares `"typescript": "^5.7.2"`, resolved to 5.9.3; `marketing/package.json:22` pins 5.9.3. `extension/package.json:20` runs `tsc --noEmit` from the extension's own node_modules, so CI's extension typecheck (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:141`) uses 5.9.3. But the extension's source is also analyzed by the root toolchain: `eslint.config.mjs:22` lists ignores for `scripts/**`, `cli/**`, `dist/**` and others but not `extension/**`, and I verified the effect directly, `npx eslint --print-config extension/src/lib/api.ts` returns a full config while `npx eslint --print-config cli/lib.mjs` returns `undefined` (the marker for an ignored path). So `npm run lint` at the root parses extension TypeScript with @typescript-eslint 8.67.0 while CI type-checks it with tsc 5.9.3, and any editor opened at the repo root resolves the root's typescript 6.0.3 for those same files. The root's Dependabot config already acknowledges this class of problem at `.github/dependabot.yml`, where the ignore list holds TypeScript majors because "@typescript-eslint ... peer range caps at <6.1.0", but that reasoning was applied only to the root manifest.
findings.impact: A developer editing extension/src sees diagnostics from TypeScript 6.0.3 in their editor that CI (5.9.3) does not produce, and vice versa. A syntax or type feature added in 6.0 compiles in the editor and fails the extension CI job, or a 5.9-only behaviour passes CI and shows as an editor error, in both cases with no obvious explanation because the version difference is invisible from the file being edited. Running eslint over the extension's build output is harmless today (I ran `npx eslint extension/dist-chrome/popup.js` and it reports nothing) but it is unintended coverage.
findings.recommendation: Align `extension/package.json:36` and `marketing/package.json:22` to the root's TypeScript major, or, if the extension must stay on 5.x, add a comment in `extension/package.json` saying why and add `"extension/dist-chrome/**"`, `"extension/dist-firefox/**"` to the `ignores` array in `eslint.config.mjs:22` so root lint never walks generated bundles.

findings.title: The packaged extension carries no license text and no third-party attribution, although it bundles the MPL-2.0 webextension-polyfill and BSD-3-Clause lit-html verbatim into background.js and content.js
findings.category: missing license and attribution in a distributed artifact
findings.description: `extension/package.json:5` declares `"license": "GPL-3.0"`, but there is no LICENSE file anywhere under `extension/` and none in the built output: `dist-chrome/` contains only assets, chunks, background.js, content.js, the three page bundles, their .map files, favicon.svg, icons/ and manifest.json. `extension/scripts/package.mjs:66` zips exactly that directory for store upload, so the Chrome Web Store and AMO packages ship with no license text. The two runtime dependencies are inlined into those bundles by the IIFE build at `extension/scripts/build.mjs:59`: `webextension-polyfill@0.12.0` is MPL-2.0 (verified from its package.json) and `lit-html@3.3.3` is BSD-3-Clause, and both appear as sources in the emitted map (`dist-chrome/content.js.map` lists `../node_modules/webextension-polyfill/dist/browser-polyfill.js` and `../node_modules/lit-html/lit-html.js` first in its `sources` array). MPL-2.0 section 3.2 requires that recipients of the binary be informed of the license and be able to obtain the source of the covered files. The source zip built by `extension/scripts/package-source.mjs` is submitted to AMO only, so Chrome Web Store users get neither a license notice nor a source pointer. That same script also has no LICENSE to include: it archives every top-level entry in `extension/` except node_modules, the dist dirs, out/, zips and tsbuildinfo, and there is no license file among them.
findings.impact: Every Chrome Web Store install of a GPL-3.0 project receives a binary with no copy of the GPL and no notice for the MPL-2.0 code compiled into it. It is a compliance gap rather than a user-facing break, but it is an avoidable one for a project whose whole pitch is open source.
findings.recommendation: Add a `LICENSE` file to `extension/` (a copy of the root GPL-3.0 text) plus a short `THIRD-PARTY.md` listing webextension-polyfill (MPL-2.0, link to its source) and lit-html (BSD-3-Clause). Copy both into the build output from `extension/scripts/build.mjs` in the same loop that copies icons (around line 103) so they land in `dist-chrome/` and `dist-firefox/` and therefore in the store zip.

findings.title: cli/package.json is publishable but incomplete: no `private` flag, a `name` that collides with the root manifest, no `repository`, and a `files` list that omits the license it declares
findings.description: `cli/package.json` declares `"name": "vulnradar"` (line 2), `"license": "GPL-3.0"` (line 5), a `bin` entry (line 7), and `"files": ["vulnradar.mjs", "lib.mjs", "README.md"]` (line 10). It has no `"private": true`, so `npm publish` from that directory would succeed. Three things are missing or wrong for that path. The `name` is identical to the root manifest's `"name": "vulnradar"` at `package.json:2`, which is only harmless because the root sets `"private": true` at line 6; the CLI does not. There is no `repository` field, so the published page would carry no source link and no npm provenance attestation. And `files` omits any license file (there is none in `cli/` to include), so a GPL-3.0 tarball would ship without its license text. On the positive side the package is genuinely dependency-free: `cli/vulnradar.mjs` imports only `./lib.mjs`, `cli/lib.mjs` imports nothing, and both use only global `fetch`, `process` and `console`, so there is no accidental dependency on the app's runtime and no lockfile is needed. This finding is the mechanical half of subdeps-01: fixing that one means publishing this manifest, and it is not ready.
findings.impact: A publish today produces a package with no repo link, no provenance, and no license file, under a name that shadows the root manifest. Minor on its own, but subdeps-01 argues the name should be claimed soon, and this is what has to be corrected first.
findings.recommendation: Before publishing, add `"repository": { "type": "git", "url": "git+https://github.com/VulnRadar/vulnradar.dev.git", "directory": "cli" }` to `cli/package.json`, add a `LICENSE` file in `cli/` and list it in `files` at line 10, and publish with `npm publish --provenance` from CI so the tarball carries a signed attestation.

findings.title: vitest collects only .test.ts, so a .test.tsx file is silently never run, and with no DOM environment or testing-library dependency no component can be rendered in a test at all
findings.description: vitest.config.ts:24 sets `include: ["tests/**/*.test.ts", "tests/**/*.spec.ts"]` and line 23 sets `environment: "node"`. Neither `.test.tsx` nor `.spec.tsx` is collected, and package.json declares no jsdom, happy-dom, @testing-library/react, or @testing-library/dom dependency (grep returns nothing for all four). Counted: tests/ holds 356 `.test.ts` files, 0 `.spec.ts`, and 0 `.test.tsx`. The 8 files under tests/components/ test only extracted pure helpers (queue-status-utils, settings-registry-utils, utils, danger-score-trend), not components. The mechanical failure: a contributor adds `tests/components/scanner/scan-form.test.tsx`, runs `npm test`, gets a normal green run with no warning that their file was not collected (vitest reports nothing about files outside `include`), and ships. Even a `.test.ts` file that imported a component would fail, since `environment: "node"` supplies no document.
findings.impact: Two effects. First, a contributor can believe they have shipped a test that has never run once, which is worse than no test. Second, none of the 266 .tsx files under components/ has any behavioural test, so hook state, conditional rendering, and event handlers are covered only by the typechecker. Given the AUDIT-011 critical finding was a UI regression (admin row actions invisible but still hit-testable on touch), that gap is the one most likely to recur.
findings.recommendation: Add `"tests/**/*.test.tsx"` and `"tests/**/*.spec.tsx"` to `include` in vitest.config.ts:24 so a .tsx suite cannot be silently skipped. If component tests are wanted, add jsdom plus @testing-library/react as devDependencies and set `environment` per file via the `// @vitest-environment jsdom` docblock rather than switching the whole suite off node.

findings.title: Fourteen tests assert only .not.toThrow(), and two of them name a behavioural contract the assertion never checks
findings.description:
A scripted pass over all 4,494 it/test blocks found 14 whose every expect matcher is `not.toThrow`. Most are honest ("does not throw on truncated markup"), but two claim a behaviour they do not verify. tests/lib/scanner/safety-rating.test.ts:215 is titled "falls back to a default weight for an unrecognized severity string" and its whole body is `expect(() => getDangerScore([{ severity: "unknown", title: "Something Odd" }])).not.toThrow()`. The fallback it names is lib/scanner/safety-rating.ts:327, `const baseWeight = SEVERITY_WEIGHTS[sev] ?? 0.1`. Exact mutation not caught: change `?? 0.1` to `?? 10` and the test passes, while every scan containing one finding with an unrecognised severity string jumps to the top of the danger scale and the site is reported unsafe. tests/lib/scanner/html/tokenizer.test.ts:103 is titled "does not create an element for an end tag with no matching start" and asserts only `expect(() => toElements(tokenize("

ok

"))).not.toThrow()`. Exact mutation not caught: make toElements emit an element for the stray ``, and the test passes while every page check that counts or walks elements sees a phantom node. The other 12 are: tests/lib/api/playground.test.ts:67, tests/lib/api/request-utils.test.ts:93, tests/lib/auth/password-hash.test.ts:45, tests/lib/backup/job-store.test.ts:53 and :57, tests/lib/database/error-log-capture.test.ts:87, tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts:72 (filed separately as tq-03), tests/lib/scanner/html/tokenizer.test.ts:68, tests/lib/scanner/page-context.test.ts:144, tests/lib/scanner/scan-jobs.test.ts:155, tests/lib/ui/url-state.test.ts:66, tests/lib/updater/job-store.test.ts:52.
findings.impact: Two named contracts, the danger-score fallback weight and the tokenizer's stray-end-tag handling, have a test that reads as covering them in a coverage review but cannot fail on a wrong answer, only on a crash. The danger score is the number shown to users as the site's safety rating, so a wrong fallback weight is directly user visible.
findings.recommendation:
In tests/lib/scanner/safety-rating.test.ts:215, assert the score itself: compare `getDangerScore([{ severity: "unknown", ... }])` against the value implied by the 0.1 weight, and add a sibling case proving an unknown severity scores strictly below an info finding. In tests/lib/scanner/html/tokenizer.test.ts:103, assert `toElements(tokenize("

ok

")).map(e => e.tag)` equals `["p"]`. Leave the other 12 as they are; their titles match what they assert.

findings.title: Thirteen tests assert only that a value exists (toBeDefined / toBeTruthy / not.toBeNull) where the contract they name is the value's content
findings.description: Scripted over all 4,494 blocks: 13 have no assertion stronger than a positive-existence matcher. The ones where the content is the actual contract: tests/lib/scanner/checks-data/_schema.test.ts:77 "every entry has required fields" loops the required list (id, title, category, severity, description, evidence, fixSteps, codeExamples) and asserts `expect(entry[field]).toBeDefined()` at lines 90 to 93, so an entry shipped with `description: ""`, `fixSteps: []`, or `codeExamples: []` passes the only required-fields guard the whole 750-plus check catalogue has. tests/lib/scanner/auth/logout-guard.test.ts:63 "returns a non-secret reason for a destructive URL" asserts only `expect(reason).toBeTruthy()`, so a reason that does leak a credential or query string passes, even though the sibling test at :55 to :60 does run a `not.toMatch(/password|cookie=|token=/i)` check for a different URL. tests/lib/scanner/registry.test.ts:119 is titled "etag-inode uses the real headers.ts detector, not configuration.ts's disabled stub" but asserts the fired finding is defined rather than asserting its identity, the way the sibling tests at :107 and :128 do. Three worker suites (tests/lib/backup/scheduled-backup-worker.test.ts:102, tests/lib/domains/reverify-worker.test.ts:167, tests/lib/notifications/posture-digest.test.ts:331) each assert `toBeDefined` on "registers a timer and cleanly cancels it" without asserting the interval passed to setInterval or that cancel actually clears the same handle. The remaining cases are weaker in form than in substance: tests/lib/auth/password-strength.test.ts:355 and :363 end in `toBeDefined` but pin the text inside the preceding `.find(w => w.includes(...))`, and the four in tests/lib/auth/authorization.test.ts (:128, :146, :159, :228) use `not.toBeNull` as an allow/deny signal that the `it.each` at :95 already backs with an exact object comparison.
findings.impact: Each of these reads as covering a named behaviour but only fails if the code returns nothing at all. The _schema.test.ts:77 case is the widest: it is the single guard over the whole JSON check catalogue and it accepts empty strings and empty arrays for every required field, so a check shipped with a blank description or no fix steps reaches the ~750 public /checks SEO pages and the scan result UI with nothing to render.
findings.recommendation: Tighten the content assertions: in _schema.test.ts:77 replace `toBeDefined` with a non-empty check per field (a string field must be a non-empty string, fixSteps and codeExamples must be non-empty arrays); in logout-guard.test.ts:63 apply the same `not.toMatch(/password|cookie=|token=/i)` assertion the sibling test at :60 already uses; in registry.test.ts:119 assert the detector's identity the way :107 and :128 do; in the three worker suites assert the interval argument passed to setInterval and that clearInterval was called with the same handle.

findings.title: Sixty-five suites index mockQuery.mock.calls positionally while the real 30-second module-level settings cache decides whether a settings query lands in that list, so running a single test with -t can fail a test that passes in a full run
findings.description: lib/config/runtime-config.ts:64 caches the whole system_settings snapshot at module scope for TTL_MS = 30_000. Because vitest isolates per file but not per test, the first it() in a file that reaches a settings read issues a `SELECT key, value FROM system_settings` through the mocked pool and warms the snapshot; every later it() in the same file does not. Any test that then reads `mockQuery.mock.calls[0]` or `[1]` is reading a different call depending on which test ran first. Three suites document the hazard in their own comments and defend against it: tests/app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.test.ts:30-38 ("whichever test first reaches the Promise.all in the route would warm it and silently change how many pool.query calls, and in what order, every later test makes"), tests/lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.test.ts:33-36, and tests/app/api/v3/history/route.test.ts:17-28, which intercepts the settings SQL inside the mock instead. 36 files call invalidateSettingsCache(). Counted: 65 files mock @/lib/database/db, do not mock @/lib/config/runtime-config, never call invalidateSettingsCache, never intercept the system_settings query, and do index mock.calls positionally. vitest.config.ts declares no setupFiles, so every suite has to remember this by hand.
findings.impact: Deterministic today only because vitest runs a file's tests in declaration order. The moment a developer narrows a run with `npx vitest run <file> -t "..."`, a different test warms the cache and the positional index points at the wrong query, producing a failure that does not reproduce in a full run. The same breaks if anyone enables sequence.shuffle or reorders tests during a refactor. The debugging cost is high because the failure looks like a real assertion failure about SQL.
findings.recommendation: Add `setupFiles: ["tests/_setup.ts"]` to the test block in vitest.config.ts and have that file call `invalidateSettingsCache()` in a global beforeEach, so the snapshot is cold for every test in every suite. That removes the hazard for all 191 DB-mocking suites at once and lets the three hand-written guards be deleted.

findings.title: Eight tests create concurrency overlap with real wall-clock sleeps instead of fake timers, in a runner the repo already documents as stalling under parallel load
findings.description: Only 12 of 356 test files use vi.useFakeTimers, and 7 use setSystemTime. Eight tests instead sleep on the real clock to let a concurrent operation interleave: tests/lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.test.ts:63, :85, :87 (10ms each), tests/lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.test.ts:465, :565 (5ms) and :494 (1ms), tests/lib/ai/verify-findings.test.ts:100 (5ms), tests/lib/scanner/protocols/banner-tls-and-capability.test.ts:328, :330 (10ms). The one with a real failure window is tests/lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.test.ts:80, "admits a priority (paid-plan) waiter before a non-priority one queued earlier": it configures BROWSERBASE_QUEUE_MAX_WAIT_MS to 2000, parks two waiters behind two 10ms sleeps, then releases one slot and asserts `paidResult.acquired` is true. If the worker process stalls for more than two seconds anywhere between line 82 and line 89, both waiters time out and the assertion fails with a message about queue priority rather than about scheduling. That stall is not hypothetical here: tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts:65-70 records that the default 5s timeout "has been observed to flake under a full parallel suite run (267 files, heavy CPU contention across workers)", and vitest.config.ts:6-9 exists specifically because worker startup was failing intermittently under memory pressure. The suite has since grown from 267 to 356 files.
findings.impact: An intermittent red CI on a test whose failure message points at browserbase queue priority, not at the runner. That is the kind of failure that gets re-run rather than diagnosed, and repeated re-runs erode trust in the suite.
findings.recommendation: Convert tests/lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.test.ts to vi.useFakeTimers with vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync, so the 2000ms wait window is simulated rather than raced. Where a real sleep is only draining microtasks (the setTimeout(resolve, 0) calls in tests/app/api/v3/scan/route.test.ts:433, tests/lib/scanner/execute-scan.test.ts:529 and friends), leave them: those are deterministic because pending microtasks always drain before a macrotask.

findings.title: The anonymous demo scan abandons runAsyncChecks after its 15 s race, leaving the work and an uncleared timer running with no accounting
findings.description: app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:215-219 builds `const asyncPromise = runAsyncChecks(url)` and races it against `new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve([]), asyncChecksTimeoutMs))` (SCAN_ASYNC_CHECKS_TIMEOUT_MS default 15000, lib/config/config-values.ts:566). When the timeout wins, the handler returns but asyncPromise keeps executing -- runAsyncChecks fans out the full live-fetch battery (~23 exposed-file probes per lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2724, plus GraphQL, bucket-listing and header probes) against the anonymous caller's chosen target with nothing left holding a reference to it. The timeoutPromise's setTimeout is never cleared, so the timer survives to its full 15 s even when the checks finish first. Contrast lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:573-647, which keeps `asyncTimeoutHandle` and clears it in a finally.
findings.impact: The one endpoint reachable with no account at all can leave outbound probe batteries running past the response, so the visible per-IP demo budget (5 per 12 hours) understates the real outbound volume, and slow targets accumulate detached work in the shared process. Bounded in practice by the per-fetch AbortSignal timeouts inside the checks, which is why this is low rather than higher.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts, hold the timeout handle and clearTimeout it after the race (as lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:647 does), and pass an AbortSignal into runAsyncChecks that is aborted when the timeout wins so the abandoned branch actually stops issuing requests.

findings.title: GET /api/v3/host/[hostname] and the badge endpoints are unauthenticated with no rate limiter, so the public-scan corpus can be scraped for free
findings.description: app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts has no getSession call and no checkRateLimit import; its GET at :70 runs two Postgres queries per request -- a host_reputation lookup at :88-103 and, when source_scan_id is set, a scan_history lookup at :140 -- and returns the full findings JSONB plus result_meta. app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/trend/route.ts, app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts and app/api/v3/whoami-ip/route.ts are in the same position (no session, no limiter), while the sibling public listing endpoint app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts:48-51 does gate on `public-scans:${ip}` and documents per-IP as "the only throttle available" for exactly this shape of route.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller can enumerate hostnames at line rate and pull the complete finding set for every publicly-listed scan, and each request costs two DB round trips plus a JSONB serialisation from a connection pool shared with the scan workers. It is free compute and free bulk export of the product's differentiating dataset, with no per-IP ceiling to make it slow. Low rather than higher because the data is public by design and both queries are indexed point lookups.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same `checkRateLimit({ key: \`public-scans:${ip}\`, ...RATE_LIMITS.publicScans })` gate used in app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts:48 to app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts, its /trend sibling and app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts (use the /64-masked key from abuse-08 so it is not trivially rotated).

findings.title: Signup returns 409 for a registered email and 200 for an unregistered one, handing back the enumeration oracle login and password-reset close
findings.description: app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:147-150 does `const existing = await getUserByEmail(email); if (existing) return ApiResponse.conflict(ERROR_MESSAGES.DUPLICATE_EMAIL);` -- a deterministic 409-vs-200 split on whether an address has an account. The rest of the auth surface works hard to avoid exactly this: login returns one generic 401 for both 'no user' and 'wrong password' and burns a dummy scrypt hash to equalize timing (app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:78-86), forgot-password always returns the same 'If an account with that email exists' message (forgot-password/route.ts:64-76), and resend-verification returns the same string on all three outcomes (resend-verification/route.ts:221-236). The route's own comment at lines 124-128 names the problem ('an attacker who rotates IPs via residential proxy can enumerate which emails are registered (409 "already in use" vs 200 success differentiates them)') and answers it with a per-email limit of 5 per hour at line 130 -- which does not remove the oracle at all, because the FIRST request for any address already answers the question. The per-IP `signup:${ip}` bucket is 5 per 15 minutes, so a single residential-proxy pool tests thousands of addresses a day.
findings.impact: Every enumeration defense elsewhere in the auth surface is nullified: an attacker confirms which of a scraped address list has VulnRadar accounts by posting each one to /signup once, then targets those addresses with credential stuffing or phishing that names the product. For a security-tools vendor, the membership list itself ('who at $COMPANY uses a vulnerability scanner') is the interesting output.
findings.recommendation: Make signup answer identically for both cases: on a duplicate email, return the same 200 `SUCCESS_MESSAGES.SIGNUP` + `requiresVerification: true` body the new-account path returns, and instead of creating a row, send the existing account an 'someone tried to sign up with your address, sign in or reset your password' email. Keep the per-email bucket as flood control. The signup form then always shows 'check your email', and the real disambiguation happens in the inbox, which only the address owner can read.

findings.title: Turning 2FA off leaves device_trust rows intact, so a previously trusted device skips the second factor when 2FA is turned back on
findings.description: app/api/v3/auth/2fa/disable/route.ts:56-59 clears `totp_enabled`, `two_factor_method`, `totp_secret`, and `backup_codes`, and app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-setup/route.ts:332-338 (DELETE) clears the first two plus email_2fa_codes -- neither deletes from device_trust. Rows written by upsertTrustedDevice (lib/auth/device-trust.ts:89-116) live for DEVICE_TRUST_DAYS, default 30 (lib/config/config-values.ts:266), and findTrustedDevice (line 14) only checks `user_id + device_fingerprint + expires_at > NOW()`. So a device trusted on day 1, with 2FA disabled on day 2 and re-enabled on day 3, still satisfies the trusted-device bypass at app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:187, app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:369, and app/api/v3/auth/discord/callback/route.ts:278 for the remaining 27 days. The two other places that rotate a credential do get this right and explicitly say why: app/api/v3/auth/reset-password/route.ts:231 and app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:348 both `DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1` alongside the session wipe, with a comment about not leaving a planted trust row behind.
findings.impact: A user who turns 2FA off and back on -- the documented way to re-enroll a new authenticator app, since app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:51-55 refuses to re-enroll while 2FA is active -- believes they have started clean. Any browser that was trusted before, including one an attacker had transient access to, keeps skipping the prompt. The trusted-devices UI (app/api/v3/auth/trusted-devices/route.ts) will list it, but nothing prompts the user to look there during re-enrollment.
findings.recommendation: Add `await pool.query("DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1", [session.userId])` to app/api/v3/auth/2fa/disable/route.ts right after the UPDATE at line 56, and to the DELETE handler in app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-setup/route.ts after line 332 -- matching what reset-password and the password-change path already do.

findings.title: validateApiKey compares the decrypted key with === and falls through to two unindexed full scans of api_keys on every failed lookup
findings.description: Two issues in the same function. (1) After the O(1) locator lookup, the key itself is checked with a plain `if (decrypted === key)` at lib/api/api-keys.ts:350 and again at :374 -- a short-circuiting comparison on a secret, in a file that otherwise reaches for keyed HMAC and bcrypt. Everywhere else in the auth surface a secret compare uses timingSafeEqual: lib/auth/password-hash.ts:92,117, lib/auth/totp.ts:179, lib/auth/pending-2fa.ts:346, lib/auth/oauth-state.ts:137, lib/auth/ipv4-echo-token.ts:248, app/api/v3/auth/2fa/verify/route.ts:233, and the nonce check at app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:131. (2) When the locator query returns no match -- which is every request carrying a wrong or made-up key -- control falls through to the legacy backfill query at line 366 (`WHERE ak.key_locator IS NULL AND ak.key_encrypted IS NOT NULL`, decrypting each returned row) and then the bcrypt fallback at line 393 (`WHERE ak.key_hash IS NOT NULL AND ak.key_locator IS NULL AND ak.key_encrypted IS NULL`, running bcrypt.compare per row at cost 12). Neither predicate is indexable, so both are sequential scans of api_keys, and both run on every single unauthenticated bad-Bearer request against any of the ~15 Bearer routes.
findings.impact: The timing side of this is largely academic (the locator already narrows the candidate set to one row and the key has 256 bits of entropy), but it is a gratuitous deviation from the rule the rest of this codebase follows. The scan side is concrete: an unauthenticated attacker sending garbage Bearer tokens forces two full table scans of api_keys per request at zero cost to themselves, and if any legacy bcrypt rows exist, one bcrypt-cost-12 verification per row per request -- roughly 250ms of CPU per legacy row, on a route with no rate limit in front of it.
findings.recommendation: Replace both `decrypted === key` comparisons in lib/api/api-keys.ts (lines 350, 374) with a length-checked `timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(decrypted), Buffer.from(key))`. Guard the two legacy fallbacks so they only run when legacy rows can actually exist: cache a boolean from a one-time `SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM api_keys WHERE key_locator IS NULL)` at module scope (invalidated on the backfill UPDATE at line 378), and skip lines 366-410 entirely when it is false. Add a partial index `CREATE INDEX ON api_keys (id) WHERE key_locator IS NULL` in instrumentation.ts if the fallback must stay unconditional.

findings.title: Changing the account email leaves every other session and trusted device alive, unlike the password change in the same handler
findings.description: PATCH /api/v3/auth/update treats email and password as the same class of 'sensitive change' at line 68 and gates both behind the same re-auth + `profile-reauth` bucket (lines 70-115). The two branches then diverge. The password branch at lines 337-356 calls deleteAllSessions(), deletes every device_trust row, mints a fresh session, and tells the user 'All other sessions have been signed out for security'. The email branch at lines 207-216 runs `UPDATE users SET email = $1, email_verified_at = NULL` plus sendEmailVerification and stops -- no session wipe, no device_trust wipe. The address the account's password-reset, 2FA email codes, and every security notification are delivered to has just changed identity, and every session that existed a moment earlier is still valid.
findings.impact: An attacker who has a session plus the password (or, for an OAuth-only account, just the session -- lines 116-122 skip the password check entirely there) repoints the account to their own address and keeps every device they were signed in on. The legitimate owner is notified at both addresses (lines 224-247), but if they respond by changing the password they will not think to also check active sessions, and the attacker's own session is not what gets killed. It is also an internal inconsistency: the handler's own comment at lines 201-206 explains that email change is an account-takeover vector, then does not apply the mitigation it applies one branch down.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts, after the email UPDATE at line 207, run the same three statements the password branch runs at lines 343-356: `deleteAllSessions(session.userId)`, `DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1`, then `createSession(...)` and set the refreshed cookie (the code at lines 393-400 can be lifted into a small helper shared by both branches), and return the same `sessionInvalidated: true` flag so the client shows the same message.

findings.title: PUBLIC_PATHS prefix matching silently exempts session-authenticated mutating endpoints from the middleware CSRF check
findings.description: middleware.ts:273-292 returns early for any path matching PUBLIC_PATHS, before the CSRF block at :316. isExemptFromCsrf (:350-368) is documented as "intentionally narrow ... every entry needs a clear non-CSRF trust boundary" and lists six exact paths, but PUBLIC_PATHS creates a second, prefix-matched exemption list that the comment does not account for. Two session-authenticated mutating endpoints land in it: "/api/v3/badge" (public-paths.ts:154) prefix-matches app/api/v3/badge/site/route.ts's POST (:14), PATCH (:64) and DELETE (:95), all of which require getSession() and write host_badges rows; and API_V3.AUTH.ACCEPT_TOS (public-paths.ts:25) covers app/api/v3/auth/accept-tos/route.ts's POST, which does `UPDATE users SET tos_accepted_at = NOW()` for the session user. Two state-changing GETs are also exempt: app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products/route.ts and setup-webhook/route.ts (public-paths.ts:130-131) create live Stripe products/prices and a live Stripe webhook endpoint, and a GET is carried by a SameSite=Lax cookie on a top-level navigation, so a link an admin clicks is enough to fire them.
findings.impact: The CSRF middleware is the app's stated defence for mutating API calls, and these routes silently sit outside it. SameSite=Lax on the session cookie still blocks the cross-site POST cases in current browsers, so this is defence-in-depth rather than a live exploit - but the GET-triggered Stripe setup routes are reachable by a plain link click from an attacker page, and any future same-site-but-different-origin position (a subdomain takeover) collapses the Lax protection for the badge and accept-tos writes too.
findings.recommendation: In middleware.ts, move the `if (pathname.startsWith("/api/v3/") && !isExemptFromCsrf(pathname))` CSRF block above the `if (isPublicPath)` early return at :273 so being publicly reachable no longer implies being CSRF-exempt, and add the genuinely unauthenticated POST endpoints (login, signup, forgot-password, reset-password, 2fa/verify, contact, demo-scan, unsubscribe) to isExemptFromCsrf only if they actually need it - they are same-origin form posts, so most will pass the check unchanged. Separately, convert app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products and setup-webhook from GET to POST since both mutate external state.

findings.title: The two Stripe setup routes hand-roll an exact role === "admin" check, bypassing requireAdmin's 2FA enforcement and locking out super_admin
findings.description: app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products/route.ts:24-36 does getSession() then `if (session.role !== STAFF_ROLES.ADMIN) return 403`, and app/api/v3/stripe/setup-webhook/route.ts:27-38 does getSession() then a raw `SELECT role FROM users` compared against the string literal "admin". Neither goes through lib/auth/authorization.ts's requireAdmin(), so neither runs passesTwoFactorEnforcement (:138): with ENFORCE_STAFF_2FA on, an admin account with totp_enabled false is refused everywhere else in the admin surface but can still call both of these and write to the live Stripe catalog (products.create / prices.create at setup-products:85 and :112) and create a live Stripe webhook endpoint (setup-webhook:85). The exact-string comparison also excludes super_admin, which every other admin route accepts via STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY - AUDIT-011#drift-21 noted that half; the 2FA-enforcement half is separate and unfiled.
findings.impact: The one class of account the ENFORCE_STAFF_2FA toggle is meant to neutralise retains write access to the production Stripe catalog and webhook configuration. Low rather than medium because the caller is still a genuine admin and the operations are near-idempotent, but it is the same bypass pattern as authz-06 and it sits on the billing integration.
findings.recommendation: Replace the hand-rolled checks in both files with `const admin = await requireAdmin(); if (!admin) return ApiResponse.forbidden(...)` from lib/auth/authorization.ts. That fixes the 2FA bypass and the super_admin lockout in one change, and removes the duplicate `SELECT role FROM users` in setup-webhook/route.ts:32.

findings.title: Scan screenshots are readable with no authentication at all, and by sequential legacy id, via the middleware's Bearer-token bypass
findings.description: app/api/v3/scan/screenshot/[id]/route.ts:38 sets `authorized = scan.is_public === true` and only falls back to a session + getTeamResourceAccess check when that is false. scan_history.is_public defaults to true (instrumentation.ts:2190), so most rows qualify. The route is not in PUBLIC_PATHS, but middleware.ts:325 lets any request through when `authorization` merely starts with "Bearer " - the string is never validated there, and this route never validates it either (it only calls getSession()). So `curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer x' https://host/api/v3/scan/screenshot/42` reaches the handler with no identity at all. resolveScanRow (lib/history/resolve-scan.ts:59-67) still matches a legacy numeric primary key alongside the opaque public_id, so the id space is `1..N` sequential. Every sibling per-scan route requires an authenticated owner or team-read (history/[id]/route.ts:117-166, history/[id]/report/route.ts:134-144); this one does not.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller can walk ids 1..N and harvest the stored page screenshot of every public scan, and confirm which scan ids exist. The images are of publicly reachable sites so the content is low-sensitivity, but for a security product it is an unauthenticated enumeration of other tenants' scan activity, and it defeats the opaque public_id the rest of the codebase moved to precisely to stop id-walking.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/scan/screenshot/[id]/route.ts, require a session before the is_public shortcut (move the `getSession()` call above :38 and 404 when there is none), so the public surface stays the token-scoped app/api/v3/shared/[token]/screenshot route it already documents at :19-21. If truly anonymous access is wanted, at minimum reject the legacy numeric id here by calling scanNumericId and only accepting a public_id match.

findings.title: jspdf and jspdf-autotable are production dependencies with zero imports, and vitest plus @vitest/coverage-v8 are in dependencies rather than devDependencies
findings.description: package.json:92-93 declares jspdf 4.2.1 and jspdf-autotable 5.0.8 as runtime dependencies. A repo-wide grep for jspdf/jsPDF across every .ts, .tsx and .mjs outside node_modules, .next and the stale worktree returns exactly one hit, and it is a comment: tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8 ('browser-rendering dependency here despite jspdf being in package.json for'). Nothing imports either package. Separately, @vitest/coverage-v8 4.1.11 (package.json:81) and vitest 4.1.11 (package.json:117) are listed under `dependencies` rather than devDependencies, so `npm ci --omit=dev` in a Docker build installs the whole test runner and its v8 coverage toolchain into the production image.
findings.impact: Three unnecessary packages are installed, audited and shipped in every production install and Docker image. The two jspdf packages are also a live supply-chain surface for code that does not exist, and their presence implies a PDF export path that a reader of package.json would go looking for.
findings.recommendation: Remove jspdf and jspdf-autotable from package.json dependencies (and update the comment at tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8), and move vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 from dependencies to devDependencies. Regenerate package-lock.json on Linux or graft the entries, per the lockfile-platform constraint this repo already documents.

findings.title: The packaged browser extension zips ~606 KB of source maps, and the newly added Chrome Web Store screenshots in extension/public/store will be copied into the next build
findings.description: extension/vite.config.ts:47 sets `sourcemap: true` and extension/scripts/build.mjs:73 sets it again for the background/content bundles. extension/scripts/build.mjs:97 then does `cp(viteOut, dist, { recursive: true })`, and extension/scripts/package.mjs:53 zips the directory with `archive.directory(dist, false)` -- no filter. The current extension/dist-chrome accordingly contains 606 KB of .map files (background.js.map 178 KB, content.js.map 151 KB, popup.js.map 80 KB, constants chunk map 74 KB, options.js.map 64 KB, plans chunk map 50 KB, welcome.js.map 8 KB) against 192 KB of actual shipped code, and both vulnradar-chrome-v0.1.8.zip and vulnradar-firefox-v0.1.8.zip are 232 KB. Separately, extension/vite.config.ts:25 sets `publicDir: extension/public`, so everything under it is copied into the build output; extension/public/store/ was just added and holds five PNGs totalling 516 KB (store_1.png 119,755 bytes through store_5.png 72,067 bytes) that exist only for the Chrome Web Store listing. dist-chrome predates that addition, so the next `npm run build` will copy them into both dist folders and both zips.
findings.impact: Users installing the extension download and store roughly three times the bytes the extension actually runs, and the next release will add another half megabyte of store-listing screenshots that the extension never references. Shipped source maps also hand a reviewer or a repackager the unminified source, which is not a secret in a GPL project but is not intentional either.
findings.recommendation: Set `sourcemap: false` for release builds in extension/vite.config.ts:47 and extension/scripts/build.mjs:73 (or gate it on the `development` mode the dev script already passes), and add a `.map` and `store/` filter to the archiver call in extension/scripts/package.mjs:53. Better: move extension/public/store/ out of publicDir entirely, e.g. to extension/store-assets/, so Vite never copies it.

findings.title: The server config module lands in the root-layout client chunk, carrying dead process.env.SMTP_PASS and BROWSERBASE_API_KEY reads into every page's JavaScript
findings.description: lib/config/constants.ts (787 lines) re-exports lib/config/config-values.ts (1,367 lines) and is imported directly by client components across the app, including ones mounted in app/layout.tsx. The compiled result is visible in the committed build: static/chunks/9711-3989d97c24edd68e.js, 18 KB and part of the /layout entry (so present on all 311 routes), contains `i.env.SMTP_HOST, i.env.SMTP_PORT, i.env.SMTP_USER, i.env.SMTP_PASS, i.env.SMTP_FROM||i.env.SMTP_USER;` and `i.env.BROWSERBASE_API_KEY&&i.env.BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID;` as bare expression statements alongside the team-role matrix and the API route table. No secret is disclosed: `i` is Next's client process shim and only NEXT_PUBLIC_-prefixed variables are inlined, so these evaluate to undefined -- but the code and the variable names ship, and every unused constant webpack cannot prove dead ships with them.
findings.impact: Every page in the app carries a slice of the server configuration module and dead environment reads for SMTP credentials and the Browserbase API key. It is bytes and noise today, and it is one careless `NEXT_PUBLIC_` rename away from becoming a real disclosure, since the read sites are already compiled into a client chunk.
findings.recommendation: Enforce the split the project already documents in CLAUDE.md: keep lib/config/client-constants.ts as the only module client components import, move the process.env-reading blocks (EMAIL_CONFIG and the Browserbase configured check in lib/config/constants.ts) into a server-only module marked with `import "server-only"`, and change the client-side imports of @/lib/config/constants over to the client-safe module.

findings.title: matchesPathPattern compiles an admin-set notification path filter to `.*` per `*` and runs it in every visitor's browser, the same backtracking shape as the robots matcher
findings.description: matchesPathPattern (lib/notifications/match-path.ts:12-22) escapes the regex metacharacters in an admin-configured `path_pattern`, replaces each `*` with `.*`, and evaluates `new RegExp(`^${escaped}$`).test(pathname)`. That is the identical construction to lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:268-273 (inj-02) and has the same exponential worst case; the module comment says it is deliberately client-safe and used from both the bell dropdown and the site-wide banner renderer (components/shared/notification-center.tsx, components/shared/site-notifications.tsx), so it executes in every visitor's browser on every route change.
findings.impact: An admin (or anyone who gains an admin session, or a compromised staff account) can set a notification targeting pattern such as `/a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*b` that hangs the main thread of every signed-in visitor's tab. Bounded because the input is admin-only, and there is no cross-tenant consequence, but it is an unnecessary self-inflicted foot-gun in shipped client code.
findings.recommendation: Replace the regex in lib/notifications/match-path.ts with a linear greedy wildcard walk (split on `*`, then advance through pathname with indexOf, anchoring the first and last segments), or reject patterns containing more than two `*` characters in the admin notification form before they are stored.

findings.title: iframe-sandbox check builds a regex by interpolating a raw URL host, so an IPv6 target's `[::1]:8080` host becomes a character class and the same-origin filter silently inverts
findings.description: The third-party-iframe filter at lib/scanner/checks/headers.ts:1422-1429 does `host = new URL(_url).host` (:1418) and then `!new RegExp(`^https?://${host}`, 'i').test(...)` on each iframe's src. `host` is interpolated with no escaping. For an IPv6 target, `new URL('http://[::1]:8080/x').host` is the literal string `[::1]:8080` (verified in Node), so the compiled regex becomes `^https?://[::1]:8080`, in which `[::1]` is a character class matching a single `:` or `1`. `new RegExp('^https?://' + new URL('http://[::1]:8080/x').host, 'i').test('http://[::1]:8080/x')` returns false (verified).
findings.impact: On a self-hosted or internal target addressed by IPv6 literal, the site's own same-origin iframes are classified as third-party and reported as unsandboxed third-party embeds: a false positive in a security report, from a check whose whole purpose is deciding first-party vs third-party. A host containing an unbalanced bracket would instead throw, and the throw is swallowed by runSyncChecks' catch (lib/scanner/engine.ts:171), silently dropping the check.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/checks/headers.ts, stop building a regex. Parse each iframe src with `new URL(src, _url)` and compare `.host` to the target's `.host` directly; that is both correct for IPv6 and cheaper. If a regex is kept, escape the host with the same `replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` used in lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:269.

findings.title: Two admin log-search endpoints still pass an unescaped ILIKE pattern, unlike the user and team search that were fixed for the same issue
findings.description: app/api/v3/admin/email-logs/route.ts:67-71 does `params.push(`%${search}%`)` then `(recipient ILIKE $n OR subject ILIKE $n)`, and app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts:61-64 does `WHERE message ILIKE $1 OR detail ILIKE $1` with `[`%${search}%`]`. Neither escapes `%`, `_` or `\` and neither adds `ESCAPE '\'`. The sibling searches were fixed for exactly this: app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:127 (`const searchEscaped = search.replace(/[\\%_]/g, '\\$&')`, with the comment 'Without this, typing "%" returns all users (full table scan)') and app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts:37/:58 both use `ESCAPE '\'`. These two were left behind. It is not SQL injection: the value is still a bound parameter.
findings.impact: An admin searching email or error logs for a literal `_` or `%` gets wrong results (every underscore matches any character), and a search of `%` degrades to a full scan of system_error_logs / the email log table, which are the two highest-volume tables in the schema. Bounded to staff users.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same one-line escape used at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:127 in both files, and add `ESCAPE '\'` to each ILIKE clause, matching app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts.

findings.title: The scheduled-scans plan limit is a read-then-insert with no guard, so concurrent POSTs let a user exceed their plan's scheduledScans cap
findings.description: POST /api/v3/schedules counts existing rows with `SELECT COUNT(*)::int as count FROM scheduled_scans WHERE user_id = $1` (app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:134-137), compares it against planLimits.scheduledScans via withinPlanLimit at :139-147, and then does an unguarded `INSERT INTO scheduled_scans ...` at :167-173. There is no row lock, no unique constraint, and no conditional INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, so two requests that both read the same count before either inserts both pass the gate. The same shape exists for the team seat cap at app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:190-205 (count, then INSERT at :214) and the team-count cap at app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:78-91. Contrast lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts, which closes exactly this race for the scan counter with a single guarded upsert (`ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... WHERE rate_limits."count" < $2`, :366-368).
findings.impact: A user (or a script) firing N parallel schedule-create requests lands N schedules where the plan allows one more, permanently over the cap until someone notices -- and each extra schedule then runs forever as an unmetered scan source (see logic-01). Bounded by how many requests overlap the same read, and self-limiting because the cap is re-read on the next single request, so the practical overshoot is small. The same argument applies to the team seat cap, where the overshoot is a paid-seat count.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts, replace the count-then-insert with a single data-modifying statement: `INSERT INTO scheduled_scans (...) SELECT $1, $2, ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scheduled_scans WHERE user_id = $1) < $limit RETURNING id`, treating a zero-row result as the over-limit rejection (skip the WHERE entirely when the limit is -1). Apply the same shape to the seat check in app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:190 and the team-count check in app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:78.

findings.title: FEATURE_SCHEDULED_SCANS is only enforced when a schedule is created; disabling it leaves every existing schedule running
findings.category: feature flag not re-checked at run time
findings.description: The FEATURE_SCHEDULED_SCANS setting is read in exactly one place on this feature's server side: POST /api/v3/schedules returns 403 'Scheduled scans are disabled on this deployment.' when it is false (app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:71-76). The worker never consults it. runDueSchedules (lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.ts:413) reads only SCHEDULE_WORKER_CLAIM_LIMIT and SCHEDULE_WORKER_BATCH_CONCURRENCY, then claims and processes every active, due row; schedulePeriodicScheduledScans (:455) is registered unconditionally from instrumentation.ts's startup sequence. Neither claimDueSchedules' WHERE clause (:125, `active = true AND next_run_at <= NOW()`) nor processSchedule's gates (:244 target safety, :261 frequency plan tier) reference the flag.
findings.impact: An operator who turns the feature off in /admin to shed load, or because scheduled scanning is causing a problem with a target, sees new schedules blocked but every pre-existing schedule keeps firing full scans on its normal cadence indefinitely. The kill switch reads as a kill switch in the admin UI and is not one. Bounded by how many schedules already exist, but on a deployment with hourly Elite schedules that is exactly the load the operator was trying to stop.
findings.recommendation: At the top of runDueSchedules in lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.ts (before the claimDueSchedules call at :415), `if (!(await getSetting("FEATURE_SCHEDULED_SCANS"))) return { processed: 0, scanned: 0, blocked: 0, planGated: 0, errors: 0 };` -- getSetting is already imported at :46 and the resolver's 30s cache TTL makes the extra read free. Returning empty stats rather than throwing keeps the failure escalator at :466 quiet.

findings.title: The staff plan floor applied on cancellation hardcodes three of the seven staff roles and omits super_admin, so those accounts drop to 'free' instead of their granted floor
findings.category: duplicated role list drifted from its source of truth
findings.description: Three separate cancellation paths reset the plan with the same hand-written CASE: `plan = CASE WHEN role IN ('admin', 'moderator', 'support') THEN 'pro_supporter' ELSE 'free' END` -- app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:640 (customer.subscription.deleted), app/api/v3/billing/subscription/cancel/route.ts:74 (immediate cancel), and app/api/v3/billing/route.ts:425 (cancel_immediately action). The canonical staff-role list is STAFF_ROLES in lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:22-30, which contains seven roles: admin, moderator, support, billing, security_analyst, content_manager, ops. The CASE covers three of them and, separately, super_admin -- whose granted floor is elite_supporter, not pro_supporter (lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:49, 62-64) -- is in none of the lists. lib/billing/staff-plan.ts's grantStaffPlan/revokeStaffPlan, which own this policy, are not called from any of the three cancel paths.
findings.impact: A billing/security_analyst/content_manager/ops staffer who cancels a real paid subscription has users.plan written to 'free' rather than the pro_supporter floor their role grants. Their enforced limits are mostly unaffected because getUserPlan (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:89) tags any STAFF_ROLES member as 'staff' and every resolver substitutes pro_supporter, so this is mainly a wrong displayed plan. A super_admin is the real case: super_admin is deliberately excluded from STAFF_ROLES (:20-21), so getUserPlan falls through to the literal column and returns 'free' -- that account is genuinely dropped to the Free tier's 25 scans/day and free-tier caps after canceling, until the next process restart, when reconcileStaffPlans (lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:253) sweeps it back to elite_supporter (and only if pre_staff_plan is still NULL).
findings.recommendation: Replace the three inline CASE expressions with a call to the module that owns the policy: after the UPDATE that clears the Stripe columns, call grantStaffPlan(userId, role) from lib/billing/staff-plan.ts (exported already), or at minimum parameterise the CASE against STAFF_ROLES plus super_admin rather than a hardcoded triple -- e.g. `plan = CASE WHEN role = 'super_admin' THEN 'elite_supporter' WHEN role = ANY($n::text[]) THEN 'pro_supporter' ELSE 'free' END` with STAFF_ROLES bound as the array.

findings.title: A lapsing Stripe subscription revokes the premium badge even when an active admin gift still entitles the user to it
findings.category: entitlement revoked without checking the other grant path
findings.description: The premium badge has two independent grant paths. The Stripe path calls grantPremiumBadge/revokePremiumBadge from lib/billing/badges.ts. The gift path awards it directly in app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1674-1691 (SELECT the 'premium' badge id, INSERT INTO user_badges if absent) when an admin runs gift_subscription. revokePremiumBadge (lib/billing/badges.ts:32-48) is an unconditional `DELETE FROM user_badges WHERE user_id = $1 AND badge_id = $2` -- it never looks at gifted_subscriptions. It is called from customer.subscription.updated whenever the resolved plan is free (app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:583), from customer.subscription.deleted (:649), and from confirmSubscription (app/actions/stripe.ts:335). The symmetric case is handled correctly in the other direction: revoke_gift only removes the badge when the user is on the free plan (app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1709-1721).
findings.impact: A user who has both an active admin gift and a Stripe subscription that then lapses, is canceled, or expires loses the premium badge even though the gift is still live and still grants them the paid plan. The badge is user-visible on shared scans, public scans and the profile (the badges query in app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.ts:114-119 reads user_badges directly), so the account silently stops being marked as a supporter while still holding a valid gifted subscription. Nothing re-grants it: the gift path only inserts at gift creation, so the badge stays missing until an admin re-issues the gift.
findings.recommendation: Make revokePremiumBadge in lib/billing/badges.ts conditional on there being no other live entitlement: guard the DELETE with `AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM gifted_subscriptions WHERE user_id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > NOW())`, which mirrors the check revoke_gift already makes in the opposite direction at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1709. That keeps all three Stripe callers (webhooks :583, :649 and app/actions/stripe.ts:335) correct without changing any of them.

findings.title: 117 of the 155 API routes bypass the ApiResponse/withErrorHandling helpers and hand-roll five different error body shapes
findings.description: lib/api/api-utils.ts already provides the canonical pieces: ApiResponse (:13-65) emits `{ error, status }` with a matching HTTP status for every 4xx/5xx class, and withErrorHandling (:263-274) converts an uncaught throw into `console.error("[API Error]", error)` plus a fixed `"An unexpected error occurred"` 500. Only 38 of the 155 route.ts files under app/api reference either one; the other 117 build responses with bare NextResponse.json, and 47 route files contain no `catch` at all. The result is five distinct error shapes in production: `{ error }` (bare NextResponse.json, the majority of the 233 `error:`-keyed literals), `{ error, status }` (ApiResponse), `{ success: false, error }` (21 occurrences, e.g. app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:299-303 and app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products/route.ts:148-152), `{ error, details, statusCode }` (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:287-294), and `{ message }` (app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:298). The shared client only understands one of them: lib/api/client.ts:46-49 reads `errorData.error` and otherwise falls back to the literal string `API error: <status>` set at :44, so a `{ message }` response surfaces to the user as "API error: 400".
findings.impact: Client code cannot render a reliable message without knowing which route it called, which is how bare status strings end up in front of users. The 47 handler-less routes also mean an unexpected throw is formatted by Next.js rather than by the app, so those responses do not carry the `{ error }` key the client expects at all.
findings.recommendation: Adopt ApiResponse as the single error constructor and wrap every handler in withErrorHandling. Do it in batches by directory rather than one sweep. Start with the five shape outliers named above so the client's single `errorData.error` read in lib/api/client.ts:46 is always satisfied.

findings.title: no-floating-promises is scoped to four auth path globs, so 86 no-op .catch handlers and 8 empty catch blocks in the scanner, billing and webhook paths pass lint
findings.description: eslint.config.mjs's type-aware block enables `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` (:126) and `no-misused-promises` (:122) only for the four globs listed at :108-113 (`lib/auth/**/*.ts`, `app/api/v3/auth/**/*.ts`, `app/api/v3/account/**/*.ts`, `app/api/v3/admin/**/*.ts`), and the main rules block (:58-92) enables no rule against empty catch blocks. A scan of the 965 source files under app/, lib/, components/, extension/src/, cli/ and scripts/ finds 8 statement-level `catch {}` blocks with a genuinely empty body, 183 with only a comment, and 86 inline `.catch(() => {})` / `.catch(() => null)` no-op handlers. Most of the 183 are deliberate and documented (a scanner check whose DNS lookup failing genuinely means no finding), which is exactly why the raw count is not itself the finding: the finding is that nothing distinguishes the deliberate ones from the ones filed above as obs-01 and obs-06, and nothing stops the next one being added.
findings.impact: The swallowed-error findings in this section (obs-01 in the scan engine, obs-06 in metering and quota refunds) all live in directories the lint rules do not cover, and none of them would be flagged today. The pattern reproduces on every new file in lib/scanner, lib/billing, lib/webhooks and lib/email.
findings.recommendation: Extend the type-aware `files` list in eslint.config.mjs:108-113 to include `lib/billing/**/*.ts`, `lib/webhooks/**/*.ts`, `lib/email/**/*.ts` and `lib/scanner/*.ts` (the orchestration files, not the 4000-line check bodies, to keep lint time bounded). Add `"no-empty": ["error", { allowEmptyCatch: false }]` to the main rules block so a new bare `catch {}` has to be written as a commented no-op or a logged one.

findings.title: The admin alert webhook that every escalation path depends on defaults to empty and has no test-delivery path, so an operator cannot know it works until an incident
findings.description: sendAdminAlert (lib/admin/alert-webhook.ts:40-44) begins `const url = await getSetting("ADMIN_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL"); if (!url) return;` and the default is the empty string (lib/config/config-values.ts:429, registered at lib/config/registry.ts:2783). Every push signal in the app routes through it: the five worker escalators via lib/admin/failure-escalation.ts:100, and the boot-time schema, stale-scan and missing-table alerts at instrumentation.ts:139, :184, :198, :3491, :3531, :3631.
