Grepping ADMIN_ALERT_WEBHOOK across app/, components/ and lib/ finds only the config registry entries and alert-webhook.ts itself: there is no route, button, or admin action that sends a test alert, and the delivery failure paths (:50-56 for an unsafe URL, :86-90 for a non-2xx response) only console.error into a log the operator would have to already be reading.
findings.impact: An operator who pastes a Slack or PagerDuty URL into the setting has no way to confirm it works. A typo, a revoked Slack webhook, or a URL that validateScanTarget (:47) now rejects produces a silent no-op, and the first time they find out is the incident the alert existed for. Until it is configured at all, the app has no push signal of any kind, which is the state a fresh install ships in.
findings.recommendation: Add a "Send test alert" action next to the ADMIN_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL setting that calls sendAdminAlert with a `severity: "warning", event: "test_alert"` payload and surfaces the delivery result (including the non-2xx status from :87) in the UI rather than only in console.error. Have sendAdminAlert return a boolean instead of void so the caller can report it.

findings.title: finalizeScanSuccess acquires a second pool connection from inside its own open transaction, which can deadlock the pool when several scans finish together
findings.description: `finalizeScanSuccess` takes a client with `pool.connect()` (lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:221), opens a transaction (line 237), and inside it calls `saveAutoTags(scanId, txUserId, findings, client)` at line 287. `saveAutoTags`'s first statement is `await loadPromotedRules()` (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:794), which on a cache miss runs `pool.query(...)` against the module-level pool (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:720) -- a second connection requested while the first is still held in an open transaction. The rules cache has a 5-minute TTL (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:702) and is also invalidated on every admin promotion, so misses are real, not theoretical.
findings.impact: With `CONFIG_DB_POOL_MAX = 10`, if ten scans finalize within the same cache-miss window every one of them holds a transaction client and waits for an eleventh connection that cannot exist. All ten stall until `connectionTimeoutMillis` fires and the scans are marked failed after their work was already done.
findings.recommendation: Call `loadPromotedRules()` before `pool.connect()` in lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:221 and pass the resolved rules into `saveAutoTags`, or have `saveAutoTags` run `loadPromotedRules` on the `executor` client it was handed rather than on the global pool (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:720).

findings.title: Three completion paths write rows one INSERT at a time where a single multi-row INSERT would do: crawl pages, AI verify verdicts, and boot-time migrations
findings.description: (a) At the end of a crawl, `for (const pr of pageResults)` runs one `INSERT INTO scan_history (...) VALUES ($1...$12) RETURNING id` per page (lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:630-650) -- up to 250 sequential round trips on the Elite plan (lib/billing/crawl-page-limits.ts:23). (b) `lib/ai/verify-findings.ts:583-593` loops the verdict map and runs one `INSERT INTO scan_finding_feedback ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` per finding, routinely 50-300 sequential inserts. (c) Boot-time passes do the same: lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:265-268 (one query per staff row, driving SELECT at :254 unbounded), lib/auth/security-migration.ts:89-98 and :123-139 (one UPDATE per row), lib/uploads/avatar-migration.ts:120-151 and :194-214 (three queries per avatar). Note the correct pattern already exists in this codebase: `saveAutoTags` builds a single multi-row INSERT (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:802-816).
findings.impact: (a) adds 250 serialized round trips to the tail of a crawl the user is already waiting on. (b) adds one round trip per finding to the AI verify flow. (c) lengthens every process start, which matters because instrumentation.ts also runs the full schema DDL at boot.
findings.recommendation: Replace each loop with one multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...) RETURNING id` built the way lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:802-816 builds its parameter list, or with `UNNEST($1::type[], ...)` for the larger sets. For (c), a single `UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...)` replaces the per-row loops.

findings.title: webhook_deliveries is written on every webhook event and never pruned, because lib/database/cleanup.ts has no retention rule for it
findings.description: `lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:111` inserts a row into `webhook_deliveries` on every delivery attempt (and the module retries once on failure, so a failing webhook writes two rows per event). The table is created at instrumentation.ts:2328 with `idx_webhook_deliveries_webhook_id ON webhook_deliveries(webhook_id, attempted_at DESC)` (:2336). Grepping lib/database/cleanup.ts for `webhook_deliveries` returns nothing -- the retention pass that prunes sessions, rate_limits, tokens, scan_finding_feedback, user_notifications, github_review_usage, ai_conversations, email_logs, system_error_logs and admin_audit_log has no rule for it. AUDIT-011's drift-25 already noted this table has no reader; combined with no writer-side retention, it accumulates forever.
findings.impact: A user with an active webhook on an hourly schedule writes ~24 rows a day per webhook, permanently. Nothing reads the table, so the growth is invisible until it shows up as disk usage and as backup/restore time on the self-hosted deployments this project targets.
findings.recommendation: Either add a retention DELETE for `webhook_deliveries` to lib/database/cleanup.ts alongside the other log tables (with an admin-configurable retention setting matching the pattern used for email_logs), or, if AUDIT-011's drift-25 conclusion holds and the table genuinely has no consumer, stop writing it in lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:111 and drop it.

findings.title: Two per-request lookups sit on the admin engine-feedback page that each pull every findings blob for a tag with no LIMIT
findings.category: N+1 with an unbounded inner query
findings.description: `for (const row of counts.rows)` at app/api/v3/admin/engine-feedback/ai-tag-candidates/route.ts:171 puts a `Promise.all` inside the loop (line 172), so the loop itself is fully sequential -- two round trips per candidate tag. The second of those (lines 182-186) is `SELECT sh.findings FROM scan_tags st JOIN scan_history sh ON sh.id = st.scan_id WHERE st.tag = $1 AND st.source = 'ai'` with no LIMIT: it pulls the complete findings JSONB of every scan carrying that tag and then flatMaps the result in JavaScript at line 191.
findings.impact: Staff-only and low frequency, so bounded in blast radius, but the page cost grows with total AI-tagged scan volume and each iteration transfers (scans with that tag) x (full findings blob) bytes. It is the same shape as perf-06's top-vulnerabilities query and will fail the same way at scale.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the `Promise.all` outside the loop so the per-tag queries actually run in parallel, add a `LIMIT` and a recency bound to the query at line 182, and project only the finding fields the candidate scoring reads rather than `sh.findings` whole.

findings.title: Three IPv6 range regexes match a single 16-bit group where the comment claims a /7 or /10, leaving fe81::-febf:: and fc00::-fcff:: unblocked
findings.description:
PRIVATE_IPV6_PATTERNS is tested against the canonical 8-group form produced by toCanonicalIPv6 (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:182-232), so each `/^xxxx:/` anchors on the full first group, not a prefix:
- lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:80 `/^fe80:/i` is commented "IPv6 link-local (fe80::/10)". fe80::/10 spans first groups fe80 through febf. `fe81::1` canonicalises to `fe81:0000:...` and matches nothing in the list, so isPrivateIP returns false for it.
- lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:81 `/^fc00:/i` is commented "fc00::/7". That /7 spans fc00 through fdff. The fd00::/8 half is covered by the separate `/^fd[0-9a-f]{2}:/i` on line 82, but fc01 through fcff match nothing.
- lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:98 `/^fec0:/i` is commented "site-local", which is fec0::/10 (fec0-feff); fec1 upward is unmatched.
The same shape is fine for the loopback and unspecified patterns (:79, :83) because those are single addresses, and for the IPv4-mapped patterns (:84-93) because they anchor on the embedded v4 octets.
findings.impact: Bounded in practice: real link-local traffic uses fe80::/64, fc00::/8 was never allocated by IANA, and fec0::/10 is deprecated. But a host that has been configured with an address in fe81::/16-febf::/16 or fc01::/16-fcff::/16 (which is legal, and which some Kubernetes and overlay-network setups do use for ULA space) is reachable through validateScanTarget with no other control in the way. It is also a latent trap: the comments assert coverage the code does not have, so a reviewer confirming "fc00::/7 is blocked" reads the comment and moves on.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts, replace lines 80, 81 and 98 with patterns that match the real prefix lengths: `/^fe[89ab][0-9a-f]:/i` for fe80::/10, `/^f[cd][0-9a-f]{2}:/i` for fc00::/7 (which then subsumes line 82), and `/^fe[c-f][0-9a-f]:/i` for fec0::/10. Or, preferably, fold this into the numeric-CIDR rewrite recommended in ssrf-03 so IPv6 ranges are expressed as prefixes rather than as regexes over a canonicalised string. Add table-driven cases to the `isPrivateIP IPv6 canonicalization` block in tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts:21 for fe81::1, fcff::1 and fec1::1.

findings.title: The BrowserBase screenshot and live-session paths validate only the entry URL; the headless browser's own redirects and sub-resource loads are never checked
findings.category: guard does not cover browser navigations
findings.description:
captureScreenshot calls validateScanTarget(targetUrl) at lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:199-203 and then sends `Page.navigate {url: targetUrl}` over CDP at :135. Everything the browser does after that is outside the Node fetch guard: a 302 the page returns, a meta refresh, a `window.location` assignment, and every image/script/XHR/iframe the page pulls. lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts has the same shape: validateScanTarget at :375, then `Page.navigate` at :280. The interactive path is the same: app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:99-108 validates the optional seed `url` once, and the user then drives the session freely from app/browser/[id]/page.tsx. safeFetch's per-hop re-validation (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:654-798) simply does not apply to any of it.

The mitigating fact, which is why this is low and not high: lib/browserbase/client.ts hardcodes BROWSERBASE_BASE_URL to https://api.browserbase.com/v1 (:43) and connects to the session over the returned `connectUrl` (:230-257). There is no local-Chrome or self-hosted-CDP fallback anywhere in lib/browserbase/, so the browser always runs in BrowserBase's cloud. The internal network a redirect could reach is BrowserBase's, not VulnRadar's, and 169.254.169.254 inside that session is BrowserBase's metadata service.
findings.impact: VulnRadar can be pointed, by any user with a plan that allows screenshots or live sessions, at a page that redirects into BrowserBase's internal network or metadata endpoint. That is a third party's blast radius rather than VulnRadar's, but VulnRadar is the vehicle, and the same code becomes a first-party SSRF the moment anyone adds a local-Chrome or self-hosted CDP option for self-hosters (which is the obvious next step for a self-hostable product that today silently disables screenshots without BrowserBase credentials).
findings.recommendation: Enable CDP request interception on the session before the first navigate: `Network.enable` plus `Fetch.enable` with a `Fetch.requestPaused` handler that runs the same isPrivateHostname/validateScanTarget check on every intercepted request URL and calls `Fetch.failRequest` when it fails. Wire it in one place, lib/browserbase/client.ts's openCdpPageSession, so page-screenshot.ts, browser-login.ts and the interactive session route all inherit it. At minimum, subscribe to `Page.frameNavigated` and abort the session when the frame URL leaves the validated host.

findings.title: Neither validateScanTarget nor safeFetch's redirect loop checks the URL scheme, so only the cross-host rule stands between a Location header and a non-HTTP outbound request
findings.description:
The scheme allowlist lives only in assertSafePublicHttpUrl (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:501-534), which safeFetch runs exactly once, on the initial URL (:562). validateScanTarget (:430-494) has no protocol check at all: it parses the URL, looks at the hostname, and returns safe/unsafe. The redirect loop then re-validates each hop with validateScanTarget alone (:746) and never re-runs assertSafePublicHttpUrl, so the next hop's scheme is unexamined. A `Location: ftp://<same-host>/x` or `Location: gopher://<same-host>:70/` passes the sameRegisteredHost test at :730-740 (identical hostname) and the validateScanTarget test at :746-752, and reaches `fetch()` at :686. It fails today only because undici refuses schemes it does not implement. file:, data:, blob: and javascript: are separately blocked, but by accident: their parsed hostname is the empty string, which never equals the initial hostname, so the cross-host branch at :736 throws first.

The same gap is why validateScanTarget is unsafe to use as a standalone guard, and it is used that way in several places: lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:199, lib/scanner/checks/tls.ts:247 and :359, lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2251. Those happen to be fed http(s) URLs by their callers, and validateScanTarget does fail closed on `file:///etc/passwd` (empty hostname to `lookup("")`, which resolves to an empty address list and hits the "resolved to no addresses" refusal at :474-479), but that is a coincidence of Node's dns.lookup behaviour, not a check.
findings.impact: No exploit today: undici rejects ftp/gopher/dict, and the schemes that would matter most (file:, data:, javascript:) are stopped by an unrelated hostname comparison rather than by a scheme check. The consequence is that the scheme allowlist is load-bearing in exactly one place and absent from the two functions that every other module treats as the guard, so a future change to the cross-host rule (for example allowing a redirect to any subdomain of the registered domain, which the walmart.com www-apex work already gestures at) silently re-opens non-HTTP outbound requests, and any new caller of validateScanTarget inherits a guard that does not check what it looks like it checks.
findings.recommendation: Two one-line changes in lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts. First, add the scheme check to validateScanTarget itself, right after `const parsed = new URL(url)` at :435: `if (!ALLOWED_PROTOCOLS.has(parsed.protocol)) return { safe: false, reason: "Only http and https URLs can be scanned." }`, which hardens every standalone caller at once. Second, in the redirect loop call `assertSafePublicHttpUrl(nextUrlObj.href)` inside a try/catch before the validateScanTarget call at :746 so each hop passes the same syntactic gate the entry URL did. Add a test to tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts asserting a `Location: ftp://example.com/` hop is refused.

findings.title: Four third-party subdomain-discovery APIs are fetched with follow-redirects and unbounded JSON/text reads, outside every SSRF and size guard
findings.description:
fetchCrtSh (lib/scanner/subdomain-discovery-engine.ts:437-450), fetchHackerTarget (:472-486), fetchSubdomainCenter (:500-512) and fetchRapidDns (:522-534), plus the remaining sources at :556, :593, :629, :667 and :705, all call the global `fetch` directly. The host is a hardcoded constant in each case and the user-supplied domain goes through encodeURIComponent, so there is no URL-injection hole. What is missing is everything else safeFetch provides: `redirect` is left at fetch's default of "follow", so any 3xx these endpoints return is followed blindly with no per-hop private-IP re-validation, and the responses are consumed with bare `await res.json()` (:448, :510) and `await res.text()` (:484) with no byte cap. `AbortSignal.timeout(10000-15000)` is passed straight to fetch here (not through safeFetch), so unlike ssrf-01 the time bound does hold, but the size bound does not.

These are free, unauthenticated, third-party endpoints (crt.sh, api.hackertarget.com, api.subdomain.center, rapiddns.io) that VulnRadar has no control over, called on behalf of a user-supplied domain.
findings.impact: A 10-second window at any reasonable bandwidth is hundreds of megabytes buffered into a string per source, and up to nine sources run per discovery. More structurally: if any of these free services is hijacked, expires, or is DNS-poisoned, a `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` is followed with no guard at all, and the response is parsed and mined for hostnames, turning a third-party outage into a metadata read on VulnRadar's own host.
findings.recommendation: Route all nine calls in lib/scanner/subdomain-discovery-engine.ts through safeFetch, the same way the subdomain HTTP probes at :854 and :865 in the same file already are, and pass `allowedHostnames: ["crt.sh"]` etc. so each source is pinned to its own host and a redirect off it is refused. Cap each read with the shared bounded reader recommended in ssrf-01 rather than `await res.json()` / `await res.text()`.

findings.title: The safe-fetch test suite covers redirects and IPv6 canonicalization but never exercises the address-range gaps, the allowedHostnames argument, or any body bound
findings.category: test gap in the SSRF guard
findings.description:
tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts is 231 lines and 18 cases. It mocks dns/promises (:6-9) and stubs global fetch (:127-131), and it does cover the things prior audits broke: IPv6 canonicalization of ::1 / ::ffff:127.0.0.1 / 64:ff9b:: forms (:21-79), resolve-to-private (:83), the metadata IP (:91), fail-closed on empty DNS (:104) and on DNS error (:204), the redirect-to-metadata and redirect-to-RFC1918 refusals (:141, :156), cross-host redirect refusal (:169), same-host rebind refusal (:184), and the non-http scheme refusal (:227). So the memory note that safeFetch had ZERO tests is stale.

What is not covered maps one-to-one onto the defects filed above:
- No case asserts any bound on the response body, in bytes or in time: the behaviour in ssrf-01 would pass the suite unchanged.
- No case for the `allowedHostnames` parameter (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:574-582), even though it is the stated containment for every active probe (lib/scanner/active-probes/shared.ts:14-19) and it is enforced only on the first hop, not on the www-apex redirect the loop permits.
- No case for the `session` parameter's credential-drop-on-redirect behaviour (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:671-680), the whole reason authenticated scanning is safe.
- No case for 100.64/10, 198.18/15 or 192.0.0.0/24 (ssrf-03), nor for the fe80::/10 and fc00::/7 prefix widths (ssrf-05).
- No case for pinToResolvedIp (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:273) or for the fact that the HTTPS branch does not pin (ssrf-02).
- No case for a hostname in decimal/octal/hex form, which currently relies entirely on getaddrinfo normalising before isPrivateIP runs.
findings.impact: The guard is the single most consequential piece of code in the product, and the parts of it that are currently wrong are exactly the parts with no test. Any of the fixes recommended in ssrf-01 through ssrf-05 can be shipped, then silently regressed, with a green suite.
findings.recommendation: Extend tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts with: a case that stubs fetch with a Response over a never-ending ReadableStream and asserts safeFetch's consumer stops at the byte cap and within the deadline; a case asserting safeFetch rejects a hostname absent from allowedHostnames, and one asserting the www-apex redirect hop is re-checked against that list; a case asserting session headers are attached on-origin and absent after a redirect; table cases for 100.100.100.200, 198.18.0.1, 192.0.0.1, fe81::1, fcff::1 in the existing isPrivateIP block at :21; and a case asserting the fetch dispatcher connects to the validated IP for an https target once ssrf-02 is fixed.

findings.title: The crawl page picker is the best-built selection UI in the product and should be kept as is
findings.description: components/scanner/crawl-url-selector.tsx (283 lines), rendered from app/dashboard/page.tsx:963-970. Persistent footer toolbar with 'N of M selected (max L)', a search filter, and Select all / Clear all. Pre-selects up to the plan cap at :55-64; over-cap rows are disabled at 40% opacity with an explanatory banner. useModalA11y provides focus trap, Escape and focus restore. Mobile works at 320px via max-h-[80vh] with a min-h-0 flex-1 scroll list and text-base sm:text-xs to stop iOS zoom. The backend is a real bulk endpoint: one request carries the whole array and app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.ts:235-272 re-validates and re-enforces the plan cap server-side.
findings.impact: None. Recorded so it is not swept up in a bulk-action removal pass: deleting it does not remove clutter, it removes the crawl feature or forces every crawl to scan every discovered page at the user's expense.
findings.recommendation: Keep. Two optional nits: the rows are buttons with aria-pressed and a fake check glyph rather than real checkboxes, so assistive tech does not announce them as checkboxes; and defaulting to everything pre-selected means a user who wants three pages must deselect the rest.

findings.title: Admin badge multi-select conveys selection only visually and commits without a transaction
findings.description: components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:1162 (literally commented 'Badges - multi select'), state at :160-161, revoke chips at :1177-1233, award dialog at :1270-1360, commit at :434-453. The shape is right: selections queue as a staged diff, surface in the save-confirmation modal as +3 badges / -2 badges, and can be unqueued before commit. Three defects: the toggles are plain buttons with no aria-pressed, so selected state is conveyed only by ring-2, line-through and a title attribute; the commit is Promise.all of N separate PATCHes with no transaction; and each fires its own toast (app/admin/page.tsx:568) while racing on the single shared actionLoading string (:516, :586).
findings.impact: Low traffic, but a screen-reader user cannot tell which badges are staged, and a partial failure leaves partial awards with a burst of contradictory toasts.
findings.recommendation: Keep it. Add aria-pressed to both toggle sets, replace the N toasts with one summary toast, and either sequence the commit or accept the partial-failure risk explicitly. Roughly 30 lines. If removal is preferred instead, UserDetailPanel has exactly one importer (app/admin/page.tsx:147) and award_badge/revoke_badge survive independently.

findings.title: Empty leftover directory at app/api/v3/admin/bulk/
findings.description: Empty directory left over from commit 52656312 ('remove bulk user actions'). Git does not track empty directories, so it survives only in the working tree. Useful precedent found alongside it: lib/changelog/data.ts:1063 records 'Removed Bulk User Actions' - the admin Users tab previously had exactly this kind of select-up-to-200 feature and it was deleted outright on blast-radius grounds.
findings.impact: None functional. Noted because the precedent is directly relevant to the bulk-01 decision.
findings.recommendation: rmdir.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md states the brand is cyan/teal at ~190 degrees; every shipped surface is blue #60a5fa at 213 degrees
findings.description: app/globals.css:178, lib/config/config-values.ts:188 (CONFIG_PRIMARY_COLOR = "#60a5fa"), lib/config/brand.ts:16-21, public/og-image.svg:36,58 and the five store PNGs all agree on blue #60a5fa (213 94% 68%). The only 190 degree hue left in the system is --chart-1 (app/globals.css:197), which is unused. app/global-error.tsx:10 still hardcodes BRAND_TEAL = "#0891b2", a stale cyan matching nothing.
findings.impact: Every future contributor and every AI agent reading CLAUDE.md is told the wrong brand colour on line 1, which is how stale cyan keeps reappearing.
findings.recommendation: Correct CLAUDE.md line 1 to blue #60a5fa (213 degrees) and fix the BRAND_TEAL constant in app/global-error.tsx:10. See audits/AUDIT-011/design-language.md for the full extracted spec.

findings.title: Inter and JetBrains Mono are imported and never applied; the site ships in system-ui
findings.description: app/layout.tsx:39-43 imports Inter and JetBrains_Mono from next/font/google but assigns both to underscore-prefixed unused consts, and their --font-inter and --font-jetbrains-mono variables are never applied. app/layout.tsx:170 is <body className="font-sans antialiased"> and tailwind.config.mjs has no fontFamily extension, so the real stack is Tailwind v4's ui-sans-serif / ui-monospace defaults.
findings.impact: Either two font downloads are being paid for and discarded, or the intended typography was never shipped. Both are worth knowing before any design work.
findings.recommendation: Decide which was intended: wire the CSS variables into tailwind.config.mjs, or remove the imports. Note the system stack is what every existing surface was visually tuned against, so switching to Inter is a visual change, not a no-op.

findings.title: components/ui/badge.tsx is the one primitive that hardcodes Tailwind palette colours and ignores dark mode
findings.description: components/ui/badge.tsx:16-19 defines info as bg-blue-500/10 text-blue-600, success as bg-green-500/10 text-green-600, warning as bg-amber-500/10 text-amber-600 and error as bg-red-500/10 text-red-600. These bypass the token set and do not respond to dark mode. The codebase is otherwise clean: zero bg-gray-*, text-gray-*, bg-slate-*, bg-zinc-* or border-gray-* anywhere in app/ or components/. Related: app/globals.css:9 safelists literal palette colours for role badges, :487-575 hardcodes hover and selection surfaces as literal hsl() with !important, --surface-1/2/3 are defined at :210-213 and used nowhere, and --sidebar-* is wired into tailwind.config.mjs:64-73 but never defined in CSS so those utilities resolve to nothing. Separately components/badge/badge-preview.tsx:114 uses text-emerald-500 where every other success indicator uses text-[hsl(var(--success))].
findings.impact: Four badge variants render the same colour in both themes, and the variant names (info/success/warning/error) form a second severity vocabulary competing with the real one.
findings.recommendation: Move the four variants onto --success, --warning and --destructive tokens. Fix badge-preview.tsx:114. Remove the dead --surface-* and --sidebar-* declarations.

findings.title: isNavItemActive has two identical ternary branches, so NavItem.exact does nothing
findings.description: components/docs/docs-nav.ts:152-154 is `return item.exact ? pathname === item.href : pathname === item.href;`. NavItem.exact is declared at components/docs/docs-types.ts:12 and set on /docs at docs-nav.ts:21. Used by docs-sidebar.tsx:48 and docs-mobile-nav.tsx:94.
findings.impact: Correct today only because every nav href is a distinct page. A future prefix-matched entry will silently fail to highlight.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the non-exact branch as `pathname === item.href || pathname.startsWith(`${item.href}/`)`, or delete the helper and inline the equality.

findings.title: Seven touch targets under 44px in the docs and legal navigation, worst at 20px
findings.description: components/legal/legal-toc.tsx:26-28 has no vertical padding at all, giving about 20px, and it is the primary navigation for 15-clause legal documents. Others: app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:433 about 26px; components/docs/docs-code-block.tsx:53-60 about 27px; components/legal/legal-nav.tsx:45 about 30px; components/docs/docs-toc.tsx:73-78 about 32px and this is the mobile TOC (xl:hidden); components/docs/docs-code-tabs.tsx:39 about 36px; components/docs/docs-mobile-nav.tsx:81 about 36px.
findings.impact: Legal and docs navigation is hard to operate accurately on a phone.
findings.recommendation: legal-toc.tsx:28 add py-2 -my-0.5 min-h-11 flex items-center; docs-toc.tsx:74 py-2.5; docs-code-block.tsx:54 px-2.5 py-2; docs-code-tabs.tsx:39 py-2.5; docs-mobile-nav.tsx:81 p-2.5 min-h-11 min-w-11.

findings.title: The only non-responsive multi-column grid in the content surface is on the docs setup page
findings.description: app/docs/setup/page.tsx:78 is `grid grid-cols-3 gap-2 sm:gap-4` with no responsive prefix. At 375px each tile gets about 109px with about 89px of content, so 'systemd / PM2' and '5 min deploy' wrap to two lines and the tiles end up uneven. It does not overflow, and the sm: override shows it was hand-tuned.
findings.impact: Minor visual inconsistency on the setup page, which is a high-intent page for self-hosters.
findings.recommendation: grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-3 gap-2 sm:gap-4.

findings.title: The changelog has no pagination fallback, so without IntersectionObserver it is a permanent loading state
findings.description: components/changelog/changelog-list.tsx:156-169 renders a sentinel div reading 'Loading more releases...' whenever hasMore. IntersectionObserver (:59) is the only path past the first four releases. Separately, if CHANGELOG were empty, visibleCount is 0 and hasMore false, so the page renders a header followed only by 'The beginning of VulnRadar'.
findings.impact: Without IntersectionObserver the page shows four releases and a spinner-shaped dead end.
findings.recommendation: Render a real <button onClick={() => setVisibleCount(c => c + LOAD_MORE_BATCH)}>Load more</button> alongside the sentinel, and add an explicit empty branch.

findings.title: Two tablist implementations declare tab roles with no tabpanel, aria-controls or arrow-key navigation
findings.description: components/docs/docs-code-tabs.tsx:30-49 and app/docs/api/playground/page.tsx:420-443 render role="tablist" with role="tab" buttons, but the controlled CodeBlock at :51 is not role="tabpanel" and nothing carries aria-controls or aria-labelledby. Arrow-key roving focus, which the tab role implies, is absent.
findings.impact: Assistive tech announces a tab widget and then behaves like plain buttons, which is worse than plain buttons.
findings.recommendation: Either complete the pattern (panel gets role="tabpanel", id and aria-labelledby; buttons get id and aria-controls; add arrow keys) or drop the ARIA roles. For two or three code samples, dropping the roles is the better trade.

findings.title: Dead configuration objects and constants, including a FEATURES object where seven of eight members are unread
findings.description: The FEATURES object at lib/config/constants.ts:778-786 has exactly one live member: a grep for FEATURES.[A-Z_]+ outside lib/config returns one hit, lib/hooks/use-client-config.ts:33 reading .PDF_REPORTS. The other seven (DEMO_MODE, TEAMS, API_KEYS, WEBHOOKS, SCHEDULED_SCANS, BULK_SCANS, EMAIL_NOTIFICATIONS) are read nowhere; the underlying CONFIG_FEATURE_* values are alive via the registry, so only this convenience object is dead. Also dead: the DATABASE object (:478-484, no matches for DATABASE.[A-Z_]), PATTERNS (:338), PAGINATION (:500), ENTERPRISE_EMAIL (:641), AUTH_SESSION_MAX_AGE (:242), API_KEY_SCOPE_DESCRIPTIONS (client-constants.ts:346), CONFIG_API_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS (config-values.ts:660), CONFIG_FOOTER_TEXT (:191), HISTORY_REPORT (client-constants.ts:151, zero web callers - the export menu regenerates all five formats client-side, and only the extension uses the route). Catalog helpers getFreePlan (catalog.ts:305), isPaidPlan (:309) and getApiLimitForPlan (:318) have tests as their only callers. Five unused skeleton exports at components/admin/shared/skeleton.tsx:18,40,62,90,114 (about 110 lines). components/auth/auth-layout.tsx:9-11 documents a width="wide" prop no caller uses - see auth-11, which is the screen it was written for. lib/config/public-paths.ts:66 lists ROUTES.GDPR_REQUEST as "/legal/privacy#gdpr" but middleware.ts:265 matches on pathname, which never contains a fragment, so the entry can never match (harmless, line 49 covers it).
findings.impact: Cleanup only, but the HISTORY_REPORT case has a real consequence: the server route additionally runs attachRemediation (app/api/v3/history/[id]/report/route.ts:149-155), so extension-exported reports and web-exported reports are not byte-identical.
findings.recommendation: Deletions need owner sign-off. The one to act on regardless is the report divergence: decide whether the extension and the web app should produce the same file, and make them agree.

findings.title: Two archival and delivery tables are written on every event and read by nothing
findings.description: webhook_deliveries (instrumentation.ts:2328) is written on every attempt at lib/webhooks/delivery.ts:111 and never SELECTed; its index on (webhook_id, attempted_at DESC) is shaped for a UI that was never built. Already recorded as AUDIT-009 #185 and still open. admin_audit_log_archive (lib/database/audit-log-archive.ts:47) is created and INSERTed at :89, and a repo-wide grep returns only that file.
findings.impact: A user whose webhook is failing has no way to see why, despite the data being captured. Purged compliance history is unviewable by any screen, route or export, which undermines the point of archiving it.
findings.recommendation: Add a delivery log to Profile > Developer > Webhooks and an 'Archived batches' view to Admin > System > Audit Log. Both are read-only views over data that already exists.

findings.title: Webhook signing secrets cannot be rotated, unlike API keys
findings.description: webhooks.secret (instrumentation.ts:2313) is returned once at creation (app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:123) and the only UPDATE (app/api/v3/webhooks/[id]/route.ts:215) cannot set it. API keys have both rotate and revoke routes.
findings.impact: A leaked webhook secret can only be addressed by deleting the webhook and recreating it, which breaks the consumer's configuration.
findings.recommendation: Add a rotate path and a 'Rotate signing secret' control, mirroring the API key flow.

findings.title: API keys silently 403 from a new network because bound_ip is never shown and cannot be reset
findings.description: api_keys.bound_ip (instrumentation.ts:382) is enforced under API_KEY_IP_BINDING_ENABLED and auto-pins on first use (lib/api/api-keys.ts:213-266, :234). getUserApiKeys at :615-626 does not select it, no component references it, and there is no reset path.
findings.impact: When the feature is enabled, a key that worked yesterday starts returning 403 from a new network with no visible cause and no way to fix it short of issuing a new key.
findings.recommendation: Show the bound IP on the API keys list and add a 'Reset binding' action.

findings.title: Two parsed environment variables are never consulted, one of them documented
findings.description: CONTACT_EMAIL is parsed at lib/config/env.ts:85 and appears in .env.example and the docs, but the contact route sends to NOREPLY_EMAIL (app/api/v3/contact/route.ts:146). STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY is parsed at :60 while only the NEXT_PUBLIC_ variant is ever read.
findings.impact: A self-hoster sets CONTACT_EMAIL as documented and contact mail goes elsewhere.
findings.recommendation: Either honour CONTACT_EMAIL in the contact route or remove it from env.ts, .env.example and the docs. Remove the unused STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY parse.

findings.title: Five admin actions have a backend case and no UI dispatch, and one has a toast with no backend case
findings.description: update_password (app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:732-754, sets a password and wipes sessions), revoke_all_sessions (:756-766, duplicating revoke_sessions at :824 which additionally emails), set_scan_limit (:1523, see drift-05), make_admin (:702) and remove_admin (:717, both superseded by set_role) all exist with no dispatch; they appear in components/admin/config.ts only as audit-log labels, and revoke_all_sessions is acknowledged as a naming bug at config.ts:303-306. export_data (:1272-1311, returns user, scans, apiKeys and badges) is likewise undispatched. Conversely app/admin/page.tsx:557 maps a send_email success toast for an action the PATCH switch has no case for, so it would 400. enable_user (:934) and delete_user/delete_account (:1985-1986) are unused aliases. Note the route's own comment at :779-786 argues against admin-set passwords, so update_password likely wants deleting rather than exposing.
findings.impact: Dead server-side surface plus one UI path that can only fail. export_data is the one with genuine user value, since GDPR export currently has no admin-side equivalent.
findings.recommendation: Wire export_data with a downloadBlob mirroring components/admin/audit/audit-log.tsx:90-107. Delete the rest, including the send_email toast.

findings.title: Seven client-sent fields are ignored by their handlers, one of them silently discarding user-chosen support categories
findings.description: app/api/v3/contact/route.ts:15-21 defines CATEGORY_LABELS for bug, feature, security, help and staff_application, then :109 does CATEGORY_LABELS[category] || "Other". The form offers nine (components/contact/contact-types.ts:27-82); billing (:58), enterprise (:64) and feedback (:76) are POSTed verbatim and land in the support inbox labelled 'Other'. Others: source: "bulk" sent at app/dashboard/page.tsx:753 while app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:374 computes source itself, so bulk scans are recorded as ordinary Web scans; authenticated and staff query params sent by components/shared/notification-center.tsx:293-296 and components/shared/site-notifications.tsx:683-686 to a route that derives both from the session and never reads searchParams, with the comment at site-notifications.tsx:678-682 now actively wrong in claiming they are enforced server-side; message_type hardcoded by mass-email-manager.tsx:132 and never read; userId in the 2FA verify body (components/auth/login-2fa-form.tsx:70,72) deliberately not destructured; baseUrl in the AI-config save (profile-ai-settings-tab.tsx:115,139) used only as an equality check, so sending it can only ever produce a 400.
findings.impact: The contact one is the only one with real user cost: triage information the user explicitly selected is discarded, and three categories are indistinguishable from 'Other' in the support inbox.
findings.recommendation: Add billing, enterprise and feedback to CATEGORY_LABELS - a one-line fix. Delete the dead params and the incorrect comment at site-notifications.tsx:678-682.

findings.title: The browser sessions API documents a TTL default 60 seconds below the real value and omits two accepted fields
findings.description: app/docs/api/page.tsx:525 and :539 advertise ttlSeconds and expiresInSeconds of 300, and :541 states ttlSeconds is hard-clamped to BROWSERBASE_MAX_TTL_SECONDS 'default 300 = 5 minutes'. The real value is 360 (lib/config/config-values.ts:913-914) and the route's floor is 30s (app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:52). The docs never mention the viewport body field (:34) nor the legacy ttl alias (:49).
findings.impact: viewport is unreachable from both surfaces: no UI control (see drift-21) and undocumented for API callers, who are currently its only possible consumers.
findings.recommendation: Correct 300 to 360 in both places, document viewport and the ttl alias, and add the resolution and session-length controls to components/scanner/scan-actions-menu.tsx:381-384.

findings.title: The opt-in screenshot wait is capped at 30 seconds, longer than the entire rest of the scan
findings.description: lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:812 awaits the screenshot with CONFIG_SCAN_SCREENSHOT_MAX_WAIT_MS = 30_000 (lib/config/config-values.ts:1013).
findings.impact: Only affects users who tick the box, but when it bites it more than doubles the wait.
findings.recommendation: Reduce the cap, or render results first and let the screenshot populate asynchronously.

findings.title: GitHub AI repo-review endpoint makes real GitHub API calls before its quota/rate gate
findings.description: POST /api/v3/scan/github calls getRepoInfo and listRepoTree (real GitHub API requests using the user's connected token) before checkGithubReviewQuota runs. Every other AI-adjacent or expensive endpoint in this app (chat, verify, verify-batch, bulk scan, crawl, discover, demo-scan, browser sessions) goes through checkRateLimit first; this one has no per-request throttle at all, only a per-day quota check that happens after the two GitHub API round-trips. Impact is mostly limited to the calling user's own GitHub API rate limit rather than a shared resource, so this is low severity, but it's the one gap in an otherwise consistently-applied pattern. Evidence: app/api/v3/scan/github/route.ts lines 73-119 (getRepoInfo/listRepoTree calls precede the checkGithubReviewQuota call at line 116); no import of checkRateLimit anywhere in that file (confirmed via grep, contrasted with every sibling route under app/api/v3/scan/).
findings.recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Add a checkRateLimit gate (a new named limit, e.g. githubReview) at the top of the handler, before any GitHub API call, mirroring the pattern already used everywhere else.

findings.title: vibe-generic-error-message: vibe-generic-error-message fires on i18n/translation JSON blobs, not just "page scripts" as its own evidence text claims
findings.description: The check requires hasScript(body) (true on virtually every modern page, since it only checks for the presence of any `<script>` tag anywhere) and then does an unscoped body-wide match for quoted common error phrases. It doesn't scope the phrase search to actual script content, so a quoted JSON string value anywhere on the page (e.g. an SSR framework's embedded i18n/state blob) satisfies it just as well as an actual catch-block string literal. Verified: `<script>window.__i18n = {"errors":{"generic":"Something went wrong"}};</script>` matches. Trigger: Any Next.js/Nuxt/similar SSR page that embeds a translation dictionary or initial-state JSON blob containing a friendly error string like `{"generic":"Something went wrong"}` — a completely standard i18n pattern, not evidence of swallowed exceptions.
findings.recommendation: Require nearby error-handling context (similar to how vibe-weak-random requires a nearby security term): only fire when the matched phrase is within ~150 chars of `catch\s*\(|\.catch\s*\(|onerror|addEventListener\s*\(\s*["']error`, so the phrase is confirmed to be inside actual exception-handling code rather than a data/string constant.

findings.title: firebase-config-exposed: firebase-config-exposed fires on the standard, required Firebase SDK initialization call present on virtually every Firebase-based site
findings.description: One of the three patterns is a bare `/firebase\.initializeApp\s*\(/` match. Per Firebase's own documentation, the client-side Firebase config object (including its apiKey) is explicitly NOT a secret — it is a public identifier, and access is controlled via Firebase Security Rules, not by hiding this call. Calling firebase.initializeApp() is mandatory for every single Firebase web app (Auth, Firestore, Realtime DB, etc.), so this pattern matches on essentially 100% of legitimate Firebase usage. Trigger: Any site using Firebase Authentication, Firestore, or Realtime Database — an extremely common choice for hobbyist projects, startups, and production SaaS alike — will contain `firebase.initializeApp({...})` in its bundled JS as required, standard SDK setup.
findings.recommendation: Remove the bare `firebase.initializeApp(` and `firebaseConfig[:=]` patterns (presence alone is not a finding per Firebase's own security model). Rely on the already-correctly-scoped secret-firebase-api-key-public detector (which requires "firebase" context near an actual AIzaSy* key) for the real signal, or repurpose this check to look for an actual misconfiguration indicator (e.g. permissive Firestore/RTDB security rules text, or a databaseURL referenced without any corresponding auth check) rather than SDK presence.

findings.title: sri-missing: Flags Google Tag Manager / Analytics / Stripe.js / PayPal SDK scripts, which are documented as SRI-incompatible
findings.description: sri-missing flags every external <script src> lacking an integrity attribute with no allowlist. Several extremely common third-party scripts are served without stable, versioned URLs and are documented by their vendors as incompatible with SRI (the vendor updates the file's contents in place; an integrity hash would break the site the next time the vendor deploys a fix). This includes Google Tag Manager (googletagmanager.com/gtm.js, gtag/js), Google Analytics (google-analytics.com/analytics.js), Stripe.js (js.stripe.com/v3/), and the PayPal SDK (paypal.com/sdk/js). Trigger: Any site embedding `<script src="https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js?id=GTM-XXXXXXX"></script>` (one of the most widely deployed script tags on the web) with no integrity attribute -- required to be absent by GTM's own design.
findings.recommendation: Add a host allowlist of known dynamically-served, SRI-incompatible script hosts (googletagmanager.com, google-analytics.com, googlesyndication.com, js.stripe.com, checkout.stripe.com, www.paypalobjects.com, connect.facebook.net, cdn.segment.com, static.hotjar.com, js.intercomcdn.com, widget.intercom.io, snap.licdn.com) and exclude script tags whose src hostname matches it from the noSRI filter.

findings.title: sri-stylesheet-missing: Flags Google Fonts stylesheet links, which cannot carry a stable SRI hash by design
findings.description: sri-stylesheet-missing flags every external <link rel=stylesheet> without an integrity attribute. Google Fonts' CSS endpoint (fonts.googleapis.com/css or /css2) deliberately serves different CSS content per requesting User-Agent (different @font-face src URLs/formats for different browsers), so no single, stable content hash exists for it -- SRI is fundamentally incompatible with this and similar UA-negotiated stylesheet services, not merely omitted by site owners. Trigger: Any of the enormous number of sites using `<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Roboto">` for web fonts.
findings.recommendation: Exempt fonts.googleapis.com (and similarly UA-negotiated stylesheet CDNs, e.g. use.typekit.net) from this check's noSRI filter.

findings.title: charset-meta-missing: Only checks for <meta charset> in the body; ignores an equally valid charset= on the Content-Type header
findings.description: The check (lines 1272-1278) only regex-matches `<meta[^>]+charset=` in the HTML body and never inspects the response's Content-Type header for a charset parameter, even though declaring charset via the HTTP header is equally valid and defeats the same UTF-7/encoding-inheritance attack this check targets. HTTP-header charset declaration is the default behavior of many production stacks. Trigger: Any server responding `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` (the default for Express's res.send/res.type, and common on many Nginx/production configs) without an inline `<meta charset>` tag -- genuinely safe from the attack this check targets, but flagged anyway.
findings.recommendation: Before falling back to the body regex, check `h(headers, "content-type")` for a `charset=` parameter (e.g. `/charset\s*=/i.test(contentType)`) and return null if present.

findings.title: expect-ct-missing: Flags absence of the Expect-CT header, which is deprecated and unsupported by modern browsers
findings.description: Chrome removed support for Expect-CT in 2022 and MDN documents it as deprecated/on track for removal; Certificate Transparency is now enforced independently by browsers and CAs. Virtually every modern site -- including ones with excellent security postures -- correctly lacks this header today, for the same reason this codebase already disabled nel-header-missing and age-header-reveals-cdn in headers.ts ('optional... its absence is not a vulnerability'). Trigger: Any HTTPS site scanned in 2024+ (i.e. effectively every site, since no current browser honors this header) gets an info-level finding for not sending a header no browser checks anymore.
findings.recommendation: Disable this detector (return null unconditionally), consistent with how nel-header-missing/age-header-reveals-cdn/x-request-id-exposed were handled elsewhere in this codebase, with a comment noting Expect-CT's deprecation.

findings.title: x-xss-protection-disabled: Flags X-XSS-Protection: 0, which is the current recommended value, not a vulnerability
findings.description: Explicitly setting `X-XSS-Protection: 0` is the value recommended by the OWASP Secure Headers Project and by Mozilla's own HTTP Observatory scoring (which treats '0' as a pass), because the legacy XSS Auditor/filter this header controls was found to itself introduce exploitable XSS and information-disclosure bugs in old IE/Chrome, and has since been removed entirely from all modern browsers. The detector's own message concedes the header is deprecated yet still returns a finding. Trigger: Any security-conscious site following current OWASP/Mozilla guidance that explicitly sends `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (the recommended configuration, especially alongside a strong CSP) is penalized for doing the currently-correct thing.
findings.recommendation: Disable this detector (return null unconditionally), matching the file's established pattern for deprecated/non-issue headers (see nel-header-missing, age-header-reveals-cdn, x-request-id-exposed).

findings.title: cookie-expires-too-far: Long-expiry check has no sensitivity filter, unlike every sibling cookie check in this file
findings.description: Every other per-attribute check in cookies.ts that cares about risk (cookie-httponly-missing, cookie-secure-missing, cookie-samesite-missing, cookie-no-secure-prefix, session-cookie-flags) first filters to cookies whose name suggests session/token/auth/jwt. cookie-expires-too-far (lines 203-226) has no such filter -- it fires on ANY cookie, sensitive or not, with Max-Age/Expires over 1 year. Long-lived, non-sensitive analytics/marketing cookies with multi-year lifetimes are standard on the web. Trigger: Google Analytics' `_ga` cookie (2-year default expiry) or LinkedIn's `bcookie` (2 years) or HubSpot's `hubspotutk` (13 months) -- present on a huge fraction of real-world sites and entirely non-sensitive, yet flagged 'Cookie Expires/Max-Age Exceeds 1 Year' on every scan.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same sensitivity filter used by the file's other per-attribute checks (cookie name includes session/token/auth/jwt) before evaluating expiry length, so only long-lived authentication/session cookies are flagged.

findings.title: iframe-third-party-without-sandbox: Flags common trusted third-party embeds (YouTube, Google Maps, Stripe Elements, reCAPTCHA) for lacking sandbox
findings.description: The check (lines 1366-1387) flags any third-party <iframe> without a sandbox attribute, with no allowlist. Widely embedded, functionally-required third-party iframes -- YouTube/Vimeo video embeds, Google Maps embeds, Stripe/PayPal payment element iframes, reCAPTCHA/hCaptcha/Cloudflare Turnstile challenge iframes -- routinely omit sandbox because it is well known to break their required functionality (postMessage, same-origin storage, popups, presentation API), and developers deliberately don't add it. Trigger: Any page with `<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID">` or `<iframe src="https://www.google.com/maps/embed?...">` -- extremely common, legitimate embeds with no sandbox attribute.
findings.recommendation: Add an allowlist of common trusted embed hosts that are known to require unsandboxed operation (youtube.com, youtube-nocookie.com, google.com/maps, vimeo.com, js.stripe.com, checkout.stripe.com, google.com/recaptcha, challenges.cloudflare.com) and skip them in the noSandbox filter.

findings.title: clipboard-hijack-pattern: Matches the common, benign 'append source URL on copy' attribution snippet used by many blogs/news sites
findings.description: The pattern only requires a `copy` event listener followed within 200 characters by `clipboardData.setData`/`setData('text`. This exact shape is also the well-known, widely-published technique many blogs and documentation/news sites use to append a 'Read more at <url>' or attribution line whenever a visitor copies page text -- a benign SEO/anti-scraping courtesy, not a hijack. The evidence text ('matches a pattern used for clipboard-hijacking attacks (e.g. swapping copied crypto addresses)') is reported regardless of whether anything crypto/address-related is actually happening. Trigger: The standard copy-attribution snippet: `document.addEventListener('copy', function(e){ e.clipboardData.setData('text/plain', document.getSelection() + '\n\nRead more at ' + location.href); e.preventDefault(); });` -- present on many blogs/news sites -- fires the 'clipboard-hijacking' finding.
findings.recommendation: Require evidence that the ORIGINAL selection is discarded rather than included/appended -- e.g. only flag when the setData call's argument does not reference `getSelection()`/`selection` at all (a pure replacement, not an append), or narrow the pattern to require an address/URL-looking regex literal (crypto wallet patterns, `bc1`/`0x` prefixes) nearby. At minimum, soften the evidence wording so it doesn't assert a crypto-swap attack when only a plain URL suffix is being appended.

findings.title: rate-limiting: Fires on static documentation pages whose URL merely contains '/api/'
findings.description: Lines 122-149: `isApiPath` is satisfied by any URL containing `/api/` anywhere in the path, with no check that the response is actually an API response rather than an HTML documentation page. Any API-reference/docs page hosted under a path like `/api/authentication` or `/docs/api/...` -- a very common URL shape for developer documentation -- qualifies, and since a plain HTML docs page naturally carries no X-RateLimit-* headers, the check fires 'No rate-limiting headers detected. API endpoints may be vulnerable to abuse.' on a static prose page that isn't an API endpoint at all. Confirmed real-world instance: Stripe's own authentication documentation page is served at the URL path `/api/authentication` (docs.stripe.com/api/authentication) and returns `text/html`, not JSON. Trigger: GET https://docs.stripe.com/api/authentication (a static HTML documentation page, not an API endpoint)
findings.recommendation: Before treating the URL-shape match as sufficient, also check the response Content-Type and bail out for HTML: `const contentType = headers.get("content-type") || ""; if (/text\/html/i.test(contentType)) return null;` inserted right after the isApiPath check.

findings.title: supply-chain-dockerfile-exposed: docker-compose.yml version regex only matches a bare integer, missing the near-universal decimal version syntax
findings.description:
Line 118: `/^version:\s*["']\d+["']$/m` requires the quoted version to be `\d+` with nothing else, so it matches `version: '3'` but NOT `version: '3.8'`, `version: '3.9'`, `version: '2.4'`, etc. In practice the overwhelming majority of real-world docker-compose.yml files pin a dotted Compose spec version (`'3.8'`, `'3.9'`, `'2.1'`...) rather than a bare digit, so this branch of the check almost never actually fires on real exposed compose files even though the sibling `image:` condition is satisfied, making this a 'check that can basically never fire' bug on the format it was written to detect. Trigger: A leaked docker-compose.yml containing `version: '3.8'
services:
  web:
    image: myapp:latest` -- the extremely common modern Compose file shape.
findings.recommendation: Change the regex to `/^version:\s*["']\d+(?:\.\d+)?["']$/m` to accept an optional decimal component.

findings.title: reflected-input-xss: Finding ID distinguisher (form.action alone) collides when two different forms share the same action URL
findings.description: buildFinding("reflected-input-xss", url, form.action) passes form.action as the id distinguisher, and generateId() in lib/scanner/_helpers.ts hashes checkId+url+distinguisher into the finding id. When two distinct `<form>` elements on the same page submit to the same action (a common pattern: a header 'quick search' box and a body 'advanced search' form both posting to `/search`, or a main contact form and a newsletter-signup mini-form both posting to `/submit`), and both independently reflect their own per-form canary unescaped, both findings get the exact same `id` (same checkId, same url, same distinguisher). _helpers.ts's own doc comment for generateId explicitly warns this is the failure mode the distinguisher parameter exists to prevent: 'without a per-hit distinguisher every hit... would collapse onto the exact same id... a false_positive mark on one hit... silently suppressing the other, unrelated hit too' -- but the distinguisher chosen here (bare form.action) doesn't actually guarantee uniqueness across forms. Trigger: A page with a header search widget and a separate body search form, both `<form method="GET" action="/search">` but with different field names (e.g. `q` vs `query`), where both reflect their submitted canary unescaped. Both vulnerable forms produce identical finding ids; a user who reviews the surfaced finding and marks it a false positive (scan_finding_feedback is keyed on this id) silently suppresses the report for the other, genuinely-vulnerable form on future scans too.
findings.recommendation: Make the distinguisher unique per probed form rather than per action URL, e.g. change the call to `buildFinding("reflected-input-xss", url, `${form.action}:${form.testableFields.join(",")}`)`, or include the form's index in the `forms` array, so two forms with the same action but different field sets (or the same field set, via an index) still produce distinct ids.

findings.title: Badge stats endpoint compares the share token in plaintext against scan_history.share_token instead of the hashed lookup used identically elsewhere, and silently ignores host_badges auto-updating tokens
findings.description: app/api/v3/badge/[token]/stats/route.ts queries `WHERE sh.share_token = $1` (the raw plaintext token from the URL) rather than hashing it and comparing against share_token_hash, unlike the sibling badge image route (app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts) and the shared-report route (app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.ts), both of which deliberately hash first with a comment citing AUDIT-004#secrets-01 ('so the plaintext token is never compared directly in the DB'). Since share_token_hash is a Postgres GENERATED column computed from share_token in the same row, this isn't a new confidentiality gap (the plaintext already lives in that row either way) and 256 bits of entropy makes any timing-based guessing attack infeasible regardless -- so this is a consistency/defense-in-depth gap, not a demonstrated exploit path. Separately, this endpoint never queries host_badges at all, so it silently 404s for any of the new auto-updating badge tokens created via POST /api/v3/badge/site -- a functional gap parallel to the two routes it's supposed to mirror. Evidence: app/api/v3/badge/[token]/stats/route.ts:19-25 (`WHERE sh.share_token = $1`, no hashing, no host_badges fallback) vs. app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts:39-73 and app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.ts:24-60 (both hash-then-compare and both fall back to host_badges).
findings.recommendation: NOT YET APPLIED -- reported for review. Recommendation: Hash the incoming token with SHA-256 and compare against share_token_hash for consistency with the two sibling routes, and add the same host_badges fallback query so stats work for auto-updating badges too.

findings.title: webhook_deliveries audit table is write-only -- nothing ever reads it
findings.description: instrumentation.ts creates webhook_deliveries this session and lib/webhooks/delivery.ts writes to it correctly on every attempt, but no route or UI component ever selects from it. The partial index's shape (scoped to webhook_id, ordered by attempted_at DESC) strongly implies a delivery-history UI was intended but never built.
findings.recommendation: Either add a GET delivery-history endpoint + UI, or note in code that this is intentionally admin/DB-only for now.

findings.title: broadcast_messages.sent_by is left NULL on a message's initial send, only populated on resend
findings.description: The sent_by column is correctly bound where it's set, but the admin features route only sets it in the resend action branch, never in the initial send path. A broadcast's first send leaves sent_by NULL, so "Sent by X" only appears in the admin UI after a resend.
findings.recommendation: Set sent_by = user.id in the initial send branch too, not just resend.

findings.title: lib/billing/billing.ts is a fully dead file, including the old Stripe Checkout Session flow deleted elsewhere this session
findings.description: getUserPlan is superseded by lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts's staff-role/gifted-subscription-aware version. The same file's createSubscriptionCheckout has zero callers anywhere except its own test suite, already true before this session. The real live checkout path is app/actions/stripe.ts; billing.ts just never got the same cleanup as the Elements-based route deleted this session.
findings.recommendation: Remove billing.ts or fold any still-wanted pieces into daily-limits.ts; lib/billing/index.ts's star-export of it can go too.

findings.title: Downgrade plan leaves 4 performance indexes behind that the matching upgrade added
findings.description: Live-verified: ran the real 3.0.0-to-2.0.0 downgrade against a migrated scratch DB. All 26 steps succeeded, restored the exact 34-table v2.0.0 set, no data loss. However idx_admin_audit_admin_created, idx_admin_audit_target_user, idx_api_usage_key_used, and idx_scan_history_user_scanned are absent from the downgrade's dropIndexes list and remain in place afterward. Cosmetic only, no data loss or functional break, but the downgraded schema isn't byte-for-byte identical to a true v2.0.0 install.
findings.recommendation: Add the 4 missing index names to the downgrade export's dropIndexes list in 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs, matching how idx_scan_history_status_pending_running is already handled.

findings.title: audit:v2-tables only validates the 15 legacy v1-to-v2 tables; a clean run proves nothing about tonight's v2.0.0-to-3.0.0 migration
findings.description: Ran fresh: 0 issues, exactly as expected. But scripts/_lib/audit-v2-tables.mjs's hardcoded TABLES list only cross-checks instrumentation.ts against versions/_snippets.mjs (the 1.0.0-to-2.0.0 migration). It has zero awareness of 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs or any v3.0.0 table/column, so it cannot catch and does not catch the gap in migration-01.
findings.recommendation: Extend audit-v2-tables.mjs (or add a sibling script) to also cross-check every v3.0.0-fingerprint table plus every CREATE TABLE/ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN in instrumentation.ts against 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs's addTables/addColumns, or clearly document that its 0-issues result only covers the frozen v1-to-v2 boundary.

findings.title: db:migrate and db:create cannot be driven non-interactively -- piped stdin hangs forever
findings.description: Each prompt in _lib.prompts.mjs and _lib.target.mjs opens a brand-new readline.Interface and closes it after a single answer. When multiple newline-separated answers are piped into stdin at once, Node's readline greedily buffers the whole pipe into the first Interface; only the first line is consumed before that Interface is discarded, and every later prompt then blocks forever with no timeout or error. Reproduced twice. Both scripts must be run attached to a real TTY with a human typing each answer; they cannot be scripted, used in CI, or wired into an automated deploy step.
findings.recommendation: Create one shared readline.Interface per script run in _lib.prompts.mjs and _lib.target.mjs and reuse it across every ask/askYesNo/chooseDatabase call instead of opening and closing a new one per question.

findings.title: lib/webhooks/detect-type.ts has no test file
findings.description: detectWebhookType() (4 branches: discord.com, discordapp.com, hooks.slack.com, generic fallback) shared by the webhook create and edit routes has zero test coverage. Low risk, pure string-matching, no security implication, but trivial to close.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/webhooks/detect-type.test.ts covering all four branches.

findings.title: lib/hooks/use-client-config.ts has no test file
findings.description: useClientConfig() (fetches /api/v3/config/client, falls back to compiled defaults on failure or before the fetch resolves) has no corresponding test. Has real branch logic worth covering (successful fetch overriding defaults, fetch failure keeping defaults, unmount-during-fetch).
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/hooks/use-client-config.test.ts using renderHook, mocking fetch for the success/failure/slow-unmount cases.

findings.title: debug-endpoint rated high while the near-identical sensitive-endpoints check is rated low
findings.description: Both checks fire on the same evidence class -- an unverified path-fragment string (e.g. '/debug/', '/trace/') appearing anywhere in the page body, with no confirmation the endpoint is reachable or that the string isn't from an observability/tracing vendor's own URLs (Datadog, OpenTelemetry, etc. commonly reference '/trace/' paths in their own tags). debug-endpoint was rated high, four tiers above the equivalent-strength sensitive-endpoints check (low), for the same 'found a suspicious substring in a huge page/JS bundle' evidence pattern the audit is specifically targeting.
findings.recommendation: Downgraded debug-endpoint severity high -> low for parity with sensitive-endpoints.

findings.title: iframe-srcdoc-no-sandbox mistyped as 'header' (93% confidence) and described as generic third-party src widgets
findings.description: The JSON 'type' field controls the engine-confidence score assigned to a finding (header=93%, body-pattern=70% per registry.ts); this check's detector is a pure body regex on iframe srcdoc attributes but was typed 'header', overstating confidence for one of the more FP-prone categories. Its description also talked about 'third-party widgets (Stripe, YouTube)' loaded without sandbox, which describes src= iframes, not the srcdoc= iframes this specific check actually inspects -- confusing overlap with the separate iframe-sandbox-missing check.
findings.recommendation: Corrected type header -> body-pattern and rewrote the description/riskImpact to describe srcdoc-specific inline-HTML risk instead of generic third-party embeds.

findings.title: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: open-form-action's third-party allowlist (stripe/paypal/google only) is likely too narrow for real-world marketing pages
findings.description: The check flags any POST form whose action points to an external domain not in {stripe.com, paypal.com, google.com}, at medium severity. Large real-world sites commonly embed newsletter/contact forms hosted by Mailchimp (*.list-manage.com), HubSpot (hsforms.com), Typeform, Formspree, SurveyMonkey, etc., none of which are allowlisted -- plausible to false-positive on an ordinary marketing site. Left unfixed because deciding which third parties are 'legitimate enough' to allowlist is a product/policy call, not a pure bug fix, and an incomplete allowlist just moves the false-positive boundary rather than eliminating it.

findings.title: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: content.ts's postmessage-origin and client-side.ts's postmessage-no-origin-check are near-duplicate detectors
findings.description: Both fire on the identical evidence: any addEventListener('message', ...) in the page with no '.origin' usage anywhere in body, both at severity high. A page with an unvalidated postMessage listener produces TWO separate high-severity findings under two different check IDs (content and client-side categories) for one real signal, double-counting it in the danger score. Left unfixed because the right resolution -- retire one, or make them meaningfully distinct (e.g. one requires a nearby dangerous sink) -- is a design decision about which category should own postMessage-origin detection, not a pure bug fix, and I did not want to unilaterally deprecate a check ID that other code/AI-verification logic might reference.

findings.title: cookie-domain-broad severity inconsistent with its own sibling check's documented rationale
findings.description: cookie-domain-broad (medium) fires on Domain=.example.com (leading dot) while cookie-domain-no-leading-dot (low) fires on Domain=example.com (no leading dot). cookie-domain-no-leading-dot's own description already states 'RFC 6265bis deprecates the leading dot, and modern browsers treat both forms identically' -- per RFC 6265 Sec 5.2.3 the leading dot is stripped on receipt and has zero effect, so both forms are equally subdomain-wide with identical real-world risk, yet one was scored 2 tiers higher than the other for the same effective exposure. A broad cookie domain is also completely standard, intentional practice at any company with subdomain-wide SSO.
findings.recommendation: Lowered cookie-domain-broad from medium to low to match cookie-domain-no-leading-dot, and noted the RFC 6265 rationale directly in its description.

findings.title: ~15 more api.json entries typed 'header' despite their detectors reading only body/URL, understating regex-guess uncertainty
findings.description: Beyond the mass-assignment and graphql-introspection entries (scanner-16/18), soap-endpoint, xml-rpc, api-graphql-batch-queries, api-graphql-error-stack-trace, api-openapi-default-values-sensitive, api-openapi-server-url-leak, and api-jwt-hs256-weak-secret are pure body regexes with zero header interaction but were typed 'header' (93% confidence); api-graphql-suggestions-enabled, api-graphql-error-stack-trace, api-openapi-security-scheme-weak, api-jsonp-callback, api-soap-wsdl-publicly-accessible, and api-websocket-no-origin-validation read both url and body (no header at all) but were also typed 'header'; api-bearer-header-leak reads only the URL string.
findings.recommendation: Corrected each to 'body-pattern' (70% confidence), 'combined' (85%), or 'url-check' (82%) matching what the paired detector in api.ts actually inspects.

findings.title: api-rate-limit-per-ip-no-auth read an unrelated response header as evidence and overclaimed 'no authentication required'
findings.description: One firing branch treated a response carrying x-forwarded-for (a client-IP-forwarding header, rarely present on a response at all) as evidence that rate limiting is 'keyed only on client IP' -- the two facts are unrelated. Separately, the evidence text asserted 'no authentication required' from the scanner's own request lacking an Authorization header, which is true of nearly every passive scan regardless of whether the endpoint actually requires auth; a properly protected endpoint returning 401 with rate-limit headers attached would look identical to this detector.
findings.recommendation: Removed the x-forwarded-for branch (kept only the x-ratelimit-limit signal) and reworded evidence to prompt verification of the auth requirement rather than assert its absence. Also softened api-rate-limit-headers-not-enforced-on-paths's evidence, which asserted a X-RateLimit-Remaining absence means the 'cap not enforced' as fact when a server may only emit that header near the limit.

findings.title: api-graphql-error-stack-trace's bare stacktrace-key match claimed GraphQL context it never verified
findings.description: One branch fired on any "stacktrace":" appearing anywhere in a response body with no requirement the response came from a GraphQL endpoint or carried a GraphQL error envelope, yet the evidence unconditionally states 'GraphQL error.extensions.stacktrace leaked' -- a stack trace leaking from a non-GraphQL API (a real bug, but a different check's concern) would be mislabeled.
findings.recommendation: Added a GraphQL-context gate (/graphql URL or a JSON 'extensions' object present, which is where the GraphQL spec places error extension data) before either stacktrace pattern is evaluated.

findings.title: api.ts and supply-chain.ts detectors never excluded doc/tutorial <pre>/<code> blocks, unlike vibe-code.ts's already-fixed equivalent
findings.description: None of api.ts's body-regex detectors (soap-endpoint, xml-rpc, api-jwt-hs256-weak-secret's jwt.sign(...) pattern, etc.) or supply-chain.ts's config-file fingerprint detectors (lockfile/requirements/Gemfile/composer/Dockerfile/.env) excluded <pre>/<code>/<kbd>/<samp> regions before matching, the same gap already fixed for vibe-code.ts (AUDIT-008 vibe-01) because this product's own /docs pages, and any tutorial/blog post, render example payloads and config snippets as literal text in those tags.
findings.recommendation: Wrapped every detector in both files with stripDocBlocks() at export time, mirroring vibe-code.ts's existing wrapper pattern exactly. No effect on the primary detection case (a raw exposed file/API response has no HTML tags to strip).

findings.title: vibe-loose-equality-auth rated high but scans client-delivered JS, where the pattern is almost always harmless UI-gating
findings.description: This check is a body-pattern scan of the page's own delivered scripts, not server source. 'role == "admin"' or similar in a browser bundle is overwhelmingly ordinary client-side conditional rendering (show/hide an admin link) driven by a value the server already decided was safe to send -- not the actual authorization boundary, which lives server-side and is never visible in the response body being scanned. Rating this high implies a near-certain auth bypass; in practice it is nearly always benign UI code.
findings.recommendation: Downgraded severity high -> low and added a caveat to the description clarifying the client-side context and that this should prompt checking the real backend logic, not be read as confirmation of a bypass.

findings.title: Audit log readable by support-tier staff (AUDIT-004#audit-01 / AUDIT-005#audit-01 deferred)
findings.description: GET /api/v3/admin?section=audit was gated by requireStaff() which allows any staff role including support (view-only). The admin audit trail contains admin IPs, action details, and references to target users — data that exceeds the support tier's need-to-know.
findings.recommendation: Added STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY guard at the top of the section=audit branch: if hierarchy[session.role] < hierarchy.moderator (< 2) → 403. Moderator and admin can still read the log.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-007 authorization sweep
findings.evidence: requireStaff() passes for role=support (STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY.support = 1); the section=audit branch had no secondary role check. Any authenticated support account could read the full audit log.

findings.title: Raw invite token exposed in POST /api/v3/teams/members response body
findings.description: The invite endpoint returned the raw 256-bit token in the JSON response. The token is a secret — only the invited recipient should possess it via email. Returning it in the response exposes it to server logs, APM tools capturing response bodies, and XSS payloads running in the admin's session.
findings.recommendation: Removed token from the response. The invite link is delivered by email; the API caller only needs confirmation the invite was sent.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-007
findings.evidence: return NextResponse.json({ message: 'Invite sent.', token }); — line 188.

findings.title: X-DNS-Prefetch-Control set to 'on' in next.config.mjs, conflicting with middleware 'off'
findings.description: next.config.mjs set X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: on with a comment indicating a scanner false positive drove the change. middleware.ts correctly set the same header to 'off'. The net value was non-deterministic across deployment environments.
findings.recommendation: Reverted next.config.mjs to 'off'. Both layers now consistently set X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-007
findings.evidence: next.config.mjs line 141: value: 'on' — comment: 'scanner flagged off as a performance issue'.

findings.title: .npmrc probe revealed first 8 characters of auth token in evidence
findings.description: The /.npmrc probe extracted and stored the first 8 characters of the _authToken value in the finding evidence. Even a partial token reduces brute-force search space and confirms the token format.
findings.recommendation: Evidence now states registry type (npmjs.org, GitHub Packages, etc.) with no token characters included.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-006 Engine 3.0.0 probe hardening
findings.evidence: evidence field: `tokenHint: match[1].slice(0, 8)` — partial token chars stored in scan results.

findings.title: checkXForwardedHostInjection read 65,536 bytes to find a 28-char marker string
findings.description: The X-Forwarded-Host injection probe read up to 65,536 bytes of response body — 8x more than any other probe — to search for a 28-character marker string. This wastes memory and increases scan time unnecessarily.
findings.recommendation: Reduced to 8192 bytes, consistent with the rest of the probe functions.
findings.fixedIn: AUDIT-006 Engine 3.0.0 probe hardening
findings.evidence: body.slice(0, 65536) — all other probes use 8192 bytes.

findings.title: Admin read operations produce no audit trail (AUDIT-004#audit-01 carry-over)
findings.description: Admin GET endpoints (user lookup, team listing, scan history browsing, notification reads) write nothing to admin_audit_log. An insider threat or compromised admin account can exfiltrate user data with no forensic trail.
findings.recommendation: Call logAuditAction for significant read operations (user detail views, bulk exports). Summarize targets rather than logging full payloads.

findings.title: Admin read operations produce no audit trail
findings.description: Admin GET endpoints (user lookup, team listing, scan history browsing, notification reads) write nothing to admin_audit_log. An insider threat or compromised admin account can exfiltrate user data with no forensic trail.
findings.recommendation: Call logAuditAction for significant read operations (user detail views, bulk exports). Summarize targets rather than logging full payloads.

findings.title: SECURITY_ALLOW_NON_BROWSER_API env var not declared in env schema
findings.description: lib/api/csrf.ts and middleware.ts read process.env.SECURITY_ALLOW_NON_BROWSER_API to bypass the CSRF/origin check in development. This flag was not declared in lib/config/env.ts, so it was unvalidated, undocumented in env.example, and silently ignored if mistyped.
findings.recommendation: Add SECURITY_ALLOW_NON_BROWSER_API to the env schema as an optional boolean; reference the parsed value instead of raw process.env.
findings.fixedIn: security(AUDIT-004): BrowserBase IDOR fix, env schema, GH Actions SHA pinning
findings.fixSummary: SECURITY_ALLOW_NON_BROWSER_API added to OptionalSchema in lib/config/env.ts with a comment explaining the intent and production danger. Startup validation now catches typos in the var name.

findings.title: Unsubscribe endpoint leaks email PII and allows disabling security notifications
findings.description: GET /api/v3/account/unsubscribe returns the user's email address in the response body (PII in GET response).
